unsureList.text: Property taxes depend on the value of possessions such as homes, land, and vehicles and may be paid periodically.
unsureList.best: Property taxes are based on the value of an individual’s property, including houses, land, and cars. Property tax bills may be paid annually, semi-annually, or monthly.

unsureList.text: Sales taxes are calculated from purchase prices, collected by sellers, and remitted to the government.
unsureList.best: Sales taxes are based on the sales price of an item and are typically collected by the business selling the item. The business, such as a retail store, submits sales tax payments to the government. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Explain why federal income-tax amounts differ among individuals and households.
unsureList.best: Explain why individuals and households pay different amounts of federal income tax in the U.S.

unsureList.text: Income, deductions, and credits affect the federal income tax an individual or household owes.
unsureList.best: The amount of income tax paid by an individual or household varies based on the individual’s or household’s income level, as well as tax deductions and tax credits.

unsureList.text: The progressive federal tax system generally applies higher rates to higher-income earners.
unsureList.best: The U.S. federal income tax (and some state income tax) is progressive, meaning that individuals and households earning higher incomes pay higher tax rates.

unsureList.text: Tax deductions lower taxable income; examples include eligible mortgage interest, retirement contributions, donations, taxes, and medical expenses.
unsureList.best: Individuals and households may qualify for specific tax deductions, which reduce their taxable income and thus the taxes owed. Tax deductions may include interest on a home mortgage, contributions to retirement accounts, the value of charitable donations, the amount paid in state and local taxes, and some medical expenses.

unsureList.text: Tax credits directly reduce taxes owed and may cover children, care, education, or qualifying purchases.
unsureList.best: Individuals and households may qualify for specific tax credits, which directly reduce the amount of taxes owed. Tax credits may include a child tax credit, a child or dependent care tax credit, an education tax credit, or credits for specific purchases.

unsureList.text: Determine and explain the parts of an individual’s pay stub.
unsureList.best: Determine and describe components of an individual’s pay stub.

unsureList.text: A pay stub shows gross earnings, required and optional deductions, and net pay.
unsureList.best: An individual’s pay stub includes gross income (pay), mandatory and voluntary deductions, and net income (pay).

unsureList.text: Gross income is total pay for a period, determined by salary, hours, contracts, or another compensation method.
unsureList.best: Gross income is the total amount of income earned during a pay period. Gross income is determined by an annual salary (divided into pay periods), hours worked during a pay period, a specific contracted amount, or another compensation scheme.

unsureList.text: Mandatory deductions, including income and payroll taxes, are required by law and withheld by employers.
unsureList.best: Mandatory deductions from gross income are required by federal, state, and/or local laws and must be withheld by an employer. These deductions typically include income taxes and specific payroll taxes.

unsureList.text: Voluntary deductions fund benefits such as health coverage, care accounts, life insurance, retirement savings, and union dues.
unsureList.best: Voluntary deductions from gross income include any money the individual has set aside for employer-sponsored benefits such as health insurance, health and/or dependent care savings plans, life insurance plans, retirement savings, and union dues.

unsureList.text: Pretax deductions reduce taxable income and can encourage saving by lowering tax liability.
unsureList.best: Some deductions are pretax deductions, which means the income allocated to these items is not included as part of taxable income. Pretax deductions can be an incentive to save because they reduce an individual’s tax liability.

unsureList.text: Net pay is earnings remaining after all deductions and can differ substantially from gross income.
unsureList.best: Net income or net pay is the amount of money an individual receives from an employer (as a paycheck) after all deductions are removed and may differ significantly from gross income.

unsureList.text: Identify insurable risks individuals may encounter.
unsureList.best: Identify types of insurable risks individuals face.

unsureList.text: People face financial and physical risks, including accidents and illnesses that can impair their ability to work.
unsureList.best: Individuals face a variety of personal financial and physical risks; for example, the risk of a car accident that causes expensive damage or an illness that limits a person’s ability to work.

unsureList.text: Insurable risks are chance-based, measurable, and statistically predictable potential losses.
unsureList.best: Insurable risks are risks that involve a potential loss due to chance, such as an accident or weather event. In order to be considered insurable, a risk must also be quantifiable and statistically predictable, which means that an insurer can estimate the cost and likelihood of a potential loss.

unsureList.text: Personal risk concerns insurable threats to an individual’s health or well-being.
unsureList.best: Personal risk is an insurable risk involving the health and well-being of the insured individual, such as injury from an accident or suffering due to illness.

unsureList.text: Property risk concerns potential damage or loss involving an insured person’s belongings, home, or vehicle.
unsureList.best: Property risk is an insurable risk involving property loss, such as damage to the insured individual’s home or car.

unsureList.text: Liability risk involves harming another person’s property or physical well-being.
unsureList.best: 5.2.A.1 Individuals face a variety of personal financial and physical risks; for example, the risk of a car accident that causes expensive damage or an illness that limits a person’s ability to work.

unsureList.text: Describe insurance types individuals use to limit financial losses.
unsureList.best: Describe types of insurance individuals use to protect themselves from financial loss. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Health, auto, homeowners, renters, and life insurance protect against different insurable financial losses.
unsureList.best: Individuals can purchase different types of insurance, such as health insurance, auto insurance, homeowner’s insurance, renter’s insurance, and life insurance, to protect themselves from financial loss due to insurable risks.

unsureList.text: Policyholders pay premiums for selected coverage and can submit claims after covered losses.
unsureList.best: Insurance buyers pay an annual, semi-annual, or monthly premium for an insurance policy with a desired amount of coverage, and they can file a claim for reimbursement in the event of a financial loss.

unsureList.text: Health insurance helps pay for necessary medical care and may be partly employer-funded.
unsureList.best: Health insurance reimburses policy owners for medically necessary health care and in some cases preventive care. Health insurance may be provided as an employee benefit where the employer pays some or all of the premiums.

unsureList.text: Auto, homeowners, and renters insurance may reimburse property losses and liability costs.
unsureList.best: Auto, homeowner’s, and renter’s insurance policy holders can file claims for reimbursement for financial losses to personal property, as well as the cost of legal liability for any damage they cause to other people or property.

unsureList.text: Life insurance pays beneficiaries after the insured’s death to replace income or meet future financial needs.
unsureList.best: Life insurance provides funds to designated beneficiaries in the event of the insured person’s death and is often intended to replace lost income, pay end-of-life expenses, and/ or fund dependents’ future financial needs.

unsureList.text: Extended warranties and service contracts can provide insurance-like protection for costly purchases.
unsureList.best: Extended warranties and service contracts on expensive purchases such as cars or appliances may serve as a type of insurance. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Recommend insurance coverage suited to a household’s needs and willingness to accept risk.
unsureList.best: Recommend appropriate insurance coverage based on an individual’s or household’s risk tolerance and needs.

unsureList.text: Some coverage is legally required; for example, states commonly require auto liability insurance and mortgage lenders require property insurance.
unsureList.best: Some types of insurance are required; legal requirements vary between states (and nations). Most U.S. states require auto liability insurance, and lenders who provide home mortgages require homeowners to buy property insurance.

unsureList.text: Lower-risk-tolerance individuals may choose broader coverage and higher premiums, while others may accept higher deductibles and out-of-pocket costs.
unsureList.best: Individuals are typically able to decide how much insurance to purchase and how much risk to bear themselves. Individuals with low risk tolerance may purchase more comprehensive insurance with higher premiums to avoid unanticipated costs later, while individuals with higher risk tolerance may purchase less comprehensive insurance or insurance with higher deductibles, knowing that they may face higher out-of-pocket costs in the event of an emergency.

unsureList.text: People with dependents may need additional health, vehicle, and life insurance protection.
unsureList.best: Individuals with dependents may require more insurance, such as family health insurance, insurance on multiple vehicles, and more life insurance to provide for dependents’ future financial needs.

unsureList.text: Safer behavior, such as careful driving or avoiding smoking, can lower insurance premiums.
unsureList.best: Individuals can reduce insurance premiums by reducing risky behavior; for example, by maintaining a good driving record (auto insurance) or by not smoking (life insurance).

unsureList.text: False information or claims by policyholders or insurers constitute criminal insurance fraud.
unsureList.best: continued on next page Misrepresentation and falsified claims by individuals are considered insurance fraud, which is a crime. Misrepresentation of policies and benefits by insurance sellers is also insurance fraud.

unsureList.text: Explain ways individuals and households can guard against financial fraud.
unsureList.best: Explain how individuals and households can protect themselves from risks associated with financial fraud.

unsureList.text: Compare lenders, resist pressure, and consult nonprofit credit counselors before accepting loan terms.
unsureList.best: Individuals and households can protect themselves from predatory lending practices and products by comparing loan terms from a variety of sources, resisting pressure to quickly agree to loan terms, and seeking advice from nonprofit credit counselors before signing a loan agreement.

unsureList.text: Assess offer credibility, protect personal information, freeze credit when needed, and seek legal help after scams.
unsureList.best: Individuals and households can protect themselves from financial fraud by evaluating the credibility of financial offers, resisting pressure to share personal or financial information online or by phone, freezing their own credit, and seeking legal aid if they have been a victim of a scam.

unsureList.text: Explain how financial planning helps achieve education, housing, retirement, and charitable-giving goals.
unsureList.best: Explain how financial planning supports an individual’s ability to achieve goals related to postsecondary education, housing, retirement, and charitable giving.

unsureList.text: Long-term goals may include funding education, purchasing a home, saving for retirement, and giving to charity.
unsureList.best: Long-term individual or household financial goals often include paying for postsecondary education (either for oneself or for a dependent), buying a home, and/or saving for retirement.

unsureList.text: Education choices depend on career aims and funding, commonly combining savings, loans, scholarships, grants, and work-study.
unsureList.best: Postsecondary education decisions, such as where to attend school and what to study, depend on individual career goals and available funding. Postsecondary education is typically financed by a combination of savings, student loans, scholarships, grants, and work- study programs. Federal student loans may have lower interest rates and more favorable repayment terms than private student loans and may be government subsidized.

unsureList.text: Housing choices depend on preferences and resources; buying usually combines a down payment with a mortgage whose payments vary by loan terms.
unsureList.best: 5.3.A.4 continued on next page Retirement decisions, such as when to retire and where to live in retirement, depend on individual preferences, personal health and well-being, and available funding. Retirement income typically comes from a combination of Social Security (in the U.S.), employer- sponsored retirement plans, personal investments, and continued earnings.

unsureList.text: Explain how personal and organizational values and capabilities influence decisions.
unsureList.best: Explain how core values and core competencies shape business and individual decision making.

unsureList.text: Core values are fundamental beliefs that direct an individual’s or business’s behavior.
unsureList.best: Core values are defining beliefs and principles that guide an individual’s or business’s actions. Examples of core values may include creativity, excellence, transparency, empathy, and reliability.

unsureList.text: Businesses express their values to unite employees and guide decisions toward a common purpose.
unsureList.best: Businesses communicate core values to align employees to a shared purpose and guide decision makers to choose courses of action consistent with the business’s beliefs and principles.

unsureList.text: Core competencies are distinctive capabilities, skills, and expertise that help achieve competitive advantage.
unsureList.best: Core competencies are an individual’s or business’s capabilities, skills, and expertise that contribute to their ability to outperform rivals and achieve competitive advantage. Examples of core competencies may include innovation, customer service, communication, ethical behavior, and efficiency.

unsureList.text: Businesses use their strengths to select opportunities and direct resources toward satisfying customers.
unsureList.best: Businesses consider their core competencies when making decisions about which opportunities to pursue and how best to allocate resources to meet customer needs.

unsureList.text: Individuals use their values and abilities to evaluate education, career, and employment options.
unsureList.best: 1.5.B Develop or evaluate a vision statement and/or mission statement based on a business’s goals and values. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Create or assess vision and mission statements using organizational goals and values.
unsureList.best: 1.5.B.3 Vision statements and mission statements communicate long-term goals and core values to internal audiences to guide decision making and provide a shared sense of purpose. These statements also inform potential customers and investors of the business’s goals and values.

unsureList.text: Describe a vision statement as a concise summary of values and future aspirations.
unsureList.best: A vision statement provides a concise description of a business’s core values and aspirations.

unsureList.text: Explain how vision and mission statements guide decisions and communicate goals to stakeholders.
unsureList.best: Vision statements and mission statements communicate long-term goals and core values to internal audiences to guide decision making and provide a shared sense of purpose. These statements also inform potential customers and investors of the business’s goals and values.

unsureList.text: Explain that businesses pursue profitability, missions, goals, competitiveness, and long-term viability.
unsureList.best: Businesses seek to achieve and increase profits, fulfill their stated missions and goals, and remain competitive and viable in the long term. Businesses can improve profits by increasing revenues and/or by decreasing costs.

unsureList.text: Describe social enterprises as organizations combining profit-seeking with social objectives.
unsureList.best: 1.5.C Describe the goals of businesses, social enterprises, and nonprofit organizations.

unsureList.text: Explain that nonprofits serve the public good, reinvest surplus, and often depend on grants and donations.
unsureList.best: Nonprofit organizations serve the public good rather than generating profit for their owners. Any surplus funds (i.e., revenues in excess of costs) must be reinvested in the organization by law. Nonprofits often rely on grant funding and donations as part of their revenue.

unsureList.text: Identify how businesses address customer problems, needs, and wants.
unsureList.best: Identify ways businesses address customers’ problems, needs, and wants. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: A business produces and distributes goods or services, regardless of its size or customer reach.
unsureList.best: A business is an organization or entity that produces and distributes products, inclusive of goods and/or services. A business can be any size—based on geographic reach, number of employees, or revenues—and serve customers face-to-face or virtually.

unsureList.text: A customer buys a product, while a consumer uses it; these may be different people.
unsureList.best: A customer is an individual or business that purchases a good or service. A consumer is an individual who uses a good or service, whether or not they are the buyer.

unsureList.text: Businesses identify market opportunities, create solutions, and choose which customers and needs to serve.
unsureList.best: Businesses identify customer problems, needs, and wants (market opportunities) and develop goods and services to address them, which achieves problem-solution fit. Businesses cannot satisfy all potential customers; they must select which problems, needs, and wants they will focus on and which customers to serve.

unsureList.text: Distinguish between creating value for customers and capturing value through pricing.
unsureList.best: Distinguish between value creation and value capture.

unsureList.text: Businesses create value by offering products that address customer problems, needs, or wants.
unsureList.best: 1.1.A Identify ways businesses address customers’ problems, needs, and wants. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Businesses capture value when their selling price exceeds production cost.
unsureList.best: Value capture occurs when businesses are able to charge customers a higher price for a product than it cost to produce. BUSINESSCASE Students explore how an entrepreneur identifies a customer problem, need, or want. PROJECTLINK Customer Task 1: Identify and describe a customer’s problem, need, or want.

unsureList.text: Explain how sellers and buyers interact to establish market prices.
unsureList.best: Explain how sellers and buyers interact in a market, establishing a market price.

unsureList.text: Markets are physical or virtual settings where businesses and customers exchange products.
unsureList.best: Businesses operate within markets, which can be local, regional, or global. A market is any physical or virtual space where businesses (the sellers) interact with their customers (the buyers).

unsureList.text: Voluntary exchange generates seller revenue and gives buyers needed or desired products.
unsureList.best: The voluntary exchange of goods and services within markets generates revenue for sellers and creates value for buyers who obtain products they need or want.

unsureList.text: Competition between sellers and buyers tends to establish a prevailing market price.
unsureList.best: 1.2.A Explain how sellers and buyers interact in a market, establishing a market price.

unsureList.text: Develop or assess a business plan for achieving competitive advantage.
unsureList.best: Develop or evaluate a business’s plan to achieve competitive advantage in a market. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Competitive advantage enables a business to outperform rivals, increasing market share and potentially profits.
unsureList.best: Competitive advantage is the ability to outperform rivals (other businesses) in the same market, leading to increased market share and potentially to increased profits.

unsureList.text: Market competitiveness depends on rivals, product differences, and competitors’ ability to offer lower prices.
unsureList.best: Markets vary in competitiveness based on the number of rival businesses and product offerings, the degree to which businesses create differentiated products (products with distinguishing features), and the extent to which rival businesses are able to offer identical or similar products at a lower price.

unsureList.text: A market’s competitiveness influences the strategies businesses use to gain advantage.
unsureList.best: The competitiveness of a given market determines the strategies a business will use to seek competitive advantage.

unsureList.text: Commodity businesses may seek advantage through efficiency that permits the lowest possible prices.
unsureList.best: Markets for many agricultural goods or other commodities tend to be highly competitive. Businesses in these markets may seek competitive advantage by producing as efficiently as possible in order to charge the lowest price possible.

unsureList.text: Businesses with differentiated products can compete through quality, features, service, price, or marketing.
unsureList.best: In competitive markets with differentiated rival products, businesses may seek competitive advantage by demonstrating to customers how their products are superior to rival products. Businesses may do this by developing higher-quality products, unique product features, better customer service, lower prices, or more effective marketing.

unsureList.text: Businesses may build entry barriers through patents, regulations, supplier access, startup costs, or scale.
unsureList.best: 1.2.B.7 A market without competition, in which only one business operates and produces a unique good or service, is a monopoly. A business that has the advantage of not having to compete for customers may seek to protect this position by maintaining barriers to entry.

unsureList.text: A monopoly has one seller and may preserve its position by maintaining entry barriers.
unsureList.best: A market without competition, in which only one business operates and produces a unique good or service, is a monopoly. A business that has the advantage of not having to compete for customers may seek to protect this position by maintaining barriers to entry.

unsureList.text: Describe political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal market factors.
unsureList.best: 1.3.A.1 PESTELfactorsarethepolitical,economic,social, technological,environmental,andlegalfactors thatshapethebusinesslandscapeandimpact thetypesofbusinessthatareviableinamarket.

unsureList.text: PESTEL factors shape the business environment and determine which businesses can succeed in a market.
unsureList.best: 1.3.B Explain how PESTEL factors influence business viability and career opportunities in a market.

unsureList.text: Political factors include policies and political conditions affecting trade, taxes, subsidies, mandates, bans, and stability.
unsureList.best: Political factors are policies and political dynamics that affect market activity such as trade policy, taxes and subsidies, mandates, bans, and political stability.

unsureList.text: Social factors include demographics, cultural norms, lifestyles, and population trends influencing consumers and markets.
unsureList.best: Social factors are trends in society and culture that affect consumers, and therefore market activity, such as consumer demographics, cultural norms, lifestyle trends, and the population growth rate.

unsureList.text: Environmental factors include geography, resources, waste policies, and customer environmental attitudes.
unsureList.best: 1.3.B.5 Environmental factors influence business viability because climate, access to resources, and the occurrence of natural disasters may constrain businesses’ abilities to produce and distribute goods and services. In addition, customers’ environmental perspectives may influence purchasing decisions.

unsureList.text: Explain how PESTEL factors affect business viability and career opportunities.
unsureList.best: Explain how PESTEL factors influence business viability and career opportunities in a market.

unsureList.text: Political systems and policies encourage some business activities and discourage others through taxes, subsidies, mandates, and bans.
unsureList.best: Political factors influence business viability because the overall political system and specific policies incentivize some business activities while disincentivizing others. Subsidies and mandates are used to support specific business activities, while bans are used to limit specific business activities. Taxes are collected to fund governments and may also have the effect of limiting specific business activities.

unsureList.text: Economic conditions affect spending, so businesses may thrive in either strong or weak economies depending on customer needs.
unsureList.best: Economic factors influence business viability because the overall stability and performance of the economy influence the levels and types of spending by consumers, businesses, and government. Most businesses are more likely to thrive in a strong, stable economy, but some businesses thrive by meeting customer needs in a weak or unstable economy.

unsureList.text: Social demographics, norms, and trends shape consumer needs and business viability.
unsureList.best: Social factors influence business viability because meeting consumer needs and wants is vital to achieving viability for consumer- oriented businesses, and these needs and wants are influenced by consumer demographics, cultural norms, and trends.

unsureList.text: Available technology affects production, distribution, and communication, influencing business viability.
unsureList.best: Technological factors influence business viability because systems for production, distribution, and communication with customers are dependent on available technologies.

unsureList.text: Climate, resources, disasters, and environmental preferences can constrain operations and influence purchases.
unsureList.best: Environmental factors influence business viability because climate, access to resources, and the occurrence of natural disasters may constrain businesses’ abilities to produce and distribute goods and services. In addition, customers’ environmental perspectives may influence purchasing decisions.

unsureList.text: Laws and regulations affect operating costs and whether particular business activities are legal.
unsureList.best: Legal factors influence business viability because they affect operating costs and the legality of some operations.

unsureList.text: Career opportunities depend partly on which businesses are viable in a location.
unsureList.best: Career opportunities in a market can be determined by the types of businesses that are viable, based on how PESTEL factors impact the location.

unsureList.text: Changes in PESTEL factors can alter business conditions and local job availability.
unsureList.best: Changes in PESTEL factors may alter the business landscape and job availability within an existing market; for example, some employees face layoffs during economic downturns.

unsureList.text: Apply PESTEL analysis to judge a market’s attractiveness and risks.
unsureList.best: Apply the PESTEL framework to evaluate the attractiveness and potential risks of a market.

unsureList.text: Businesses assess relevant PESTEL factors and their effects on a product’s or business idea’s market prospects and risks.
unsureList.best: Businesses evaluate market opportunities using the PESTEL framework, which involves identifying the relevant PESTEL factors and assessing how each relevant factor impacts the attractiveness and potential risks of the market, specific to their product or business idea.

unsureList.text: Businesses are more likely to enter markets whose PESTEL conditions fit their models, resources, processes, and customers.
unsureList.best: A business is more likely to enter a market where PESTEL factors align with its business model, considering resources and production processes as well as potential customers. For example, a tech business is more likely to locate in a market with relatively inexpensive access to high-speed internet and electricity, while a farm-to-table restaurant is more likely to locate in a market with customers who prioritize locally grown food.

unsureList.text: Changing PESTEL factors can affect customers, operations, distribution, resources, and a business’s viability.
unsureList.best: Changes in PESTEL factors may impact the viability of a business in an existing market because of their influence on customer needs, wants, and ability to buy a product; available production and distribution systems; and access to resources.

unsureList.text: An entrepreneur creates a business while accepting its risks and possible rewards.
unsureList.best: An entrepreneur is an individual who develops a new business and assumes the risks and potential rewards.

unsureList.text: Businesses generate ideas by observing, interviewing, surveying, researching gaps, and experimenting with new capabilities.
unsureList.best: Entrepreneurs and existing businesses generate new product ideas using a variety of strategies, such as observing, interviewing, and surveying potential customers to identify needs; investing in market and technical research to identify market gaps; and developing new capabilities through experimentation.

unsureList.text: Explain new-product risks and why entrepreneurs and businesses accept them.
unsureList.best: 1.4.A Describe strategies entrepreneurs and businesses use to generate new product ideas.

unsureList.text: New products require costly financial, physical, and human resources without guaranteeing sufficient revenue or profit.
unsureList.best: Bringing a new product to market incurs risk because it requires financial, physical, and human resources, which have costs, and there is no guarantee that a new product will generate enough revenue to cover the costs or earn profits.

unsureList.text: Potential profits, solving problems, and pursuing passions can motivate businesses to accept new-product risks.
unsureList.best: 1.4.A.1 An entrepreneur is an individual who develops a new business and assumes the risks and potential rewards.

unsureList.text: Use entrepreneurial design thinking to create and validate a business or product idea.
unsureList.best: Apply an entrepreneurial design-thinking process to the generation and validation of a new business or product idea. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Use observation, interviews, and surveys to verify that a clearly defined problem affects multiple potential customers.
unsureList.best: An entrepreneurial design-thinking process begins with observing, interviewing, and/ or surveying potential customers to identify and validate a problem, need, or want. At this stage, validation means gathering evidence that the problem, need, or want exists, can be clearly defined, and is experienced by multiple potential customers.

unsureList.text: After validating a problem, develop a solution through brainstorming, sketching, and prototyping.
unsureList.best: After an entrepreneur or existing business has identified and validated a problem, need, or want, the entrepreneur or existing business will develop a potential solution (product idea), which may involve brainstorming, sketching, and prototyping.

unsureList.text: Test an initial product idea by collecting customer feedback on a simple minimum viable product.
unsureList.best: After an initial product idea is developed, the entrepreneur or existing business will validate the idea by gathering initial feedback on a minimum viable product (MVP) from potential customers. The MVP is the simplest version of the product idea, with only core features, and may be a sketch, a description, or a model.

unsureList.text: Explain how and why businesses promote ethical conduct.
unsureList.best: Explain how and why businesses encourage ethical behavior.

unsureList.text: Explain how unethical conduct and incentive systems can encourage people to pursue personal benefits improperly.
unsureList.best: 1.6.A Explain how and why businesses encourage ethical behavior.

unsureList.text: Identify ways businesses promote ethics, including codes, training, consequences, and leadership example.
unsureList.best: Businesses can encourage ethical behavior by implementing codes of conduct, training employees to follow ethical guidelines, imposing internal repercussions for ethical transgressions, and modeling ethical behavior.

unsureList.text: Explain how ethical practices affect customer loyalty, employee relationships, reputation, and profitability.
unsureList.best: Ethical business practices can also attract both customers and employees and contribute to brand loyalty. A business’s response to unethical behavior or an ethical dilemma may affect customer and employee relationships, public perception of the business, and profitability.

unsureList.text: Explain how leaders address ethical dilemmas.
unsureList.best: Explain how business leaders respond to ethical dilemmas.

unsureList.text: Define an ethical dilemma as a conflict among values or between values and business goals.
unsureList.best: Ethical dilemmas in business exist when a core value, such as transparency, fairness, and empathy, conflicts with other core values or with business goals or practices.

unsureList.text: Explain how leaders consider stakeholders, reputation, and company culture when responding to ethical dilemmas.
unsureList.best: Business leaders facing ethical dilemmas of- ten consider the impact of potential responses on various internal and external stakeholders, as well as the impact on reputation and com- pany culture.

unsureList.text: Explain how leaders choose responses by weighing stakeholder effects or following organizational values and goals.
unsureList.best: To respond to an ethical dilemma, business leaders often evaluate the benefits and costs of potential responses for each stakeholder group and choose the course of action that results in the greatest total benefit or the least total harm. Alternatively, business leaders may choose a course of action that is most consistent with the business’s vision and/or goals.

unsureList.text: Describe major business structures and compare their advantages and disadvantages.
unsureList.best: Describe the major types of business organization and their relative advantages and disadvantages.

unsureList.text: Identify sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLCs, and corporations as major business structures.
unsureList.best: The major types of business organization are sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company (LLC), and corporation.

unsureList.text: Explain how unincorporated structures and LLCs preserve owner control but may limit growth funding.
unsureList.best: A business owner can retain control over decision making and profits by organizing their business as a sole proprietorship, partnership, or LLC; however, they may be limited in their ability to grow the business because these types of businesses have less access to funding.

unsureList.text: Compare personal liability for sole proprietors and partners with the liability protection of LLCs.
unsureList.best: Sole proprietors and partners are personally liable for all business debts and obligations; however, they can avoid personal liability for business debts by organizing as LLCs.

unsureList.text: Explain how corporations trade owner control for greater funding, growth potential, and separate business liability.
unsureList.best: 1.7.A.2 A business owner can retain control over decision making and profits by organizing their business as a sole proprietorship, partnership, or LLC; however, they may be limited in their ability to grow the business because these types of businesses have less access to funding.

unsureList.text: Explain that sole proprietors manage all business areas and may perform several specialized roles.
unsureList.best: continued on next page Sole proprietors have primary responsibility for all aspects of their businesses and may play multiple roles, including chief executive officer (CEO), marketer, product developer, financial manager, and operations manager.

unsureList.text: Explain that partners share broad responsibilities and typically divide roles by strengths and interests.
unsureList.best: Partners have primary responsibility for all aspects of their business and play multiple roles, which are typically divided according to each partner’s strengths and interests.

unsureList.text: Explain that growth and complexity lead businesses to assign responsibilities to specialized teams.
unsureList.best: As a business grows in size and complexity, managing all aspects of it requires more employees with specific skills, which leads many businesses to organize roles and responsibilities into specialized departments (or teams).

unsureList.text: Describe executive leaders’ and managers’ responsibilities and reporting relationships in large businesses.
unsureList.best: Many large businesses employ executive leaders (e.g., CEOs) who are responsible for the overall vision, operations, strategy, and performance of the business as well as managers who lead the specialized departments and report to the executive leaders. In a corporation, the executive leaders report to the board of directors and shareholders.

unsureList.text: Explain how specialized departments build expertise and improve efficient, effective service to customers.
unsureList.best: 1.7.C Explain how and why large businesses organize responsibilities into a structure that includes leadership and management of specialized departments as well as outsourcing.

unsureList.text: Explain why businesses outsource activities to improve efficiency, reduce costs, or obtain missing expertise.
unsureList.best: Businesses may outsource functions to other businesses when doing so is likely to increase efficiency or reduce costs. For example, a business may outsource functions when it lacks employees with specific skills or when existing labor costs are high.

unsureList.text: Explain how sales and marketing attract and retain customers through research, selling, branding, and relationships.
unsureList.best: Sales and marketing departments conduct market research, develop sales strategies, manage brands, and build customer relationships to attract and retain customers.

unsureList.text: Explain how research and development improves goods, services, and processes through innovation.
unsureList.best: Research and development departments innovate around new and existing goods, services, and processes to better meet customers’ needs and wants.

unsureList.text: Describe how operations manage production or service delivery processes.
unsureList.best: 1.8.A Describe factors businesses consider when developing a production process.

unsureList.text: Explain how accounting tracks financial activity and prepares statements to assess business health.
unsureList.best: Accounting departments track expenditures and earnings and prepare financial statements to monitor the financial health of a business.

unsureList.text: Explain how finance obtains and manages funds and recommends performance improvements using financial data.
unsureList.best: Finance departments secure and manage the use of funds and use financial data to recommend strategies for improving a business’s performance.

unsureList.text: Describe how human resources recruits, trains, and evaluates employees for business needs.
unsureList.best: Human resources departments recruit, train, and oversee the evaluation of employees to ensure that a business has a workforce with the knowledge, skills, and abilities to produce and provide the product, market to customers, make sales, and manage finances.

unsureList.text: Compare artisan production, which relies on skilled labor, with technology-intensive mass production.
unsureList.best: Businesses establish processes for producing and distributing their goods and/or services. Some businesses that produce goods choose artisan processes, which require skilled labor and attention to detail, while others choose mass-production processes, which typically require technology, assembly lines, and machinery to produce a larger quantity of goods.

unsureList.text: Explain how customer priorities, capabilities, and competition influence production-process choices.
unsureList.best: 1.8.C Explain how a business’s competitive advantage strategy influences supply chain decisions.

unsureList.text: Develop or describe a product supply-chain plan.
unsureList.best: Develop or describe a supply chain plan for a product.

unsureList.text: Explain how supply chains connect participants from raw-material acquisition through customer delivery.
unsureList.best: Businesses connect all of the individuals and businesses involved at each stage of the production and distribution process—from acquiring raw materials to final customer delivery—through supply chains, which may be local, regional, or global. Supply chains for goods differ from supply chains for services.

unsureList.text: Describe how goods move from materials and components through manufacturing, storage, distribution, and retail.
unsureList.best: 1.8.B.1 Businesses connect all of the individuals and businesses involved at each stage of the production and distribution process—from acquiring raw materials to final customer delivery—through supply chains, which may be local, regional, or global. Supply chains for goods differ from supply chains for services.

unsureList.text: Describe service supply chains involving employees, resources, and systems for in-person or virtual delivery.
unsureList.best: In the supply chain for a service, businesses acquire the employees, resources, and delivery systems needed to provide the service to customers either in person or virtually.

unsureList.text: Explain how cost, quality, efficiency, convenience, and risks affect supplier selection.
unsureList.best: Businesses consider cost, quality, efficiency, convenience, and risk when choosing suppliers. Risks such as natural disasters, political instability, resource shortages, production errors, and supplier reputation may delay product delivery or increase costs, threatening competitive advantage and profits.

unsureList.text: Explain how competitive strategy influences supply-chain choices.
unsureList.best: Explain how a business’s competitive advantage strategy influences supply chain decisions.

unsureList.text: Explain how low-price strategies favor mass production, cost reduction, and scalable supply chains.
unsureList.best: Businesses seeking competitive advantage through low prices typically use mass production and build supply chains focused on reducing costs, for example, through the use of cheaper resources and more efficient production processes. Some businesses scale their operations—building new, higher- capacity, and/or more efficient supply chains designed to achieve revenue increases that are greater than cost increases.

unsureList.text: Explain how quality-focused businesses select high-quality resources and production methods.
unsureList.best: Businesses seeking competitive advantage through the provision of high-quality goods and services, whether through artisan or mass-production processes, build supply chains that use high-quality resources and production methods.

unsureList.text: Explain how entry barriers can involve exclusive supplier or distributor agreements.
unsureList.best: Businesses seeking competitive advantage through barriers to entry build supply chains that include exclusive or restrictive agreements with suppliers or distributors; for example, agreements that prevent a supplier from selling component parts to rivals or prevent a retailer from distributing rival products.

unsureList.text: Explain why marketers gather customer information and how they use it.
unsureList.best: Explain why and how marketers collect customer data. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Marketing includes identifying customer problems, needs, and wants, then promoting, selling, and delivering products.
unsureList.best: Marketing is all of the activities businesses undertake to identify customers’ problems, needs, and wants as well as to promote, sell, and deliver products.

unsureList.text: Customer information helps businesses choose whom to serve, what to offer, and how to market profitably.
unsureList.best: Customer data helps marketers determine which customers a business should serve, which products to produce, and how to market products effectively and profitably.

unsureList.text: Marketers gather customer information about demographic and psychographic characteristics.
unsureList.best: Marketers collect a wide variety of data pertaining to customers. This data includes demographic and psychographic characteristics.

unsureList.text: Businesses obtain customer information through digital tools, traditional research, and purchases from other companies.
unsureList.best: 2.1.C.1 Businesses use a variety of tactics to build strong customer relationships, including personalized service, rewards programs for frequent buyers, and customer feedback opportunities (e.g., satisfaction surveys). Social media and the internet make it easier for businesses to employ these tactics.

unsureList.text: Use market segmentation to find target customers and create customer profiles.
unsureList.best: Use market segmentation to identify target customers and develop a customer profile. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Market segmentation groups potential customers by shared demographic and psychographic traits to reveal differing needs.
unsureList.best: Market segmentation is a way to aggregate potential customers into groups, called market segments, based on shared demographic and psychographic characteristics. Market segmentation helps businesses better understand the needs and wants of different groups within a market and how their products might address these needs and wants.

unsureList.text: A customer profile is a fictional representative containing target customers’ demographic, psychographic, and preference information.
unsureList.best: A business may create customer profiles to personify its target customers. A customer profile is a fictional description of a specific sample customer, incorporating demographic and psychographic data as well as the individual’s wants, needs, and preferences.

unsureList.text: Targeting and profiling help businesses design more appealing and cost-effective products and marketing.
unsureList.best: Identifying target customers and developing customer profiles helps businesses design products and marketing elements (e.g., branding, pricing, and advertising) that appeal to the targeted customer population, which is typically more effective and less costly than appealing to a wide audience. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Explain why customer relationships matter and plan ways to strengthen them.
unsureList.best: Describe the purpose of building customer relationships and develop a plan to build customer relationships.

unsureList.text: Businesses build relationships through personalized service, rewards, feedback, social media, and internet-based interactions.
unsureList.best: Businesses use a variety of tactics to build strong customer relationships, including personalized service, rewards programs for frequent buyers, and customer feedback opportunities (e.g., satisfaction surveys). Social media and the internet make it easier for businesses to employ these tactics.

unsureList.text: Strong relationships can lower customer acquisition costs and raise profits through customer referrals.
unsureList.best: Strong customer relationships can reduce customer acquisition cost, potentially increasing profits, because satisfied customers may refer new customers. Customer acquisition cost is calculated by dividing the total marketing, advertising, and sales costs associated with acquiring customers by the total number of customers.

unsureList.text: Strong relationships can increase customer lifetime value through loyalty and repeat purchases.
unsureList.best: Strong customer relationships can increase the lifetime value of each unique customer, potentially increasing profits, because satisfied customers have more brand loyalty and make repeat purchases. The lifetime value of a customer is the estimated amount of money that the customer will spend on the business’s products over time.

unsureList.text: Explain how customer-data practices can expose consumers and businesses to privacy, identity-theft, and fraud risks.
unsureList.best: Explain how the collection and use of customer data may make customers vulnerable to privacy infringement, identity theft, and fraud and create risks for businesses.

unsureList.text: Collecting and storing personal information may violate privacy, especially without clear customer awareness or consent.
unsureList.best: Collecting, compiling, and storing customer data such as consumers’ online searches, purchases of goods and services, credit card numbers, social media posts, and geographic location may violate consumers’ privacy, particularly when consumers are unaware that their data is being collected or uninformed about how it may be used.

unsureList.text: Poorly protected customer information can enable data breaches, fraud, and identity theft.
unsureList.best: Customer data that is not properly secured may make individual consumers or businesses vulnerable to data breaches, fraud, and identity theft.

unsureList.text: Businesses must weigh data-use benefits against customer loss, value conflicts, reputational damage, and other risks.
unsureList.best: Businesses that collect, compile, store, and use customer data must balance the benefits of using this data against the potential risks to the business, including loss of customers, violation of core values, and harm to the business’s reputation.

unsureList.text: Explain why and how consumers decide what to buy.
unsureList.best: Explain why and how consumers make buying decisions. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Consumers purchase goods and services for needs and wants; price, features, availability, and advertising affect choices.
unsureList.best: Consumers buy goods and services to meet basic needs and wants. When rival goods that meet the same needs and wants are available, consumer decisions regarding which products to buy are influenced by prices, differentiated product features, availability, and advertising.

unsureList.text: Some purchases involve systematic comparison, while smaller purchases are often habitual; rational evaluation requires time and information.
unsureList.best: Consumers make some buying decisions, especially consequential ones like a home purchase, using a rational process of systematically evaluating alternative products, but many smaller buying decisions, such as buying a coffee on the way to work, are habitual or routine. A rational decision-making process helps consumers identify products that best address their needs and wants but also incurs costs, including time spent gathering information.

unsureList.text: Age, education, income, budget, occupation, and lifestyle influence consumers’ needs, wants, and ability to pay.
unsureList.best: Personal factors, such as age, sex, education, income level, budget, occupation, and lifestyle, shape buying decisions by influencing what a consumer needs and wants and what they can afford.

unsureList.text: Values, beliefs, perceptions, learned associations, and motivations shape attitudes toward products and willingness to buy.
unsureList.best: 2.2.A.5 Social and cultural factors, such as peers, family, social status, cultural norms, and media, shape consumer buying decisions by influencing what is acceptable, desirable, or appropriate to buy.

unsureList.text: Peers, family, social status, cultural norms, and media influence what consumers consider acceptable or desirable.
unsureList.best: Social and cultural factors, such as peers, family, social status, cultural norms, and media, shape consumer buying decisions by influencing what is acceptable, desirable, or appropriate to buy.

unsureList.text: Store conditions, timing, and product availability create temporary influences that encourage or discourage purchases.
unsureList.best: Situational influences, such as store design (noise, lighting, and organization), timing, and product availability, influence consumer buying decisions by creating temporary conditions that can encourage or discourage buying. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Describe how legal and technological changes affect consumer purchasing patterns.
unsureList.best: Describe the impact of legal and technological factors on consumer purchasing patterns.

unsureList.text: Purchasing patterns describe consumers’ usual timing, frequency, and quantities, influenced by location, income, family, and friends.
unsureList.best: A purchasing pattern is a consumer’s typical routine for making purchases, including timing, frequency, and quantity of purchases. Factors such as where an individual lives and works, their income level, and the purchasing patterns of their family and friends help determine their purchasing patterns.

unsureList.text: Laws shape purchasing by restricting products or transaction conditions and may encourage substitute products.
unsureList.best: Laws influence consumer purchasing patterns when they regulate what consumers can buy and when and where they can buy specific items. Consumer protection laws, for example, are designed to help individuals avoid fraudulent products and/or products that may be unsafe for them. These legal factors can give rise to substitute products, as consumers find new ways to address their needs and wants when existing products are more difficult to obtain.

unsureList.text: Technology and innovation introduce products and shopping methods that change how consumers meet needs and wants.
unsureList.best: Technology and innovation make new products accessible, which influences consumer purchasing patterns. For example, the internet in the 1990s and the advent of smartphones in the 2010s both facilitated new ways of shopping, finding information, and accessing entertainment, which changed how customers met their needs and wants.

unsureList.text: Evaluate Cialdini-based sales approaches and create an appropriate sales tactic.
unsureList.best: Evaluate sales tactics that draw upon Cialdini’s principles of influence, and develop a sales tactic. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Cialdini’s influence principles explain psychological reasons people comply; marketers use them to encourage purchases.
unsureList.best: The principles of influence, developed by psychologist Robert Cialdini, are psychological factors that cause people to comply with a request. Marketers use tactics based on these principles to motivate consumers to buy products.

unsureList.text: Scarcity tactics increase desire by making products seem rare or available for only a limited time.
unsureList.best: 2.2.C.1 The principles of influence, developed by psychologist Robert Cialdini, are psychological factors that cause people to comply with a request. Marketers use tactics based on these principles to motivate consumers to buy products.

unsureList.text: Authority tactics use experts or credentials to make consumers more likely to follow recommendations.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s authority principle states that individuals tend to obey or follow authority figures. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by using expert spokespeople, such as doctors, to endorse products or by emphasizing the credentials of service providers.

unsureList.text: Consensus tactics use favorable customer feedback to suggest that many people approve of a product.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s consensus principle states that individuals tend to follow social-group norms. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by promoting positive customer feedback to create a sense that most consumers like a product.

unsureList.text: Liking tactics feature relatable people and personal rapport to make consumers more receptive.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s liking principle states that individuals are more likely to be influenced by people they like or relate to. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by featuring people who look and act like the target customer in advertising and by building personal rapport with consumers.

unsureList.text: Reciprocity tactics provide samples, trials, or gifts that encourage recipients to respond with a purchase.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s reciprocity principle states that individuals feel obligated to reciprocate when given something of value. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by offering free trials, samples, and gifts, which can make the recipient feel compelled to buy something in return. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Consistency tactics connect products with consumers’ self-images and encourage behavior aligned with their identities.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s consistency principle states that individuals tend to repeat behavior that aligns with their self-image. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by appealing to their identity; for example, by promoting a product as something health-conscious consumers buy.

unsureList.text: Unity tactics build group identity or community, making members more receptive to influence.
unsureList.best: Cialdini’s unity principle states that when individuals perceive that they are part of a group, they are more likely to be influenced by the group. Marketers apply this principle to motivate consumers by building a sense of community among target customers; for example, by asking them to join an exclusive online group or inviting them to cocreate products.

unsureList.text: Market researchers collect both numerical and descriptive information.
unsureList.best: Market researchers collect both quantitative and qualitative data.

unsureList.text: New-product businesses research desirability, feasibility, and viability before committing substantial resources.
unsureList.best: Businesses developing new products use market research to evaluate the desirability, feasibility, and viability of a product before committing significant resources to bring the product to market.

unsureList.text: Explain how existing businesses use research to understand changing needs, identify innovations, and retain or expand market share.
unsureList.best: Businesses with existing products use market research to better understand customers’ changing needs and wants, identify opportunities for product innovation, and develop strategies to retain or grow market share. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Conduct and interpret secondary research to evaluate a market opportunity.
unsureList.best: Conduct and interpret secondary-source research to assess a market opportunity.

unsureList.text: Explain how secondary and primary research reveal customers, competitors, market conditions, and PESTEL influences.
unsureList.best: Businesses use both secondary-source research and primary-source research to learn about customers, competitors, and the market landscape, including the PESTEL factors influencing market opportunities.

unsureList.text: Describe secondary research sources and the market information they provide, including size, trends, segments, and customer influences.
unsureList.best: Secondary-source research involves gathering quantitative and/or qualitative information from a variety of external sources, including government, commercial, and academic publications and databases. These sources often contain detailed information on a variety of topics including market size (in dollars and in total customers), market trends, market segments, and factors that influence customer decisions, which can inform a business’s understanding of the potential viability of its product.

unsureList.text: Explain why businesses interpret secondary research, including competitor information, when assessing a product opportunity.
unsureList.best: Businesses typically interpret secondary- source research findings, including detailed information about rival businesses, to assess the market landscape for a product idea because it is more cost-effective than conducting extensive primary-source research.

unsureList.text: Conduct and interpret primary research testing hypotheses about target customers and their preferences.
unsureList.best: Conduct and interpret primary- source research to test a business hypothesis related to target customers and/ or customer preferences.

unsureList.text: Describe primary research methods businesses use to test customer and preference hypotheses.
unsureList.best: 2.3.C.3 When conducting primary-source research, businesses may choose the research method or combination of methods based on the types of data the business needs to test its hypotheses.

unsureList.text: Define a business hypothesis and explain why businesses test assumptions before acting.
unsureList.best: A business hypothesis states an assumption related to a customer, product, or market. Businesses typically test the validity of their assumptions (hypotheses) before committing to a course of action.

unsureList.text: Explain how needed data determines the choice or combination of primary research methods.
unsureList.best: When conducting primary-source research, businesses may choose the research method or combination of methods based on the types of data the business needs to test its hypotheses.

unsureList.text: Explain when surveys are appropriate for collecting extensive quantitative data representing a population.
unsureList.best: Businesses may use surveys when they need a large amount of quantitative data that reflects the views of a population in order to test a hypothesis.

unsureList.text: Explain when focus groups and interviews provide detailed qualitative insights from a small number of people.
unsureList.best: Businesses may use focus groups and one- on-one interviews when they need in-depth, qualitative data from a small number of individuals, such as highly engaged customers or potential customers, in order to test a hypothesis. These methods allow for follow-up questions and discussions that elicit detailed explanations.

unsureList.text: Explain how experiments and observations measure customer behavior in controlled or natural settings.
unsureList.best: Businesses may use experiments and observations when they need data on customer behavior, rather than opinions, in order to test a hypothesis. These methods allow researchers to gather information about how customers behave in either a controlled environment (in an experiment) or a natural environment (in an observation).

unsureList.text: Explain how A/B testing compares authentic customer responses to two viable alternatives.
unsureList.best: Businesses may use A/B testing (a type of experiment) when they need to measure authentic customer responses to two viable alternatives in order to test a hypothesis. This method allows researchers to gather information about specific customer preferences in a real-world environment. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Explain how representative samples and unbiased questions reduce skewed research data.
unsureList.best: Businesses should take care to implement hypothesis testing in ways that reduce the risk of skewed data—both by designing research studies with sufficiently large and appropriately populated samples to reflect the population being studied and by asking unbiased questions that use neutral phrasing to avoid influencing the way respondents answer.

unsureList.text: Recognize that businesses must often decide amid limited, unclear, or contradictory research because predictions can be inaccurate.
unsureList.best: Despite the use of market research to inform decisions, businesses are not always able to accurately predict customer and market responses. Businesses often must innovate and respond to problems and opportunities using limited, unclear, or contradictory data.

unsureList.text: Explain how visualizations reveal and communicate patterns, trends, and insights for evidence-based decisions.
unsureList.best: Businesses may use a variety of data visualization tools to identify and communicate patterns, trends, and insights. Data visualizations such as bar charts, stacked bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts make it easier for stakeholders to understand complex information and make evidence- based decisions.

unsureList.text: Choose the visualization that best communicates a desired pattern, trend, or insight.
unsureList.best: Businesses select the data visualization tool that best illustrates the pattern, trend, or insight they want to communicate.

unsureList.text: Explain that bar charts compare individual data points, such as sales or business revenues.
unsureList.best: Bar charts are often used to illustrate comparisons between individual data points, such as several years of sales data for a specific business or annual revenue for different businesses in a market.

unsureList.text: Explain that stacked bar charts compare totals and their component categories.
unsureList.best: 2.3.D.1 Businesses may use a variety of data visualization tools to identify and communicate patterns, trends, and insights. Data visualizations such as bar charts, stacked bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts make it easier for stakeholders to understand complex information and make evidence- based decisions.

unsureList.text: Explain that line graphs show changes and trends over time.
unsureList.best: 2.3.D.1 Businesses may use a variety of data visualization tools to identify and communicate patterns, trends, and insights. Data visualizations such as bar charts, stacked bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts make it easier for stakeholders to understand complex information and make evidence- based decisions.

unsureList.text: Explain that pie charts show how parts comprise a whole.
unsureList.best: Pie charts are often used to illustrate part-to- whole relationships, such as the percentage of market share held by each business in a market.

unsureList.text: Identify product development’s six stages: ideation, validation, design, messaging, production, and launch.
unsureList.best: Product development is the process of creating or improving a product through research and iteration. Product development typically includes six stages: ideation, validation, design, messaging, production, and launch.

unsureList.text: Explain how ideation generates product ideas through research, development, and brainstorming.
unsureList.best: The ideation stage focuses on generating ideas for new or improved products through market research, technical research and development (R&D), and brainstorming.

unsureList.text: Explain how validation tests ideas with customers and uses MVPs to assess product-market fit.
unsureList.best: The validation stage focuses on testing product ideas with potential customers. Marketers may use an MVP (minimum viable product) to assess whether a product can achieve product-market fit, which occurs if customer demand is sufficient to generate profit.

unsureList.text: Describe how design develops prototypes, evaluates costs and features, and incorporates customer feedback.
unsureList.best: 2.4.A.6 The production stage focuses on building the product, incorporating feedback received during the design stage. Businesses determine the production process and supply chain and attempt to match production levels with customer demand.

unsureList.text: Explain how messaging creates marketing strategy, value propositions, and positioning relative to competitors.
unsureList.best: 2.4.C Explain how businesses adapt their marketing strategies to address competitive challenges throughout the product life cycle. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Explain how production builds the product, incorporates feedback, establishes supply chains, and aligns output with demand.
unsureList.best: The production stage focuses on building the product, incorporating feedback received during the design stage. Businesses determine the production process and supply chain and attempt to match production levels with customer demand.

unsureList.text: Explain how launch begins customer ordering, distribution, and marketing to the target segment.
unsureList.best: The launch stage focuses on taking orders and distributing a final product to customers. Businesses begin marketing the product to the target segment. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Explain how branding distinguishes products, builds awareness, and encourages customer loyalty.
unsureList.best: Branding is the process of developing an identity, or brand, for a business or product, which is used to distinguish it from competitors, raise customer awareness, and generate loyalty.

unsureList.text: Explain how vision and value propositions guide brand identities appealing to target customers.
unsureList.best: Businesses typically consider their vision and/ or the value proposition for a product when developing a brand identity to ensure that the brand appeals to the target customer. For example, a business that includes quick delivery in its value proposition may develop a brand identity that conveys a sense of movement or urgency.

unsureList.text: Identify brand identity elements and explain how trademarks protect them.
unsureList.best: A brand identity can be conveyed through a name, idea, term, symbol, design, or combination of these elements, which businesses often seek to protect by trademarking.

unsureList.text: Explain why businesses may offer generic products to customers prioritizing lower costs over branding.
unsureList.best: In addition to marketing products under brand names, businesses may sell generic products because some customers prioritize cost savings, which are associated with generic goods, over branding.

unsureList.text: Define the product life cycle as stages from introduction through decline shaped by changing demand.
unsureList.best: The product life cycle is a series of stages that a product passes through, from introduction (the culmination of the product development stages) to decline, dictated by changes in customer demand over time.

unsureList.text: Explain how businesses adjust marketing priorities at each life-cycle stage to grow or retain market share.
unsureList.best: At each stage of the product life cycle, businesses adapt the focus of their marketing strategies to address competitive challenges and attempt to grow or retain market share.

unsureList.text: Describe introduction-stage conditions and marketing focused on building awareness and initial demand.
unsureList.best: During the introduction stage of the product life cycle, a business launches a new product and sales volume and revenue are typically low; marketing strategy focuses on tactics to raise brand awareness to generate initial customer demand.

unsureList.text: Describe growth-stage conditions and strategies emphasizing differentiation, quality, promotion, and advertising.
unsureList.best: 2.4.C Explain how businesses adapt their marketing strategies to address competitive challenges throughout the product life cycle. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Describe maturity-stage conditions and strategies emphasizing loyalty, differentiation, lower prices, and innovation.
unsureList.best: A product enters the maturity stage when sales volume and revenue flatten, and the business seeks to retain existing market share by building brand loyalty in a saturated market. Marketing strategy during the maturity stage focuses on continued product differentiation, lower prices, and innovation.

unsureList.text: Describe decline-stage conditions and strategies involving cost reduction, redesign, or discontinuation.
unsureList.best: 2.4.C Explain how businesses adapt their marketing strategies to address competitive challenges throughout the product life cycle. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Develop and evaluate a pricing strategy.
unsureList.best: Develop and evaluate a pricing strategy. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Explain how pricing affects customer attraction, retention, revenue, profit, and business viability.
unsureList.best: A pricing strategy is a way of determining how much to charge for a product; setting the right price is critical to a business’s viability because of the role price plays in attracting and retaining customers and generating revenue and profit.

unsureList.text: Explain why price must exceed per-unit production and distribution cost for profitability.
unsureList.best: 2.5.A.6 Businesses that use penetration pricing set a low price (possibly below per-unit cost) with the intention of increasing the price later in an effort to attract price-sensitive customers away from competitors and grow market share quickly.

unsureList.text: Describe value-based pricing as charging according to customers’ perceived product value.
unsureList.best: Businesses that use value-based pricing set a price based on the perceived value or worth of the product to the customer. Businesses that produce highly differentiated or uniquely valuable products are more likely to use value- based pricing.

unsureList.text: Describe competitive pricing as setting prices relative to rivals, including premium, matching, or lower pricing.
unsureList.best: 2.5.B.1 Businesses that operate in highly competitive markets with little product differentiation have little pricing power (the ability to raise prices without risking market share), which may force them to keep prices as low as possible. Businesses that operate in less-competitive markets or sell highly differentiated products have more pricing power and can implement more profitable pricing strategies.

unsureList.text: Describe cost-based pricing as setting prices to achieve a desired profit per unit.
unsureList.best: Businesses that use cost-based pricing set the product’s price to achieve the desired per- unit profit (price minus per-unit cost) rather than considering factors such as perceived customer value or the price of rival goods. Businesses with clearly defined per-unit costs that can be communicated to customers, such as construction contractors, are more likely to use cost-based pricing.

unsureList.text: Describe penetration pricing as initially setting a low price to attract customers and rapidly gain market share.
unsureList.best: Businesses that use penetration pricing set a low price (possibly below per-unit cost) with the intention of increasing the price later in an effort to attract price-sensitive customers away from competitors and grow market share quickly.

unsureList.text: Explain how competition and product differentiation influence pricing power.
unsureList.best: 2.5.B Evaluate how market conditions affect a business’s pricing power.

unsureList.text: Explain why highly price-responsive customers limit pricing power and may reduce revenue after price changes.
unsureList.best: Businesses whose customers are highly responsive to price changes have little pricing power because a price increase may reduce revenue if customers buy significantly less of the product. While a price cut may increase product sales, sales may not increase sufficiently to compensate for the lower price, also resulting in lower revenue and profits.

unsureList.text: Explain how price elasticity measures customer responsiveness and constrains price increases.
unsureList.best: Businesses measure customer responsiveness to price changes and how price changes will impact sales and revenue by measuring price elasticity of demand. Businesses that face more elastic (responsive) demand are limited in their ability to raise prices compared to businesses that face more inelastic (less-responsive) demand.
