unsureList.text: Explain that collusion among competitors to establish prices is illegal in many jurisdictions.
unsureList.best: Colluding with competitors to set an agreed- upon price (typically used to set one higher than the competitive market price) is illegal in many countries, including the U.S.

unsureList.text: Explain that raising prices excessively during crises, known as price gouging, is illegal in many places.
unsureList.best: Price gouging—the practice of raising the price of a product with increased demand due to a crisis—is illegal in many U.S. states and in many countries.

unsureList.text: Explain that price discrimination based on protected characteristics is illegal.
unsureList.best: Price discrimination—the practice of charging different prices to different customer segments for the same product—is illegal when done on the basis of race, nationality, sex, or another protected status.

unsureList.text: Identify the marketing channels businesses can use to make products available to customers.
unsureList.best: Describe the types of marketing channels available to businesses. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Place describes where and how customers obtain products, including stores, memberships, and online locations.
unsureList.best: Place is used to describe where and how customers access products; for example, whether products are available in retail stores, in company-owned stores, through club memberships, and/or online.

unsureList.text: Marketing or distribution channels are the final supply-chain stage connecting finished products with customers.
unsureList.best: Place is determined by a business’s marketing channels (also called distribution channels), which are the final stage of a supply chain. A marketing channel consists of all of the individuals and businesses required to deliver a finished product to the final customer.

unsureList.text: Direct channels reach customers without intermediaries; indirect channels use intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers.
unsureList.best: Businesses distribute products through either direct channels, which connect them directly to their customers with no intermediaries, or indirect channels, which include intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers.

unsureList.text: Some products, including medicines and hazardous goods, must legally use particular distribution channels.
unsureList.best: Specific distribution channels are legally required for some products, such as prescription medications and products that pose health or safety risks. TOPIC2.6 Place and Channels continued on next page BUSINESSCASE Students explore how a business decides which marketing channels it should use to best reach its target customers. PROJECTLINK Operations Task 7: Select a potential marketing channel or channels.

unsureList.text: Choose and assess possible marketing channels for a product.
unsureList.best: Select and evaluate potential marketing channels for a product. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Compare channels by cost, profitability, customer experience, and ability to reach target customers.
unsureList.best: Businesses select from a variety of direct and indirect marketing channels by comparing the costs and potential profitability of each channel, the customer experience in each channel, and the ability of each channel to deliver the product to the target customers.

unsureList.text: Direct channels offer control over prices and customer experience but may cost more, reach fewer customers, and require specialized expertise.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select direct channels, such as websites or company-owned retail stores because these channels enable a business to maintain more control over pricing and the customer experience. These channels may be more costly to establish and more limited in reach, and the business may need to acquire expertise in sales and distribution.

unsureList.text: Indirect channels can lower costs and expand reach through partners’ expertise, but rivals may control distributors or retail space.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select indirect channels when they expect the expertise and networks offered by distribution partners to reduce costs and provide access to more customers. In some cases, these channels are difficult for businesses to access because distributors and retail space may already be dominated by rivals.

unsureList.text: Create or assess a coordinated marketing campaign.
unsureList.best: 2.7.A.1 A marketing campaign refers to a coordinated effort to promote a product to potential customers using all or some of the marketing tools in the promotional mix.

unsureList.text: A marketing campaign coordinates promotional activities that encourage potential customers to consider a product.
unsureList.best: A marketing campaign refers to a coordinated effort to promote a product to potential customers using all or some of the marketing tools in the promotional mix.

unsureList.text: Businesses match promotional tools to customers’ decision processes, using personalized information for significant purchases and broad messages for routine ones.
unsureList.best: Businesses strategically use different tools to address how customers make buying decisions for specific products. A customer making a consequential purchase may require detailed, personalized interaction to make a decision, while a customer making a more routine purchase may be satisfied by messages and information conveyed by mass media or direct-marketing materials.

unsureList.text: Media advertising reaches many customers simultaneously with a consistent message through outlets such as television, radio, newspapers, or billboards.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select media advertising (e.g., TV, radio, newspapers, and billboards) when they want to reach a large number of customers with the same message, such as a commercial or advertisement, at the same time. TOPIC2.7 Promotion and Marketing Communications continued on next page BUSINESSCASE Students explore how a business decides which promotional tools to use to effectively communicate with its target customers. PROJECTLINK Customer Task 8: Develop a marketing campaign, including digital marketing tools.

unsureList.text: Personal selling provides detailed information or demonstrations, often using a brief value-focused sales presentation.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select personal selling when they want to provide detailed product information or a demonstration to a potential customer. Personal selling may include a sales pitch—a short presentation that conveys the product’s value proposition—to complete a sale.

unsureList.text: Sales promotions such as discounts and coupons speed purchasing decisions or help clear excess inventory.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select sales promotions (e.g., discounts and coupons) when they want to encourage more rapid customer decision making or to reduce unsold inventory.

unsureList.text: Direct marketing uses materials such as flyers and brochures to deliver targeted messages to many prospects.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select direct marketing (e.g., flyers and brochures) when they want to reach many potential customers with a targeted message.

unsureList.text: Public relations builds a favorable public image rather than directly promoting a particular sale.
unsureList.best: Businesses may select public relations (e.g., press releases and media interviews that result in media coverage) when they want to create a favorable public image rather than advance a specific sale.

unsureList.text: Digital marketing uses internet-based tools to connect with customers; businesses increasingly shifted resources from traditional advertising to digital platforms.
unsureList.best: Digital marketing is the use of the internet and digital technology tools, such as websites, email, social media, and mobile apps, to connect with and serve customers. In the early 21st century, businesses shifted marketing resources away from traditional advertising such as newspaper, magazine, radio, and TV ads, toward digital tools and platforms.

unsureList.text: Digital tools provide more personalized, lower-cost access to global audiences and targeted customer groups.
unsureList.best: Digital marketing tools enable businesses to reach potential customers, whether global audiences or targeted customer segments, with greater personalization and at lower cost than traditional tools.

unsureList.text: Digital marketing generates extensive customer-response data, unlike many traditional methods such as television advertising and billboards.
unsureList.best: Digital marketing tools enable businesses to collect a large volume of information—known as big data—about how customers respond to marketing communication and which factors make them more likely to buy. Some traditional tools, such as personal selling, permitted this type of data collection on a small scale, but other traditional tools, such as TV ads and billboards, did not.

unsureList.text: Explain why consumers save and identify obstacles that can prevent saving.
unsureList.best: Describe reasons consumers save, and identify barriers to saving. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Consumers earn income from employment and other sources, then spend it on products meeting problems, needs, and wants.
unsureList.best: Consumers typically earn income by working for an organization such as a business, nonprofit, or government entity and spend income to buy products that address their problems, needs, and wants. Some individuals receive income from other sources, such as self-employment, rental properties, government programs, investments, or retirement accounts.

unsureList.text: Consumers save for major future purchases, emergencies, and retirement income.
unsureList.best: Consumers often save a portion of their income for significant future purchases, such as a car, a home, or college tuition. Individuals also save to prepare for future emergencies, such as job loss or illness, and to have a source of income in retirement.

unsureList.text: Saving creates an asset and may earn interest determined by rates, savings amount, account type, and economic conditions.
unsureList.best: Saving creates a personal asset and may earn interest, which can be a source of current or future income. Interest payments are determined by the interest rate, the amount of savings, the type of savings vehicle, and conditions in the economy.

unsureList.text: Automated savings, retirement plans, and health savings accounts can encourage saving through convenience or tax advantages.
unsureList.best: 3.1.B.3 Political factors influence saving because government tax policies may incentivize savings, for example, by allowing individuals to not pay income taxes on a portion of income that they place in designated accounts for retirement, health care, childcare, or other purposes.

unsureList.text: Irregular income, excessive recurring expenses, instant gratification, lifestyle inflation, and impulse buying can hinder saving.
unsureList.best: Consumers may face barriers that make saving difficult; for example, inconsistent income or recurring expenses that exceed income. Psychological forces such as instant gratification, lifestyle inflation, and impulse buying also make saving difficult. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Economic stability, income changes, and living costs influence how much disposable income individuals can save.
unsureList.best: Economic factors influence saving because the overall stability and performance of the economy affects individuals’ incomes and the cost of living. Either loss of income in a weak economy or increased cost of living in a strong economy may make saving more difficult because individuals may have less available income after paying necessary expenses.

unsureList.text: Inflation reduces savings’ purchasing power and may discourage people from saving.
unsureList.best: Inflation—an increase in the prices of goods and services—is an economic factor that erodes the purchasing power of savings because money will buy fewer goods and services in the future. The expected loss of purchasing power can disincentivize savings.

unsureList.text: Tax policies can encourage saving through tax benefits for designated retirement, healthcare, childcare, or other accounts.
unsureList.best: Political factors influence saving because government tax policies may incentivize savings, for example, by allowing individuals to not pay income taxes on a portion of income that they place in designated accounts for retirement, health care, childcare, or other purposes.

unsureList.text: Financial regulations protect savers and support the stability of banks and credit unions.
unsureList.best: Legal factors influence saving because government agencies regulate financial institutions, such as commercial banks and credit unions, to improve consumer protection and the financial stability of these institutions.

unsureList.text: Develop or assess a savings plan.
unsureList.best: Develop or evaluate a savings plan.

unsureList.text: Savings amounts depend on personal goals, income, expenses, and the barriers an individual faces.
unsureList.best: Consumers decide how much of their income to save based on their personal and financial goals as well as their current income and expenses; individuals are likely to save more if they have defined goals and face fewer barriers.

unsureList.text: Choose savings vehicles based on savings amount, goals, time horizon, PESTEL effects, and institutional costs and benefits.
unsureList.best: Consumers decide how and where to keep their savings based on how much they are saving, their goals, their available time frame, the impact of PESTEL factors, and their evaluation of the benefits and costs of various savings vehicles offered by financial institutions such as banks and credit unions. These vehicles include savings accounts, money market accounts, and certificates of deposit.

unsureList.text: Evaluate institutions and accounts using rates, fees, minimum deposits, risk, location, convenience, reputation, and associated tradeoffs.
unsureList.best: Consumers consider interest rates, fees, minimum deposit requirements, and potential risk as well as location, convenience, and reputation when selecting a financial institution and type of account. Individuals choosing a savings vehicle often face tradeoffs, such as higher minimum balances or other requirements for accounts that pay higher interest.

unsureList.text: Savings accounts are generally insured, interest-bearing deposit accounts whose rates, fees, and minimums vary by institution.
unsureList.best: 3.1.C.3 Consumers consider interest rates, fees, minimum deposit requirements, and potential risk as well as location, convenience, and reputation when selecting a financial institution and type of account. Individuals choosing a savings vehicle often face tradeoffs, such as higher minimum balances or other requirements for accounts that pay higher interest.

unsureList.text: Money market accounts are insured savings vehicles that may require larger deposits, charge higher fees, pay more interest, and offer easier cash access.
unsureList.best: A money market account is similar to a savings account and is also federally insured. Compared to a savings account, a money market account may require a larger minimum deposit, charge higher monthly fees, pay higher interest rates, and provide easier access to cash; these features differ by institution.

unsureList.text: Certificates of deposit usually offer higher interest but restrict withdrawals for a fixed period and may require larger deposits.
unsureList.best: A certificate of deposit (CD) is similar to a savings account and is also federally insured. A CD typically pays a higher rate of interest than a savings account or money market account, but depositors are restricted from withdrawing their funds for a set period of time—usually one month to five years. A CD typically requires a larger minimum deposit but no monthly fee; these features differ by institution.

unsureList.text: Checking accounts support frequent transactions; consumers compare fees, access, convenience, and interest when selecting them.
unsureList.best: Money that is not saved may be held as cash or in a checking account, which is a deposit account that is also federally insured. Checking accounts are designed for frequent transactions, such as deposits, withdrawals, debit card purchases, and payments. They typically pay little or no interest and may charge fees, such as monthly maintenance fees or overdraft fees. Consumers choose checking accounts based on factors such as fees, access (e.g., ATMs and online banking), and convenience for managing day-to-day spending and other banking transactions.

unsureList.text: Mobile payment and cryptocurrency accounts may be convenient or appreciate, but generally lack federal insurance and interest.
unsureList.best: Some individuals store savings in vehicles such as mobile payment accounts, which make the money easy to spend, or cryptocurrency accounts, which users hope will gain value as an asset. Unless offered by insured financial institutions, these vehicles are not federally insured and typically do not pay interest.

unsureList.text: Explain why consumers borrow and identify available funding sources.
unsureList.best: Describe reasons consumers borrow money and the funding sources available to them. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Consumers borrow for purchases exceeding current resources, emergencies, savings preservation, or convenience.
unsureList.best: Consumers typically borrow money because they want to spend money on goods or services that exceed their current income and accumulated savings, such as a car, a house, or college tuition. Consumers may also borrow money to address an emergency, to maintain savings while purchasing goods and services, or because of convenience.

unsureList.text: Loans create debt repaid with interest; rates and terms depend on lenders, loan type, amount, and credit history.
unsureList.best: Borrowing creates a personal liability or debt, and consumers must repay borrowed money (loans) with interest. The interest rate charged and the repayment terms vary based on the lender, the type of loan, the amount of money borrowed, and the borrower’s credit history. Loans used to buy items that can serve as collateral, such as cars and houses, are secured loans and typically have lower interest rates than general consumer loans, which are unsecured.

unsureList.text: Banks and credit unions use deposited funds to make loans to consumers and organizations.
unsureList.best: Financial institutions such as commercial banks and credit unions make loans to consumers and to businesses, nonprofits, and government entities based on the deposits received from individual savers, businesses, and other entities.

unsureList.text: Credit card companies, retailers, mortgage lenders, and alternative financial services also provide consumer loans.
unsureList.best: Credit card companies, retail stores, mortgage lenders, and alternative financial services, such as payday loans, check-cashing services, and instant tax refunds, also lend money to consumers. TOPIC3.2 Borrowing, Credit, and Debt continued on next page Required Course Content PERSONALFINANCELINK Credit Credit 12-1 Credit 12-2 Credit 12-6 Credit 12-7 Credit 12-8 Credit 12-9 Credit 12-10 Credit 12-11 Credit 12-12 Credit 12-13

unsureList.text: Consumer-protection laws require clear credit terms, regulate collections, and prohibit discriminatory lending.
unsureList.best: Consumer protection laws require lenders to communicate credit terms clearly and explicitly to borrowers; these laws also govern debt collection tactics and prohibit discriminatory lending practices. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Explain how lenders assess a prospective borrower’s creditworthiness.
unsureList.best: Explain how a lender evaluates the creditworthiness of a potential borrower.

unsureList.text: Lenders prefer borrowers with lower risk and charge higher rates to compensate for greater default risk.
unsureList.best: Lenders face the risk that a borrower will default—meaning that the borrower will not repay the loan—so they typically prefer lending to individuals who pose less risk, for example, consumers with low existing debt, high income and savings, and a history of repaying loans on time. Lenders willing to make loans to higher-risk individuals, including alternative financial services, typically charge higher interest rates.

unsureList.text: Lenders review income, savings, debt, and credit reports when judging creditworthiness.
unsureList.best: Lenders collect information about a potential borrower’s income, savings, and existing debt as well as credit reports detailing their past use of credit to determine the consumer’s creditworthiness.

unsureList.text: Credit bureaus compile reports from consumers’ financial interactions with institutions.
unsureList.best: Credit reports are created by credit bureaus (also called credit reporting agencies), which collect information each time a consumer interacts with a financial institution; for example, opening a savings account, securing a bank loan, applying for a credit card, or making a payment.

unsureList.text: Credit reports contain scores and may be provided to lenders, employers, landlords, insurers, and government agencies.
unsureList.best: A credit report includes a credit score reflecting the consumer’s past use of credit. These reports can be shared with potential lenders, potential employers, potential landlords, insurance companies, and government agencies.

unsureList.text: Recommend ways to manage existing debt or use credit.
unsureList.best: Recommend a strategy to manage a consumer’s existing debt and/ or use of credit.

unsureList.text: High debt reduces money available for saving and other expenses; larger balances or rates increase monthly payments.
unsureList.best: High levels of debt can harm a consumer’s financial condition because payments on loans reduce the amount of income available to save or use for other expenses. Larger debts and/ or higher interest rates require higher monthly payments.

unsureList.text: Income loss or unaffordable monthly payments can make loan repayment difficult.
unsureList.best: Borrowers may face difficulty repaying loans for a variety of reasons, including loss of income or monthly payments that exceed the consumer’s ability to pay.

unsureList.text: Maintain strong credit, seek improved loan terms, and quickly repay high-interest debt to reduce debt’s financial impact.
unsureList.best: Borrowers can manage the impact of debt on their finances by maintaining a high credit score, seeking better terms on loans, and repaying high-interest-rate loans (e.g., credit card debt) as quickly as possible.

unsureList.text: Improve credit scores by paying bills promptly, reducing debt, and limiting credit-card use.
unsureList.best: Strategies to improve an individual’s credit score include paying bills on time, paying off existing debt, and minimizing use of credit cards.

unsureList.text: Compare lenders and make down payments to obtain lower loan rates and fees.
unsureList.best: Borrowers can obtain better terms on loans, including lower interest rates and lower fees, by comparing the terms offered by different lenders and by making down payments on major purchases like a home or car. A down payment requires using some income or saved money to pay part of the cost of the purchase.

unsureList.text: Debt management assistance or bankruptcy may help address severe debt, including property seizure or unmanageable repayment obligations.
unsureList.best: Individuals who face negative consequences from unmanageable debt, such as property seizures, may be able to seek debt management assistance. In some cases, borrowers may seek bankruptcy—a legal process that eliminates some debts and helps the borrower set up a repayment plan for other debts.

unsureList.text: Businesses’ transactions affect their assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity.
unsureList.best: Businesses engage in a variety of financial transactions such as buying resources, receiving payment from customers, distributing profits to owners, and saving and borrowing funds. These transactions affect the business’s assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity, which is the value of the business to its owners.

unsureList.text: Consumers’ income, purchases, savings, and borrowing affect assets, liabilities, and net worth.
unsureList.best: Consumers engage in a variety of financial transactions, such as receiving income, buying goods and services, saving, and borrowing, that affect their assets, liabilities, and net worth.

unsureList.text: Businesses record transactions and prepare reports to monitor performance, guide decisions, inform stakeholders, and comply with regulations.
unsureList.best: Businesses record all financial transactions and use this data to prepare reports and financial statements that summarize the business’s financial performance. Financial statements are used to monitor the business’s financial health, guide decision making, provide accurate information to shareholders, investors, and lenders, and ensure compliance with laws and reporting regulations.

unsureList.text: GAAP requires publicly traded corporations to consistently disclose positive and negative financial information.
unsureList.best: 3.3.B Describe the roles of accounting and finance departments in the preparation, reporting, and use of financial information.

unsureList.text: Consumers benefit from organized financial tracking, such as budgeting, even though reporting is usually not required.
unsureList.best: Consumers are not usually required to record or report financial transactions; however, having an organized system, such as a budget, for tracking financial transactions helps consumers monitor their finances and make decisions aligned to their financial goals.

unsureList.text: Managerial accountants analyze information for internal planning and decision making.
unsureList.best: Managerial accountants provide financial information and analysis to managers and other internal stakeholders for the purpose of business planning and decision making.

unsureList.text: Finance departments analyze accounting data and recommend ways to improve financial performance.
unsureList.best: Finance departments are responsible for analyzing the financial data compiled by accounting departments and recommending strategies for maintaining or improving a business’s financial performance.

unsureList.text: Consumers may use financial advisors or accountants for planning, decisions, and tax preparation.
unsureList.best: Consumers may hire financial advisors and/or accountants to help with financial planning and decision making as well as tax preparation.

unsureList.text: One-time expenditures may include legal, incorporation, licensing, and equipment costs.
unsureList.best: One-time expenditures include legal fees, incorporation and licensing fees, and in some cases equipment purchases.

unsureList.text: Initial expenses include occupancy, development, marketing, insurance, and initial inventory costs that later become ongoing.
unsureList.best: A business’s initial expenses include occupancy expense, research and development, marketing, insurance, and the costs associated with production or acquisition of initial inventories. All of these expenses become ongoing once the business begins operation. TOPIC3.4 Business Expenses continued on next page Required Course Content

unsureList.text: Classify recurring costs as fixed or variable based on how they respond to production or service levels.
unsureList.best: 3.4.B.1 Businesses classify their recurring costs as either direct or indirect. Direct costs are tied to the production or delivery of specific goods or services. Indirect costs, also called operating expenses, are the costs associated with running the business.

unsureList.text: COGS includes production materials, supplies, labor, benefits, and manufacturing facility costs.
unsureList.best: Businesses that produce goods incur direct costs called the cost of goods sold (COGS). COGS typically includes the cost of raw materials, production supplies, production- related wages and benefits, and the cost to operate manufacturing facilities. The components of COGS can be either fixed or variable; rent for a factory is fixed, while raw materials costs are variable.

unsureList.text: Service businesses’ direct costs include labor, travel, and materials used to deliver services.
unsureList.best: For businesses that provide services, the direct costs are called cost of sales and include direct labor expenses, travel costs, and any materials associated with delivering the service.

unsureList.text: Operating expenses include occupancy, staff compensation, marketing, supplies, utilities, maintenance, and insurance.
unsureList.best: Businesses face recurring indirect costs, called operating expenses. These costs, which are typically fixed, include occupancy expenses, salaries and benefits for office and sales staff, marketing and advertising costs, supplies, utilities, maintenance, and insurance.

unsureList.text: Insurance protects businesses and consumers from losses, with coverage choices influenced by requirements and risk tolerance.
unsureList.best: Businesses (and consumers) buy insurance to protect against financial losses from accidents, injuries, or property damage. Some types of insurance are required—for example, workers compensation insurance—but many are optional. Businesses (and consumers) vary in their willingness to accept risk and/or pay for insurance to minimize risk.

unsureList.text: Entrepreneurs may fund startups through personal savings, bank loans, or personal credit.
unsureList.best: Many entrepreneurs initially rely on bootstrapping (i.e., using personal savings), personal bank loans, and/or personal credit to fund startup costs.

unsureList.text: Entrepreneurs compare personal funds with startup needs and calculate sales required to break even.
unsureList.best: 3.5.A.3 Entrepreneurs seek external financial capital if they lack the funds required to pay startup costs and operating costs for a sufficient period of time to break even.

unsureList.text: Businesses seek external capital when they cannot cover startup and operating costs until reaching break-even.
unsureList.best: Entrepreneurs seek external financial capital if they lack the funds required to pay startup costs and operating costs for a sufficient period of time to break even.

unsureList.text: Established businesses seek capital for product development, asset replacement, or increased sales and revenue.
unsureList.best: Established businesses seek external financial capital for a variety of reasons, including financing new product development, replacing fixed assets, and increasing sales volume and revenue.

unsureList.text: Businesses seek capital to manage cash flow when revenue collection is irregular but expenses remain due.
unsureList.best: 3.5.A.4 Established businesses seek external financial capital for a variety of reasons, including financing new product development, replacing fixed assets, and increasing sales volume and revenue.

unsureList.text: Most business financing comes through loans or equity financing.
unsureList.best: Most sources of financial capital are classified as loans or equity financing.

unsureList.text: New businesses often use friends’ and family’s loans or sell ownership shares.
unsureList.best: New businesses, typically those in operation for less than two years, often borrow money from the owners’ friends and family or use equity financing by issuing (selling) ownership shares to others, including friends and family or outside investors.

unsureList.text: Corporations can raise funds by issuing bonds or shares of stock.
unsureList.best: Businesses organized as corporations can obtain funds by issuing bonds or shares of stock. A bond represents a loan from an investor to a business. Stock is an ownership share in the business and can be sold privately or publicly. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Describe potential benefits and risks to lenders and investors providing business capital.
unsureList.best: Describe potential benefits and risks to lenders and investors who provide financial capital to businesses.

unsureList.text: Lenders and investors receive financial assets that can be resold in secondary markets.
unsureList.best: In exchange for the financial capital they provide to businesses, lenders and investors obtain financial assets—loans (including bonds) or shares of stock. These assets can be resold in a secondary market.

unsureList.text: Lenders earn interest, including from bonds; corporate bond purchasers become business lenders.
unsureList.best: Lenders receive income from interest payments on loans. A bond pays interest to the bond holder. When an individual consumer buys a corporate bond in the secondary market, they become a lender to the business.

unsureList.text: Stock investors may receive dividends, while corporations may retain earnings instead.
unsureList.best: Investors may receive income from dividends, which represent their share of a business’s profits; however, some corporations reinvest earnings into the business and do not pay dividends. When an individual consumer buys a share of stock in the secondary market, they become an investor (shareholder) in the business.

unsureList.text: Selling an asset above its purchase price produces a capital gain; asset prices respond to several forces.
unsureList.best: If an investor sells an asset at a higher price than they paid for it, they achieve a capital gain. The prices of financial assets such as bonds and stocks change in response to business performance, investor demand, and PESTEL forces.

unsureList.text: Calculate annual investment return by dividing total gains by the asset’s price.
unsureList.best: The annual rate of return on an investment is determined by dividing the total dollars gained (the sum of income and any capital gain) by the price of the asset.

unsureList.text: Poor business performance can cause lenders and investors to lose income, asset value, or invested capital.
unsureList.best: Lenders and investors risk financial loss if a business performs poorly. Lenders risk losses if the business is unable to make interest payments or repay loans. Investors risk lost income (dividends) and decreased stock value if the business’s profits decline, and they may lose their entire financial stake if a business shuts down.

unsureList.text: Risk tolerance differs among funders, and riskier investments generally require higher expected returns.
unsureList.best: Lenders and investors vary in their risk tolerance, which is their willingness to take financial risks. Some consumers and institutional lenders and investors have a high risk tolerance and will provide financial capital to fund risky or unproven ideas, while others are more cautious. Lenders and investors expect a higher rate of return when they invest in riskier assets. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Develop and evaluate funding pitches for prospective lenders or investors.
unsureList.best: Develop and evaluate a pitch to prospective lenders or investors.

unsureList.text: A funding pitch summarizes a business plan, value proposition, market research, strategy, projections, request, return, and risk.
unsureList.best: Lenders and investors often require businesses to provide a business plan that includes their value proposition, market research, marketing strategy, and financial projections to justify a specific funding request, rate of return, and level of risk. A business owner typically develops a polished pitch summarizing this key information to persuade potential lenders and investors to provide their business with capital.

unsureList.text: Funders use reports, projections, and industry data to estimate business valuation and loan repayment capacity.
unsureList.best: When evaluating a funding request from an established business, lenders and investors rely on the business’s financial reports and projections as well as external industry data to estimate the economic valuation of the business. A valuation provides prospective investors with an estimate of what an ownership share is worth and helps lenders assess the business’s capacity to repay a loan.

unsureList.text: Funding proposals improve when they demonstrate product-market fit and support financial projections.
unsureList.best: A funding request is more likely to be successful when the business provides evidence of product-market fit and a basis for its financial projections. Lenders and investors typically prefer funding projects with lower risk and higher projected returns.

unsureList.text: Funders may assess leadership qualifications and alignment between the business mission, value proposition, and their goals.
unsureList.best: In evaluating a request for financial capital, lenders and investors may also consider the qualifications of the business’s leadership team and whether the business’s value proposition and mission align with the funders’ goals. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Identify and explain the components of a business income statement.
unsureList.best: Determine and describe components of a business income statement.

unsureList.text: Revenue is income generated through a business’s primary activities, such as selling goods or services.
unsureList.best: For income statement purposes, revenue is the income generated by a business’s core activities, such as sales of goods and services.

unsureList.text: Gross profit equals revenue minus the direct production costs represented by cost of goods sold.
unsureList.best: Gross profit describes the profit earned after deducting only the direct costs of production; it is calculated by subtracting COGS from revenue.

unsureList.text: Operating expenses are indirect costs, including selling, administrative, and research and development expenses.
unsureList.best: 3.6.A.6 Operating profit is the profit earned after deducting COGS and operating expenses and represents the business’s net income before interest and taxes; it is calculated by subtracting operating expenses from gross profit.

unsureList.text: Operating profit equals gross profit minus operating expenses and shows income before interest and taxes.
unsureList.best: Operating profit is the profit earned after deducting COGS and operating expenses and represents the business’s net income before interest and taxes; it is calculated by subtracting operating expenses from gross profit.

unsureList.text: Net profit equals pretax income minus taxes and represents the owners’ earnings for the period.
unsureList.best: 3.6.A.6 Operating profit is the profit earned after deducting COGS and operating expenses and represents the business’s net income before interest and taxes; it is calculated by subtracting operating expenses from gross profit.

unsureList.text: Stakeholders use income statements to track revenue and cost trends, assess profitability, and guide improvement decisions.
unsureList.best: Income statement information is used by internal and external stakeholders to monitor trends in revenues and costs, evaluate profitability, and inform decisions related to improving future profitability.

unsureList.text: Gross profit margin, gross profit divided by revenue, assesses pricing and management of direct costs.
unsureList.best: Gross profit margin, which is calculated as gross profit divided by total revenue, is used to evaluate how successfully a business is setting prices and managing its direct costs.

unsureList.text: Operating profit margin assesses marketing, sales, administration, and control of operating expenses.
unsureList.best: Operating profit margin, which is calculated as operating profit divided by total revenue, is used to evaluate how successfully a business is marketing and selling its product(s), administering the activities of the business, and controlling operating expenses.

unsureList.text: Businesses compare profit margins with forecasts, historical results, and competitors to judge performance.
unsureList.best: Gross profit margin, operating profit margin, and net profit margin are typically benchmarked against projections, past performance, and performance by competitors as a means of determining whether the business’s financial performance is meeting expectations.

unsureList.text: Use percentage change to calculate rates of change in income, costs, profits, or margins.
unsureList.best: Businesses use the percentage change equation to determine the rate of change for any data point. For example, a business evaluating financial performance may calculate the rate of change in its income, cost, profit, or profit margin. Percent change = [(Current Value – Initial Value) / Initial Value] x 100. continued on next page

unsureList.text: Changing needs, wants, competition, and external forces create financial uncertainty; planning supports financial goals.
unsureList.best: Businesses and consumers face financial uncertainty because incomes and expenses fluctuate in response to changing needs and wants, competitive pressure within markets, and PESTEL forces. Thoughtful planning can help both businesses and consumers meet financial goals.

unsureList.text: Businesses use projected income statements and budgets to estimate revenues, expenses, and profit or loss.
unsureList.best: Businesses develop projected income statements and/or budgets to plan for revenues, costs, and resulting profit/loss for a period (e.g., a month, a quarter, or a year). Projected income statements and budgets describe estimates of all expenses involved in running the business and predicted revenues, given projected production and sales levels.

unsureList.text: Business budgets help anticipate costs, identify funding requirements, and maintain cash for obligations.
unsureList.best: Projected income statements and budgets help businesses plan for expected costs, identify funding needs, and maintain enough cash to meet current obligations.

unsureList.text: Consumer budgets allocate expected after-tax income among savings, expenses, and debt payments.
unsureList.best: Consumers use budgets to plan saving and spending allocations based on expected income. A consumer budget describes expected net pay (income after taxes and other deductions) for a period, typically a month or a year, and all planned savings and expenses including debt payments.

unsureList.text: Budgets reveal spending habits and help consumers manage debt, save, and support charitable causes while pursuing goals.
unsureList.best: Budgets help consumers identify spending patterns and assess whether they are meeting their financial goals, including managing debt, saving for future expenses, and donating to charitable organizations whose missions they support.

unsureList.text: Use recorded revenues, expenses, and taxes to prepare an income statement.
unsureList.best: Businesses use current financial data tracking revenues, expenses, and taxes to develop income statements.

unsureList.text: Forecast revenues, expenses, and taxes to prepare a projected income statement.
unsureList.best: Businesses predict future revenues and expenses (and estimated taxes) to develop projected income statements.

unsureList.text: Estimate future revenue using pricing plans, customer-demand research, and industry trends.
unsureList.best: Future revenues are estimated based on planned pricing strategies and market research about customer demand and industry trends.

unsureList.text: Estimate COGS and operating expenses from production plans, supply-chain costs, and anticipated business expenses.
unsureList.best: Future COGS and operating expenses are estimated based on planned production processes, the cost of supply chain components, and other projected expenses, such as occupancy expenses, marketing expenses, office and sales salaries, and planned research and development.

unsureList.text: Identify and explain the components of a business balance sheet.
unsureList.best: Determine and describe components of a business balance sheet.

unsureList.text: Balance-sheet assets are grouped by liquidity as current, long-term, or intangible assets.
unsureList.best: The assets listed on a balance sheet include every item of value owned by a business, grouped according to liquidity into current assets, long-term assets, and intangible assets.

unsureList.text: Liabilities are business obligations classified as current or long-term according to when payment is due.
unsureList.best: The liabilities listed on a balance sheet represent debts or obligations owed by a business, grouped into current and long-term liabilities, in order of when payment is due.

unsureList.text: Owners’ equity equals assets minus liabilities and commonly includes stock and retained earnings.
unsureList.best: Owners’ equity—the net worth of a business— is the difference between assets and liabilities. Owners’ equity is often comprised of stock and retained earnings, which are the business’s cumulative profits not paid out as dividends.

unsureList.text: Balance sheets commonly compare current financial data with figures from earlier periods.
unsureList.best: 3.7.B.1 Internal stakeholders, such as business managers and owners, as well as external stakeholders, such as lenders and investors, use balance sheets to evaluate the financial condition of a business at a point in time (e.g., the end of a year or quarter).

unsureList.text: Managers, owners, lenders, and investors use balance sheets to assess financial condition at a particular time.
unsureList.best: Internal stakeholders, such as business managers and owners, as well as external stakeholders, such as lenders and investors, use balance sheets to evaluate the financial condition of a business at a point in time (e.g., the end of a year or quarter).

unsureList.text: A balance sheet shows net worth, working-capital sufficiency, and whether debt is reasonable compared with similar businesses.
unsureList.best: A balance sheet indicates whether a business has a positive net worth, whether it has sufficient working capital to fund day-to-day operations (current assets meet or exceed current liabilities), and whether its debt level is comparable to similar businesses.

unsureList.text: Insufficient current assets may cause shutdown or bankruptcy, a legal process for liquidation, repayment, or reorganization.
unsureList.best: Business owners may shut down a business or pursue bankruptcy if the business cannot access sufficient current assets to fund operations. Bankruptcy is a legal process through which a business can liquidate assets, eliminate or repay debts, and either shut down or reorganize the business under legal supervision.

unsureList.text: Describe why people determine personal net worth.
unsureList.best: Describe the purpose of determining personal net worth. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Household net worth equals all assets, including savings, investments, property, and possessions, minus liabilities.
unsureList.best: Personal net worth is typically calculated for a household, which may include more than one individual. Net worth is determined by adding all of the household’s assets, including savings and investments, property, and personal possessions, and subtracting all liabilities.

unsureList.text: Lenders may request household net-worth information during a consumer loan application.
unsureList.best: Lenders may require information about a consumer’s household net worth as part of the loan application process.

unsureList.text: Consumers and financial planners use net worth to assess retirement savings sufficiency.
unsureList.best: Consumers and financial planners consider net worth when determining whether individuals have sufficient savings to retire.

unsureList.text: Identify and explain the components of a business cash-flow statement.
unsureList.best: Determine and describe components of a business’s cash flow statement.

unsureList.text: A cash-flow statement shows how cash inflows and outflows change the cash balance during a reporting period.
unsureList.best: A cash flow statement is a financial statement used by businesses to show how cash inflows and outflows impact a business’s cash balance over the course of a financial reporting period.

unsureList.text: Businesses monitor cash balances to pay regular expenses, lenders, and unexpected costs.
unsureList.best: Businesses closely monitor cash balances to ensure there is sufficient cash available to pay recurring expenses (e.g., payroll and rent), repay lenders, and manage unforeseen expenses.

unsureList.text: Cash inflows include customer payments, investment returns, asset sales, and new financial capital.
unsureList.best: Cash inflows increase a business’s cash balance and typically include payments from customers, interest or dividends earned on investment assets, proceeds received from the sales of a business’s assets, and/or infusions of financial capital, such as money raised by taking out a new loan.

unsureList.text: Cash outflows include payments to workers and suppliers, interest, taxes, asset purchases, debt repayment, and dividends.
unsureList.best: Cash outflows decrease a business’s cash balance and typically include payments to employees and suppliers, interest expense paid on existing loans, taxes paid to the government, money spent to purchase assets, money spent on debt repayment, and dividends.

unsureList.text: A business can end a reporting period with either positive or negative cash flow.
unsureList.best: A business’s cash flow may be positive or negative at the end of a period. BUSINESSCASE Students explore how a nonprofit identifies and addresses an annual operating deficit and an ongoing cash flow challenge.

unsureList.text: Stakeholders use cash flow to judge whether a business can meet obligations to employees, suppliers, creditors, and shareholders.
unsureList.best: The cash flow statement is used to assess a business’s ability to meet its financial obligations, including its ability to pay its employees, suppliers, creditors, and shareholders.

unsureList.text: Negative cash flow can threaten operations despite positive income; businesses may raise funds, collect receivables, or negotiate supplier terms.
unsureList.best: Negative cash flow may signal that a business is unable to pay its current expenses, which could lead to shut down or bankruptcy even if net income is positive. In such a situation, the business may need to raise more funds, collect accounts receivable faster, or obtain better terms from suppliers and lenders to continue operating.

unsureList.text: Explain why individuals or businesses may have incentives to use unethical financial management or reporting practices.
unsureList.best: Explain why an individual or a business might be incentivized to engage in unethical financial management and reporting practices.

unsureList.best: Unethical practices in finance include misuse of funds, tax evasion, embezzlement, bribery, lack of transparency, and fraud, which can include falsifying information on financial statements.

unsureList.text: Explain how access to substantial business cash can tempt individuals to steal funds, misuse money, or falsify information.
unsureList.best: Access to large sums of a business’s cash creates a situation where individuals may seek to embezzle, misuse funds, or falsify information for personal gain.

unsureList.text: Explain how misrepresenting financial conditions can affect stock prices, loan terms, or tax obligations.
unsureList.best: A business or its financial managers may be able to influence stock prices, secure better terms on loans, or avoid taxes by portraying its financial situation to stakeholders and to the government as better or worse than it really is.

unsureList.text: Explain how laws and professional standards promote ethical conduct among accounting and financial professionals.
unsureList.best: Explain how laws and professional codes of conduct encourage ethical behavior by accounting and financial managers.

unsureList.text: Identify financial misconduct that is generally illegal, while recognizing that laws and penalties differ across countries.
unsureList.best: Misusing funds, tax evasion, embezzlement, bribery, and fraud are illegal in most countries, but laws and punishments vary from country to country.

Financial market regulations are designed to ensure that investors have access to accurate information and are protected from fraud. unsureList.best: Many businesses develop internal mechanisms, such as codes of conduct, audit requirements, and cash-handling processes, to prevent unethical behavior. LEARNING OBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe management as coordinating resources and activities to achieve business goals.
unsureList.best: 4.1.A.1 Management is the process of planning, organizing, leading, and evaluating a business’s employment of human, financial, and physical resources to meet the business’s goals and objectives.

unsureList.text: Management plans, organizes, leads, and evaluates human, financial, and physical resources to meet objectives.
unsureList.best: Management is the process of planning, organizing, leading, and evaluating a business’s employment of human, financial, and physical resources to meet the business’s goals and objectives.

unsureList.text: Managers at every organizational level make decisions and lead business activities.
unsureList.best: 4.1.A.3 Managers who lead specialized departments in a business are responsible for coordinating the activities of employees to ensure that their work is aligned to the business’s vision and mission.

unsureList.text: Department managers coordinate employees’ work so it supports the business vision and mission.
unsureList.best: Managers who lead specialized departments in a business are responsible for coordinating the activities of employees to ensure that their work is aligned to the business’s vision and mission.

unsureList.text: Identify and demonstrate effective leadership and business communication abilities.
unsureList.best: Identify and demonstrate effective leadership and business communication skills.

unsureList.text: Effective leaders communicate and collaborate with supervisors, employees, customers, investors, lenders, and other stakeholders.
unsureList.best: Leadership and communication skills are valued in business because leaders and managers need to collaborate and communicate effectively with a wide variety of stakeholders, including supervisors, colleagues, employees, lenders, investors, customers, and the public.

unsureList.text: Leadership includes expressing vision, building teams, resolving conflict, and motivating people.
unsureList.best: 4.1.A.2 Management includes the decisions, actions, and leadership of managers at all levels of a business, from executive leaders to supervisors.

unsureList.text: Strong communication involves clarity, persuasion, empathetic listening, and appropriately responding to feedback.
unsureList.best: Key communication skills for leaders, managers, and employees include expressing ideas clearly, communicating persuasively, listening empathetically, and correctly interpreting and responding to feedback.

unsureList.text: Businesses employ people to produce goods, serve customers, market, sell, and manage finances.
unsureList.best: Business leaders and managers hire employees to do the day-to-day work of a business; for example, producing and providing products, marketing to customers, making sales, and managing finances.

unsureList.text: Businesses need diverse skills and backgrounds for different tasks, while outsourcing work outside their core activities.
unsureList.best: Businesses need employees with a variety of core competencies, experiences, and backgrounds because of the different types of tasks to be done, although some tasks may be outsourced, especially if they are outside the business’s core competencies and/or operating activities.

unsureList.text: Skilled, trained employees support product quality, customer service, reputation, revenue, and business viability.
unsureList.best: Hiring and/or developing skilled employees is essential to business viability because employees who lack skills or adequate training may create flawed products or provide poor service, which can cause the business to lose customers, brand reputation, and revenue. Some skills or attributes may be rare or require extensive training.

unsureList.text: Employee development can involve college, apprenticeships, workplace instruction, online courses, and continuing education.
unsureList.best: Employee training may include postsecondary education, apprentice programs, on-the- job training, online training, and continuing education.

unsureList.text: Explain how businesses compensate, motivate, and retain capable employees.
unsureList.best: Explain how businesses compensate, motivate, and seek to retain high-quality employees.

unsureList.text: Businesses may hire full-time, part-time, temporary, or contract workers.
unsureList.best: Businesses hire some employees to work full time, while others are hired as part-time, temporary, or contract employees.

unsureList.text: Compensation may use wages, salaries, commissions, piece rates, or profit sharing, depending on role, law, industry, and competition.
unsureList.best: Employees may be paid using a variety of compensation schemes such as hourly wage, annual salary, commission, piece rate pay, or profit sharing. The type of compensation depends on the industry, the employee role, legal guidelines (e.g., minimum wage), and the degree to which businesses must outbid rivals to secure high-quality employees.

unsureList.text: Employers generally set pay by considering education, skills, and productivity.
unsureList.best: Employers generally determine compensation by evaluating factors like education, skills, and productivity.

unsureList.text: Benefits may include health coverage, retirement plans, health savings accounts, disability insurance, education reimbursement, and paid leave.
unsureList.best: Employee compensation may include benefits such as contributions to health insurance, retirement savings plans, health savings plans, disability insurance, educational reimbursement programs, and paid time off.

unsureList.text: Raises, promotions, bonuses, autonomy, flexibility, recognition, and workplace culture can motivate and retain employees.
unsureList.best: Many businesses use incentives, like raises, promotions, or bonuses, to motivate and retain employees because it is typically more cost- effective to keep high-quality employees than to recruit and train new ones. Businesses may also seek to motivate and retain employees by providing them autonomy, flexible work hours or locations, recognition and rewards, flexible scheduling, and a positive workplace culture.

unsureList.text: A KPI is a measured data point showing performance, goal progress, or strategy effectiveness.
unsureList.best: A key performance indicator (KPI) is a data point used to measure a business’s performance, including progress toward short- and long-term goals and the effectiveness of strategy.

unsureList.text: Managers choose KPIs connected to mission, goals, profitability, competitiveness, viability, and industry characteristics.
unsureList.best: Managers select KPIs that relate to their stated mission and goals, profitability, and their ability to remain competitive and viable in the long term. KPIs vary based on the characteristics of the business and the industry in which it operates.

unsureList.text: Develop or interpret financial and nonfinancial KPIs to track financial health and goal progress.
unsureList.best: 4.2.B.1 Develop or interpret financial and nonfinancial KPIs to monitor a business’s financial health and progress toward goals. Businesses monitor financial health using a variety of KPIs, such as revenue, gross profit, gross profit margin, operating profit, operating profit margin, COGS, operating expenses, and cash flow.

unsureList.text: Financial-health KPIs include revenue, profit, margins, costs, expenses, and cash flow.
unsureList.best: 4.2.B 4.2.B.1 Develop or interpret financial and nonfinancial KPIs to monitor a business’s financial health and progress toward goals. Businesses monitor financial health using a variety of KPIs, such as revenue, gross profit, gross profit margin, operating profit, operating profit margin, COGS, operating expenses, and cash flow.

unsureList.text: Operations KPIs include unit cost, delivery cost, order accuracy, and on-time delivery rates.
unsureList.best: Businesses measure progress toward operations goals using a variety of KPIs, such as per-unit cost, delivery cost, order accuracy, and percentage of deliveries received on time.

unsureList.text: A benchmark is a comparison standard based on historical company data or industry performance.
unsureList.best: A benchmark is a reference point used to compare data to a standard. Businesses may base benchmarks on internal historical data or external industry standards.

unsureList.text: Businesses compare KPI results with benchmarks to evaluate performance against a recognized standard.
unsureList.best: Businesses compare KPI data to selected benchmarks to assess performance against a known standard.

unsureList.text: Explain how and why businesses create and use strategies to accomplish goals.
unsureList.best: Explain how and why businesses develop and use strategy to achieve goals.

unsureList.text: A strategy outlines how a business will pursue goals such as advantage, mission fulfillment, revenue, cost reduction, or profit.
unsureList.best: A strategy is a plan or approach to achieving a goal. Business strategy describes how a business will achieve one or more goals, such as achieving competitive advantage, fulfilling the business’s mission, increasing revenues, reducing costs, or increasing profits. Businesses pursue differing strategies based on their unique capabilities, their competitive landscape, and their industry.

unsureList.text: Businesses collect and monitor financial, customer, competitor, and market-trend data to create and adjust strategies.
unsureList.best: Businesses typically identify, gather, and track specific data to define a strategy, evaluate the effectiveness of the strategy, and modify the strategy. This data often includes information about a business’s financial performance, customers, competitors, or broader trends in the business’s market.

unsureList.text: A clear strategy aligns resources toward goals or challenges, improving the likelihood of success.
unsureList.best: Defining a clear strategy facilitates the mobilization and alignment of resources to meet an articulated goal or address a challenge, thus increasing the likelihood of success.

unsureList.text: Strategy directs decisions and tactics, which are actions intended to advance strategic goals.
unsureList.best: Businesses use strategy to guide decision making and the development of tactics, which are actions or approaches intended to advance the strategy.
