The longer and more complex a password is, the longer it will take a digital tool to crack the password.

unsureList.text: Minimum password length requirements make passwords harder and more time-consuming for digital tools to crack.

unsureList.text: Password-history settings prevent reuse by storing hashes of users’ previous passwords.

unsureList.best: Anti-malware software (sometimes called antivirus software) has tools to quarantine and remove malware that can corrupt, spy on, or destroy a system. Malware contains indicators that make it detectable; these indicators are called signatures.

unsureList.text: Select detection methods based on device performance and available processing and memory resources.
unsureList.best: Performance is a criterion for determining a detection method. Detection tools use system memory and processing power and can impact the performance of a device. Anomaly-based detection tools use more system resources than signature-based tools. Signature-based detection is a better option for devices with less powerful system resources. Many embedded devices do not have enough system resources to run any detection tools on the device.

unsureList.text: Select stronger or hybrid detection for devices handling sensitive information or critical services.

Devices that store or process sensitive information or provide critical services are more likely to be targeted by adversaries and benefit from a hybrid-detection model to offer maximum protection, when possible.

unsureList.text: Evaluate detection speed and resource demands, recognizing that intensive tools can reduce device performance.
unsureList.best: Speed and performance are factors in evaluating the impact of a detection method. Signature-based detection is faster than anomaly-based detection in general, and that effect is compounded on devices, which often lack the processing power to effectively run anomaly-based detection tools. Implementing resource-intensive detection tools on devices can degrade device performance.

unsureList.text: Evaluate detection based on attack stage and the benefits of stopping threats at the device layer.
unsureList.best: Phase of the attack is a factor in evaluating the impact of a detection method. To carry out actions on a device, adversaries must first bypass a combination of physical- or network- layer protective, deterrent, and detective security controls. Detecting and stopping an attack at the device level can prevent adversaries from accessing sensitive data or disrupting critical services.

unsureList.text: Balance false-positive rates against how easily adversaries can evade a detection method.
unsureList.best: 4.4.B.3 Sensitivity or criticality of the device is a criterion for determining a detection method. Devices that store or process sensitive information or provide critical services are more likely to be targeted by adversaries and benefit from a hybrid-detection model to offer maximum protection, when possible.

unsureList.text: Use authentication logs to identify online password attacks and respond to compromised password databases.
unsureList.best: Online password attacks can be detected in authentication logs. A single user attempting many wrong passwords is an indicator of an online password attack. If a user:password hash database has been compromised, all the user passwords in the database should be considered insecure and all users should be forced to reset their passwords.

unsureList.text: Recognize unexpected login locations, addresses, or times as possible evidence of password compromise.
unsureList.best: 4.4.D.3 An indicator of password spraying is many users trying to log in within seconds of each other from one IP address or from unusual IP addresses.

unsureList.text: Recognize password spraying through rapid login attempts against many users from one or unusual addresses.
unsureList.best: An indicator of password spraying is many users trying to log in within seconds of each other from one IP address or from unusual IP addresses.

unsureList.text: Recognize credential stuffing through rapid attempts using default username-password combinations, often from one address.
unsureList.best: An indicator of credential stuffing is a series of default user:password combinations being attempted on a device in quick succession, often from the same IP address.

unsureList.text: Explain that offline password attacks cannot be detected because they occur on the adversary’s computer.
unsureList.best: Offline password attacks can’t be detected, because the attack takes place on the adversary’s computer. AP Cybersecurity · Course Framework return to contents 113

unsureList.text: Explain how application attacks take advantage of software vulnerabilities.
unsureList.best: Explain how application attacks exploit vulnerabilities.

unsureList.text: Assess and record risks created by application and data vulnerabilities.
unsureList.best: Assess and document risks from application and data vulnerabilities.

unsureList.text: Recognize that anyone accessing a device or storage drive can read files that are not encrypted.
unsureList.best: An adversary can read any unencrypted files if they have access to the device or drive storing the files.

unsureList.text: Distinguish standard and administrative users, and explain how compromised administrative accounts provide elevated system access.
unsureList.best: Computers have standard users and administrative users. Administrative users have access to control system settings and can typically access any files or applications on a system. If regular users are given administrative privileges on a computer, and an adversary can compromise a user’s account, then the adversary will have elevated privileges on the system.

unsureList.text: Explain how weak permissions let adversaries view, change, steal, destroy files, or disrupt applications.
unsureList.best: When access control settings are weakly configured, many users often have permission to view and sometimes even edit files on a system. Adversaries can take advantage of weak access control settings to steal or destroy files or disrupt an application.

unsureList.text: Describe applications as executable programs that may run locally or on servers accessed over networks.
unsureList.best: Applications are programs that run instructions on computers; they are executable data. Some applications run locally on a user’s computer, while other applications, like web applications, run on a server and are accessed by users through a network. SUGGESTEDSKILLS

unsureList.text: Explain data validation and how accepting unexpected input enables injection attacks.
unsureList.best: 5.1.B Explain how application attacks exploit vulnerabilities.

unsureList.text: Explain SQL’s role in querying and changing databases, and why unvalidated input creates vulnerabilities.
unsureList.best: Structured query language (SQL) is a computer language used to request information from databases and make changes to databases or entries in databases. Applications that query a database using unvalidated or unsanitized input from users are vulnerable.

unsureList.text: Describe how SQL injection can expose, alter, or delete database information.
unsureList.best: 5.1.B.3 Structured query language (SQL) is a computer language used to request information from databases and make changes to databases or entries in databases. Applications that query a database using unvalidated or unsanitized input from users are vulnerable.

unsureList.text: Explain how browser-executed JavaScript may access sensitive information stored in a browser.
unsureList.best: Websites are written using hypertext markup language (HTML), and many websites use Javascript to create dynamic content on websites or web applications. Because Javascript commands run in the browser of the user visiting the website, those commands can access sensitive data stored in the browser like usernames, passwords, and cryptographic keys.

unsureList.text: Distinguish reflected and stored XSS, in which injected browser code affects one or many visitors.
unsureList.best: A cross site scripting (XSS) attack injects malicious code into a website that a user’s browser then executes. The malicious code can be embedded in a link the user clicks (a Type I or Reflected XSS attack) or it can be inserted onto a website through a comment field, forum post, or visitor log, which would affect any user visiting that website (a Type II or Stored XSS attack).

unsureList.text: Explain that buffers have fixed memory capacity and excess input can overwrite neighboring memory.
unsureList.best: When applications take user input, that input is written to a buffer. A buffer is a designated section of computer memory with a fixed size. If the amount of data the user enters exceeds the size of the buffer, it can overflow into adjacent memory locations and overwrite other parts of the computer’s memory.

unsureList.text: Describe how buffer overflows can crash systems or enable unauthorized code execution and file access.
unsureList.best: A buffer overflow attack feeds more data into memory than was allotted, which can cause a system to crash or to execute code outside the scope of a program’s security policy, effectively allowing the adversary to perform unauthorized actions on a computer, such as accessing, modifying, or deleting files.

unsureList.text: Explain that web application files reside in server directories and HTTP GET requests retrieve them.
unsureList.best: The files that run web applications are stored in directories on servers. When users access web applications, their browsers send GET requests using hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP). A GET request accesses a file somewhere in the filesystem of the server.

unsureList.text: Describe directory traversal, in which altered URLs or requests seek sensitive files outside an intended directory.
unsureList.best: 5.1.C.1 Data security risks can involve a compromise of confidentiality when unauthorized persons can access sensitive data, integrity when data can be manipulated or altered from its intended state, and availability when data can be destroyed or encrypted to prevent others from accessing it.

unsureList.text: Assess confidentiality, integrity, and availability risks from unauthorized access, alteration, destruction, or encryption of data.
unsureList.best: Data security risks can involve a compromise of confidentiality when unauthorized persons can access sensitive data, integrity when data can be manipulated or altered from its intended state, and availability when data can be destroyed or encrypted to prevent others from accessing it.

unsureList.text: Identify high risk when highly sensitive data faces a likely successful exploit.
unsureList.best: High risks from data vulnerabilities often involve highly sensitive data (e.g., data that is governed by laws or regulations) that could be compromised through a highly likely exploit. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE The company developing the next jet engine that will be used by the Air Force in its planes is storing the technical specifications for the engine on an unencrypted drive.

unsureList.text: Identify moderate risk when sensitive data lacks sufficiently strong encryption or access restrictions.
unsureList.best: Moderate risks from data vulnerabilities often involve sensitive data not having strong enough encryption or strict enough access controls. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE A company stores its customers’ PII in a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet is encrypted using a small key.

unsureList.text: Identify low risk when less sensitive data has relatively weak encryption or access controls.
unsureList.best: Low risks from data vulnerabilities often involve less sensitive information being encrypted with shorter keys or having access controls that are not strict enough. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE An organization’s CEO stores his private memos to his executive staff on a company share drive that is unencrypted and has no access controls.

unsureList.text: Choose an access control model appropriate for protecting applications and data.
unsureList.best: Determine an appropriate access control model to protect applications and data.

unsureList.text: Set permissions controlling access to files and directories on a Linux system.
unsureList.best: Configure access control settings on a Linux-based system. 5A Protecting Sensitive Data § Configure access control settings for directories and files.

unsureList.text: Explain that organizations use controls to meet legal requirements for collected, stored, processed, and transmitted data.
unsureList.best: Organizations implement specific security controls to comply with legal requirements based on the types of data they collect, store, process, and transmit.

unsureList.text: Distinguish data at rest, in transit, and in use, along with suitable protections for each state.
unsureList.best: 5.2.A Explain how the state or classification of data impacts the type and degree of security applied to that data.

unsureList.text: Explain why organizations apply stronger protection to data classified as more sensitive.
unsureList.best: Organizations often categorize data according to their sensitivity and prioritize a higher degree of security for more sensitive information.

unsureList.text: Explain that laws and regulations prescribe how certain data must be stored, transmitted, and handled.
unsureList.best: Laws and regulations can require certain types of data to be stored, transmitted, and handled according to specific rules. SUGGESTEDSKILLS

unsureList.text: Explain that regulated data must be labeled and managed according to applicable legal or regulatory requirements.
unsureList.best: Organizations that collect regulated data will label them and have policies that comply with the legal or regulatory requirements for the safe storage, transmission, and handling of these data.

unsureList.text: Describe how a cryptography policy specifies approved algorithms, key sizes, generation procedures, and storage requirements.
unsureList.best: A cryptography policy will describe the acceptable encryption protocols and key parameters for an organization and may include: § A list of encryption algorithms approved for specific uses § Minimum or maximum key lengths § Cryptographic key-generation requirements and parameters § Cryptographic key-storage requirements

unsureList.text: Describe what a web application security policy may require for vulnerability testing and remediation.
unsureList.best: A web application security policy will outline the requirements and parameters for testing and mitigating web application vulnerabilities in an organization, and it may include: § Parameters for when an application is subject to a security assessment § Timelines for remediating vulnerabilities based on level of risk § Parameters for how an application security assessment is to be carried out (e.g., using specific tools or according to specific frameworks)

unsureList.text: Explain how access control regulates subjects’ operations on protected objects.
unsureList.best: Access control enforces which users or applications (called subjects) can access, modify, add, or remove (called operations) which files or applications (called objects). Access control models describe how to determine which subjects have what type of access to which objects.

unsureList.text: Explain how role-based access control assigns permissions according to subjects’ roles.
unsureList.best: Role-based access control (RBAC) assigns every subject to a role and defines which roles have which types of access to which objects. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE An example of a role at a company might be “accountant,” and one type of object could be the payroll software. Role-based access could be used to ensure that only subjects who are assigned to the role of “accountant” have access to the payroll software object.

unsureList.text: Explain how rule-based access control uses rules to allow or deny specific access.
unsureList.best: 5.2.C.5 Mandatory access control (MAC) follows strict rules for which types of access each subject level has for objects that are above their level, at their level, or below their level. Subject and object levels are assigned by an external administrator.

unsureList.text: Explain how discretionary access control lets object owners assign permissions, with administrators able to override them.
unsureList.best: Discretionary access control (DAC) gives individual subjects the ability to set the type of access that other subjects have on objects they own. In DAC models some subjects are designated as administrators or super users, and they have the ability to override the access controls established by other subjects. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE Bob creates a file (an object) and decides to give Alice permission to edit the file, to give Frank permission to view the file only, and to deny everyone else access to the file altogether.

unsureList.text: Explain how mandatory access control assigns externally administered access levels and enforces strict rules.
unsureList.best: Mandatory access control (MAC) follows strict rules for which types of access each subject level has for objects that are above their level, at their level, or below their level. Subject and object levels are assigned by an external administrator.

unsureList.text: Explain Bell-LaPadula’s rules: subjects cannot read above their level or write below it.
unsureList.best: The Bell-LaPadula model is a MAC model that is often used by governments and military organizations to control the security of information. This model has the following two important properties: i. The Simple Security Property states that subjects may not read objects that are above their level. ii. The * (Star) Security Property states that subjects may not write to objects below their level. These rules taken together are often summarized as “write up, read down” (WURD).

unsureList.text: Apply least privilege by granting entities only the access necessary for their functions.
unsureList.best: The principle of least privilege is the idea that entities should be given exactly as much access as they need to perform their function and no more.

unsureList.text: Explain authorization as granting an entity permission for a specified type of resource access.
unsureList.best: Authorization is when an entity is granted permission to have a certain type of access to a resource. Access controls are put in place to control which users have what types of access to which data.

unsureList.text: Distinguish Linux file permissions: read, write, and execute, represented as r, w, and x.
unsureList.best: There are three types of access to a file in Linux that can be set, and they always come in the following order: i. Read access allows a user to view the contents of a file. ii. Write access allows a user to make changes to a file. iii. Execute access allows a user to run a binary file such as a program. Theseareabbreviatedrwx,respectively.Ifa useronlyhasreadandexecutepermissions (notwrite),thenitwoulddisplayasr-x.The- symbolindicatestheabsenceofthatpermission.

unsureList.text: Identify Linux permission categories in order: owner, group, and other users.
unsureList.best: the file owner, (2) the file group, and (3) all other users. The three sets are displayed with no spaces (e.g., rwxrwxrwx ).

unsureList.text: Use ls -l to view file permissions and getfacl to inspect additional permissions.
unsureList.best: To view the current permission settings for a file, use the command ls -l, which will show the current settings for the default entities. If there is a + symbol at the end of the permissions, this means that other permissions have been set for that file and it can be viewed with the getfacl command.

unsureList.text: Use chmod’s numeric or symbolic syntax to change Linux file permissions.
unsureList.best: To modify the permission settings for a file, use the chmod command. This command can be used with the numeric method or the symbolic method.

unsureList.text: Use numeric chmod values to assign read, write, and execute permissions to owner, group, and others.
unsureList.best: To use chmod in the numeric method the syntax is chmod ### filename. Each of the three ### represents one of the three entities mentioned above (the owner, the group, other nongroup users). § The first # = the owner § The second # = the group § The third # = other nongroup users The permission for each entity is determined by adding up the values for the types of access to be granted: § 0 = no permissions § 1 = execute § 2 = write § 4 = read

unsureList.text: Use symbolic chmod notation to add or remove permissions for selected user categories.
unsureList.best: Securing Applications and Data UNIT

unsureList.text: Describe cryptography, encryption, decryption, and cryptographic algorithms.
unsureList.best: The purpose of cryptography is to hide information. A cryptographic algorithm defines a process for encrypting and decrypting information. Encryption is the process of hiding the information, and decryption is the process of reversing the encryption to retrieve the original information.

unsureList.text: Explain how encryption combines plaintext with a key to produce ciphertext.
unsureList.best: An encryption algorithm defines a process for combining the information to be encrypted with a predefined key. The information to be encrypted is called the plaintext. The output of the encryption algorithm is called the ciphertext.

unsureList.text: Explain that larger keyspaces make randomly discovering encryption keys more difficult.
unsureList.best: The number of possible keys that can be used in an encryption algorithm is called the keyspace. The larger the keyspace, the longer it will take an adversary to discover the correct key by random chance.

unsureList.text: Use command-line, specialized, or web tools to perform symmetric encryption and decryption.
unsureList.best: Symmetric encryption and decryption can be performed using the command line, specialized software, or web-based tools. § On a command line interface, users can encrypt or decrypt with OpenSSL. § Specialized software like AES Crypt is an open source tool that can encrypt and decrypt files. § There are many web-based tools for encrypting and decrypting files.

unsureList.text: Use OpenSSL commands to encrypt and decrypt files with AES.
unsureList.best: 5.3.B.3 Symmetric encryption and decryption can be performed using the command line, specialized software, or web-based tools. § On a command line interface, users can encrypt or decrypt with OpenSSL. § Specialized software like AES Crypt is an open source tool that can encrypt and decrypt files. § There are many web-based tools for encrypting and decrypting files.

unsureList.text: Distinguish symmetric encryption using one key from asymmetric encryption using two keys.
unsureList.best: Cryptographic algorithms are classified by whether they use one key or two keys. § Symmetric encryption algorithms use the same key to encrypt and decrypt information. § Asymmetric encryption algorithms use two different keys—one to encrypt information and the other to decrypt information. SUGGESTEDSKILLS

unsureList.text: Differentiate block encryption, which processes fixed-size chunks, from stream encryption, which processes data continuously.
unsureList.best: Cryptographic algorithms are also classified by whether they process information one bit at a time or in fixed-size chunks of bits. § Block encryption handles information in fixed-size chunks called blocks, producing an output block for each input block. § Stream encryption handles input information continuously, producing output one element at a time.

unsureList.text: Identify AES as a widely used symmetric encryption algorithm for securing various data and communications.
unsureList.best: Computer-based encryption algorithms operate on binary data. The most common symmetric encryption algorithm is the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). AES encryption is used to secure Wi- Fi transmissions, internet browsing, file encryption on disks, and hardware-level encryption on processors.

unsureList.text: Explain that AES uses 128-bit blocks and that longer keys improve security but increase processing time.
unsureList.best: AES is a symmetric key block cipher that encrypts data in 128-bit blocks (16 bytes). AES can operate with keys of varying lengths. Longer keys produce more secure encryption but require more time to encrypt and decrypt.

unsureList.text: Explain how asymmetric encryption enables secure communication without a prearranged shared secret.
unsureList.best: Asymmetric encryption allows users to communicate securely without prearranging a shared secret key.

unsureList.text: Describe public and private key pairs, their inverse relationship, and their encryption and decryption roles.
unsureList.best: 5.4.A.3 Once the receiver generates the key pair, the private key must be stored securely. If the private key is exposed, shared, stolen, corrupted, or compromised the key pair must be deleted and a new key pair must be generated, because the security of the encryption algorithm rests on the security of the private key. The public key is published for anyone to view and use.

unsureList.text: Explain that senders encrypt data with recipients’ public keys, which recipients decrypt using private keys.
unsureList.best: 5.4.A.2 When using asymmetric encryption, each entity that will be receiving data must first generate a key pair. Key pairs are binary strings of equal length that are generated at the same time through a mathematical process. One key is designated as the public key and the other as the private key. The keys are mathematical inverses of each other— each key reverses its partner. Either key can be used to encrypt information, but only the other key in the key pair will then be able to decrypt it.

unsureList.text: Explain how key length affects encrypted-data security.
unsureList.best: Explain why the length of a key impacts the security of encrypted data.

unsureList.text: Explain that an n-bit key has a keyspace of 2ⁿ and that longer keys provide more possibilities.
unsureList.best: Longer keys result in larger keyspaces. For binary keys, ann-bit length key has a keyspace of2n.

unsureList.text: Calculate the average guesses needed to discover an n-bit key by random guessing.
unsureList.best: Using an application to randomly guess an n-bit length encryption key means that on average an adversary will be able to guess the correct key in2 2 n / or2n 1 − guesses.

unsureList.text: Explain that longer keys improve security but require more encryption and decryption time.
unsureList.best: Although longer keys are more secure, they also require more time to encrypt and decrypt messages.

unsureList.text: Explain why key-length recommendations increase as computational power improves.
unsureList.best: Computational processing power and efficiency continue to improve, allowing software to guess keys faster. Key-length recommendations for both symmetric and asymmetric encryption algorithms are periodically increased to account for increased processing power.

unsureList.text: Compare key lengths only within the same cryptographic algorithm.
unsureList.best: Key-length comparison is only valid when comparing keys for the same cryptographic algorithm. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLES § An AES 256-bit key is more secure than an AES 128-bit key. § An RSA 4096-bit key is more secure than an RSA 2048-bit key. § RSA and AES keys cannot be directly compared to one another in determining the level of security.

unsureList.text: Identify RSA and elliptic curve cryptography as asymmetric algorithms used for encryption, signatures, and certificates.
unsureList.best: Common asymmetric encryption algorithms include RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). Asymmetric algorithms are used in many applications, including digital signatures and digital certificates. 136 AP Cybersecurity · Course Framework return to contents

unsureList.text: Explain why private keys require secure storage and replacement after compromise.
unsureList.best: 5.4.B.3 Although longer keys are more secure, they also require more time to encrypt and decrypt messages.

unsureList.text: Use command-line, specialized, or web tools for asymmetric encryption and decryption.
unsureList.best: As with symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption and decryption can be performed using the command line, specialized software, or web-based tools. § On a command line interface, users can encrypt or decrypt with OpenSSL. § Specialized software like RSA Encryption Tool is an open source tool that can encrypt and decrypt files. § There are many web-based tools for encrypting and decrypting files.

unsureList.text: Identify secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles.
unsureList.best: Identify the application security principles of secure by design and security by default.

unsureList.text: Explain that secure-by-design incorporates security throughout product development, beginning with design.
unsureList.best: Secure by design is an initiative that encourages companies to include security in all phases of product development including design. When organizations implement secure by design, security is a design principle not just a technical feature.

unsureList.text: Describe secure-by-design principles involving customer outcomes, transparency, accountability, leadership, and organizational structure.
unsureList.best: Secure by design includes three design principles: iii. Companies should build organizational structure and leadership to implement secure by design. Companies need leaders who are focused on security and have a security-first posture.

unsureList.text: Explain that secure-by-default products enable security features automatically.
unsureList.best: Companies should take ownership of customer security outcomes. Companies should build products that meet the security needs of their customers.

unsureList.text: Identify control characters that can surround and affect user input.
unsureList.best: When users enter input into an application, the application typically encases that input in special characters to process it. The characters that encase the user input are called control characters and include the single quote, the double quote, and the semicolon.

unsureList.text: Explain how validating and sanitizing input prevents malicious characters and application attacks.

unsureList.text: Evaluate how effectively a method detects attacks against applications or data.
unsureList.best: Evaluate the impact of a method for detecting attacks against an application or data.

unsureList.text: Explain how honeypots expose attempted access to seemingly valuable but fabricated data.
unsureList.best: A honeypot is a file that appears as if it contains valuable data (e.g., credit card information, PII, passwords), but the data in the file are fake. A system can alert defenders if someone attempts to access the honeypot. Since the honeypot is a fake file, there is no legitimate reason to be accessing it, and any attempted access would be an indicator of malicious activity.

unsureList.text: Consider control cost when selecting detection methods such as honeypots, hashes, or DLP services.
unsureList.best: Cost is a criterion in determining detective controls. Detective controls like honeypots and using hash values to check data integrity are inexpensive. Some organizations invest in third-party data loss prevention (DLP) services, which monitor data access, usage, and transmission by users throughout the organization to detect suspicious activity; DLP services provide strong detection capabilities at a higher cost.

unsureList.text: Monitor more sensitive or critical applications and data more closely.
unsureList.best: Sensitivity or criticality of data or applications is a criterion in determining detective controls. More sensitive or critical data or applications are more likely targets of an adversary and should be monitored more closely.

unsureList.text: Determine whether a file changed by verifying its hash.
unsureList.best: Identify whether a file has been altered by verifying its hash.

unsureList.text: Use cryptographic hashes to detect unexpected changes to data.
unsureList.best: 5.6.A Explain how to detect attacks on data. ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Explain that identical inputs produce repeatable hashes, enabling change detection.

unsureList.text: Calculate file hashes using command-line tools, websites, or specialized software.
unsureList.best: 5.6.D.3 A file can be hashed and its hash output recorded. Then it can be hashed again later, and the second hash output can be compared to the previous hash output for the same file. If a file’s hash changes, then the file was altered between when the first and second hashes were generated. AP Cybersecurity · Course Framework return to contents

unsureList.best: Apply detection techniques to identify and report indicators of application attacks by analyzing log files.

unsureList.text: Use access logs and accounting data to identify unusual or malicious activity.
unsureList.best: 5.6.A.2 A honeypot is a file that appears as if it contains valuable data (e.g., credit card information, PII, passwords), but the data in the file are fake. A system can alert defenders if someone attempts to access the honeypot. Since the honeypot is a fake file, there is no legitimate reason to be accessing it, and any attempted access would be an indicator of malicious activity.

unsureList.text: Explain why automated tools augment log analysis to achieve timely detection.
unsureList.best: 5.6.C.2 Some DLP tools, honeypots, and realtime automated log analysis provide alerts as an attack is happening. These tools allow for a prompt response that can stop an attack before it does more harm. Retrospective log analysis and the use of cryptographic hashes to verify data integrity identify attacks after they have occurred.

unsureList.text: Compare real-time detection with retrospective logs and hashes for identifying and responding to attacks.
unsureList.best: Some DLP tools, honeypots, and realtime automated log analysis provide alerts as an attack is happening. These tools allow for a prompt response that can stop an attack before it does more harm. Retrospective log analysis and the use of cryptographic hashes to verify data integrity identify attacks after they have occurred.

unsureList.text: Account for legal or regulatory monitoring requirements associated with data classifications.
unsureList.best: Classification of data is a criterion in determining detective controls. Data that have been classified as private, educational, healthcare, or financial often have legal or regulatory detection and monitoring requirements.

unsureList.text: Recognize false negatives when hashes or honeypots fail to detect data theft or unaccessed targets.
unsureList.best: False negatives can occur in applications and data attack detection. Cryptographic hash functions only detect if data have been altered. An adversary could view and steal data without altering it, and a cryptographic hash function would not detect this. Honeypots cannot detect adversaries that do not attempt to access them. 142 AP Cybersecurity · Course Framework return to contents

unsureList.text: Detect SQL injection indicators in logs, including quotes, Boolean tests, comments, and SQL keywords.
unsureList.best: SQL injection attacks can be detected by reviewing application and server logs of user input for SQL control words and symbols such as: § A single or double quote character: ``, ` § Boolean conditions like OR 1=1 § A double dash (which indicates a comment in SQL): -- § SQL control words (always in capital letters) like WHERE, IN, FROM

unsureList.text: Detect XSS indicators by identifying suspicious script tags in user input.
unsureList.best: XSS attacks can be detected by reviewing user input for suspicious tags, particularly the <script>...</script> tag.

unsureList.text: Detect possible buffer overflows by checking request fields, including URL, cookie, query-string, and total lengths.
unsureList.best: For web applications, buffer overflows can be detected by checking the amount of data the user is sending to the web application in their request. The fields commonly checked are the URL length, cookie length, query string length, and total request length. Long strings in any of these fields can be an indicator of an attempted buffer overflow attack.

unsureList.text: Recognize directory traversal attempts by identifying ../ sequences in HTTP GET paths within application or server logs.
unsureList.best: Directory traversal attacks can be detected by reviewing application and server logs. HTTP GET requests that include paths with sequences of../ are indicators of an adversary attempting a directory traversal. AP Cybersecurity · Course Framework return to contents 144

changes.from: Explain reasoning through commentary that connects selected evidence to a claim.

changes.from: A writer’s tone expresses attitude toward a subject through word choice and writing style.

changes.from: Readers infer tone from word choice, especially from words’ positive, negative, or other connotations.

changes.from: Because arguments participate in ongoing discourse, effective writers usually avoid absolute claims, reasoning, and evidence.

changes.from: Sentence arrangement can emphasize particular ideas.

changes.from: Design features such as italics and boldface can create emphasis.

unsureList.text: Recognize that a text’s rhetorical situation includes its exigence, purpose, audience, context, and message.
unsureList.best: AP English Language and Composition Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | Return to Table of Cont © 2024 College Boar ents d The rhetorical situation of a text collectively refers to the exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, and message.

unsureList.text: Exigence is the circumstance or motivation that prompts a writer to create a text.
unsureList.best: The exigence is the part of a rhetorical situation that inspires, stimulates, provokes, or prompts writers to create a text.

unsureList.text: A text’s purpose is what its writer wants to accomplish, and a text may have multiple purposes.
unsureList.best: The purpose of a text is what the writer hopes to accomplish with it. Writers may have more than one purpose in a text. continued on next page

unsureList.text: An audience shares some beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds while also having individual characteristics.
unsureList.best: An audience of a text has shared as well as individual beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds.

unsureList.text: Writers produce texts within a context shaped by time, place, and occasion.
unsureList.best: Enduring Understanding Skill Essential Knowledge RHS-1 Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation. 1.A Reading – Identify and describe components of the rhetorical situation: the exigence, audience, writer, purpose, context, and message.

unsureList.text: Writers express positions through claims that need support or defense.
unsureList.best: Writers convey their positions through one or more claims that require a defense.

unsureList.text: Writers support claims using evidence, reasoning, or both.
unsureList.best: Writers defend their claims with evidence and/or reasoning.

unsureList.text: Strong claims spark interest and need defense rather than merely stating obvious facts.
unsureList.best: Effective claims provoke interest and require a defense, rather than simply stating an obvious, known fact that requires no defense or justification.

unsureList.text: Writers incorporate quoted, paraphrased, or summarized source material into their own arguments and ideas.
unsureList.best: Writers relate source material to their own argument by syntactically embedding particular quoted, paraphrased, or summarized information from one or more sources into their own ideas.

unsureList.text: Writers pursue their purposes by connecting with an audience’s emotions and values.
unsureList.best: To achieve a purpose, writers make choices in an attempt to relate to an intended audience’s emotions and values.

unsureList.text: Arguments persuade or encourage action through rhetorical appeals.
unsureList.best: ~15 CLASS PERIODS UNIT

unsureList.text: Carefully chosen evidence supports an argument’s validity and reasoning, engages audiences, and builds credibility.
unsureList.best: Strategically selected evidence strengthens the validity and reasoning of the argument, relates to an audience’s emotions and values, and increases a writer’s credibility.

unsureList.text: Arguments need enough high-quality evidence to provide appropriate support.
unsureList.best: An effective argument contains sufficient evidence; evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the argument.

unsureList.text: A thesis is the central claim a writer supports through evidence-based reasoning.
unsureList.best: A thesis is the main, overarching claim a writer is seeking to defend or prove by using reasoning supported by evidence.

unsureList.text: A thesis may be implicit or explicit; when directly stated, it is called a thesis statement.
unsureList.best: CLE-1.I A thesis is the main, overarching claim a writer is seeking to defend or prove by using reasoning supported by evidence.

unsureList.text: Use commentary to show the logical connection between evidence and the claim it supports.
unsureList.best: Effective use of evidence uses commentary to establish a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim it supports.

unsureList.text: Introduce source material with commentary that integrates it appropriately into the argument’s reasoning.
unsureList.best: Writers introduce source material by using commentary to properly integrate it into their line of reasoning.

unsureList.text: In a synthesis argument, consider, explain, and incorporate other writers’ arguments into your own.
unsureList.best: Synthesis requires consideration, explanation, and integration of others’ arguments into one’s own argument.

unsureList.text: Recognize that writers can establish a line of reasoning before reaching a thesis.
unsureList.best: Writers may lead readers through a line of reasoning and then arrive at a thesis.

unsureList.text: Recognize that writers can state a claim first and then develop reasoning to support it.
unsureList.best: Writers may express a claim and then develop a line of reasoning to justify the claim.

unsureList.text: Use commentary to explain evidence’s significance and relevance to the argument’s reasoning.
unsureList.best: Commentary explains the significance and relevance of evidence in relation to the line of reasoning.

unsureList.text: Understand that paragraph order reveals an argument’s line of reasoning.
unsureList.best: The sequence of paragraphs in a text reveals the argument’s line of reasoning.

unsureList.text: Recognize that weaknesses in reasoning can make an argument illogical or misleading.
unsureList.best: REO-1.E The sequence of paragraphs in a text reveals the argument’s line of reasoning.

unsureList.text: Understand that methods of development help organize reasoning and let audiences follow an argument.
unsureList.best: Methods of development are common approaches writers frequently use to develop and organize the reasoning of their arguments. A method of development provides an audience with the means to trace a writer’s reasoning in an argument.

unsureList.text: Identify narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, and description as common development methods.
unsureList.best: Some typical methods of development are narration, cause- effect, comparison-contrast, definition, and description.

unsureList.text: Use narration by presenting details about real experiences and reflecting on their significance.
unsureList.best: When developing ideas through narration, writers offer details about real-life experiences and offer reflections and insights on the significance of those experiences.

unsureList.text: Use cause-effect development by presenting causes, consequences, or linked causes and effects.
unsureList.best: When developing ideas through cause-effect, writers present a cause, assert effects or consequences of that cause, or present a series of causes and the subsequent effect(s).

unsureList.text: An introduction identifies the subject or writer and may orient, engage, or focus the audience using varied rhetorical techniques.
unsureList.best: The introduction of an argument introduces the subject and/ or writer of the argument to the audience. An introduction may present the argument’s thesis. An introduction may orient, engage, and/or focus the audience by presenting quotations, intriguing statements, anecdotes, questions, statistics, data, contextualized information, or a scenario.

unsureList.text: A conclusion unifies the argument and may provide significance, implications, action, solutions, a summary, or a connection to the introduction.
unsureList.best: The conclusion of an argument brings the argument to a unified end. A conclusion may present the argument’s thesis. It may engage and/or focus the audience by explaining the significance of the argument within a broader context, making connections, calling the audience to act, suggesting a change in behavior or attitude, proposing a solution, leaving the audience with a compelling image, explaining implications, summarizing the argument, or connecting to the introduction.

unsureList.text: A thesis may preview an argument’s reasoning without listing every point, analytical aspect, or specific supporting evidence.
unsureList.best: A thesis statement may preview the line of reasoning of an argument. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an argument, aspects to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in an argument. unsureList.text: Comparison-contrast development establishes a category, then examines similarities or differences using comparable categories.
unsureList.best: When developing ideas through comparison-contrast, writers present a category of comparison and then examine the similarities and/or differences between the objects of the comparison. When analyzing similarities and/or differences, like categories of comparison must be used.

unsureList.text: Definition or description develops ideas by relating an object’s characteristics, features, sensory details, examples, or illustrations.
unsureList.best: When developing ideas through a definition or description, writers relate the characteristics, features, or sensory details of an object or idea, sometimes using examples or illustrations.

unsureList.text: Body paragraphs advance an argument by making claims, supporting them with evidence, and explaining their contribution to the reasoning.
unsureList.best: The body paragraphs of a written argument make claims, support them with evidence, and provide commentary that explains how the paragraph contributes to the reasoning of the argument.

unsureList.text: Coherence operates across sentences, paragraphs, and the entire text through logical connections between ideas.

unsureList.text: Repetition, synonyms, pronoun references, and parallel structures can signal or build relationships among textual elements.
unsureList.best: Repetition, synonyms, pronoun references, and parallel structure may indicate or develop a relationship between elements of a text.

unsureList.text: Transitions create coherence by showing relationships among ideas across sentences, paragraphs, or sections.
unsureList.best: Transitional elements are words or other elements (phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs) that assist in creating coherence among sentences, paragraphs, or sections in a text by showing relationships among ideas.

unsureList.text: Transitions can introduce evidence or show how it relates to other ideas or evidence within a paragraph or text.

unsureList.text: Words communicate both dictionary definitions and associated or implied meanings.
unsureList.best: Words have both connotative and denotative meanings.

unsureList.text: Descriptive modifiers provide information and convey the writer’s perspective toward what they describe.
unsureList.best: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, not only qualify or modify the things they describe but also convey a perspective toward those things.

unsureList.text: Specific word choices minimize confusion and can help audiences recognize the writer’s perspective.
unsureList.best: Precise word choice reduces confusion and may help the audience perceive the writer’s perspective.

unsureList.text: Effective synthesis selects relevant information from multiple sources and integrates precise source material into an argument.
unsureList.best: When synthesizing, writers draw upon arguments from multiple sources, strategically select the most relevant information, and combine apt and specific source material as part of their own argument.

unsureList.text: Sources contribute information to arguments, but their reliability and credibility vary.
unsureList.best: CLE-1.P When synthesizing, writers draw upon arguments from multiple sources, strategically select the most relevant information, and combine apt and specific source material as part of their own argument.

unsureList.text: A source’s position differs from its perspective, which reflects its background, interests, and expertise.
unsureList.best: A position and a perspective are different. Sources may have the same position on a subject, yet each comes from a different perspective based on their background, interests, and expertise.

unsureList.text: Strong arguments recognize evidence biases and limitations and address them in their reasoning.
unsureList.best: When incorporating evidence or sources into an argument, the strongest arguments recognize and acknowledge the biases and limitations of the material and account for those limitations in their reasoning.

unsureList.text: A source’s treatment of alternative positions indicates how biased it may be.
unsureList.best: The degree to which a source does or does not consider other positions reflects the degree to which that source is biased.

unsureList.text: New evidence may require revising the thesis or changing the argument’s reasoning.
unsureList.best: STL-1.F A writer’s shifts in tone from one part of a text to another may suggest the writer’s qualification, refinement, or reconsideration of their perspective on a subject.

unsureList.text: Changes in tone can signal qualification, refinement, or reconsideration of the writer’s perspective.
unsureList.best: A writer’s shifts in tone from one part of a text to another may suggest the writer’s qualification, refinement, or reconsideration of their perspective on a subject.

unsureList.text: Failing to recognize subject complexities can produce oversimplified claims or broad generalizations.
unsureList.best: A lack of understanding of the complexities of a subject or an issue can lead to oversimplification or generalizations.

unsureList.text: Writers use modifiers to qualify claims or limit an argument’s scope.
unsureList.best: Enduring Understanding Skill Essential Knowledge CLE-1 Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments. 3.C Reading – Explain ways claims are qualified through modifiers, counterarguments, and alternative perspectives. 4.C Writing – Qualify a claim using modifiers, counterarguments, or alternative perspectives.

unsureList.text: Sentences contain clauses, including at least one independent clause, to express ideas.
unsureList.best: Writers express ideas in sentences. Sentences are made up of clauses, at least one of which must be independent.

unsureList.text: Subordination and coordination show intended relationships between ideas within sentences.
unsureList.best: Subordination and coordination are used to express the intended relationship between ideas in a sentence.

unsureList.text: Coordination commonly presents ideas as balanced or equal.
unsureList.best: STL-1.I Subordination and coordination are used to express the intended relationship between ideas in a sentence.

unsureList.text: Subordination commonly presents ideas as unequal or imbalanced.
unsureList.best: STL-1.I Subordination and coordination are used to express the intended relationship between ideas in a sentence.

unsureList.text: Arranging clauses, phrases, and words can emphasize ideas.
unsureList.best: STL-1.H The arrangement of sentences in a text can emphasize particular ideas.

unsureList.text: Following established grammar and mechanics conventions enables clear communication.
unsureList.best: Grammar and mechanics that follow established conventions of language enable clear communication.

unsureList.text: Punctuation can clarify, organize, emphasize, indicate purpose, add information, or shape tone.
unsureList.best: Punctuation(commas,colons,semicolons,dashes,hyphens, parentheses,quotationmarks,orendmarks)advancesawriter’s purposebyclarifying,organizing,emphasizing,indicating purpose,supplementinginformation,orcontributingtotone.

unsureList.text: Writers use comparisons such as metaphors, analogies, similes, or anecdotes to connect with audiences and advance their purposes.
unsureList.best: Writers may make comparisons (e.g., similes, metaphors, analogies, or anecdotes) in an attempt to relate to an audience. Effective comparisons must be shared and understood by the audience to advance the writer’s purpose.

unsureList.text: Syntax and diction shape how audiences perceive writers and can affect their willingness to accept an argument.
unsureList.best: Writers’ choices regarding syntax and diction influence how the writer is perceived by an audience and may influence the degree to which an audience accepts an argument.

unsureList.text: Word choice can reveal bias and influence a writer’s credibility with a particular audience.
unsureList.best: Word choice may reflect writers’ biases and may affect their credibility with a particular audience.

unsureList.text: Because audiences differ and change, writers should adapt evidence, organization, and language to their intended audience’s perspectives and needs.
unsureList.best: Because audiences are unique and dynamic, writers must consider the perspectives, contexts, and needs of the intended audience when making choices of evidence, organization, and language in an argument.

unsureList.text: A writer’s style combines word choice, syntax, and writing conventions.
unsureList.best: A writer’s style is made up of the mix of word choice, syntax, and conventions employed by that writer.

unsureList.text: Writers can use style to communicate complex or ironic perspectives, including contrasts with audience expectations or values.
unsureList.best: UNITOVERVIEW(cont’d) Enduring Understanding Skill Essential Knowledge STL-1 The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make. 7.A Reading – Explain how word choice, comparisons, and syntax contribute to the specific tone or style of a text. 8.A Writing – Strategically use words, comparisons, and syntax to convey a specific tone or style in an argument.

unsureList.text: Modifiers qualify or clarify information and should be placed near the words they modify to minimize ambiguity.
unsureList.best: Modifiers—including words, phrases, or clauses—qualify, clarify, or specify information about the thing with which they are associated. To reduce ambiguity, modifiers should be placed closest to the word, phrase, or clause that they are meant to modify.

unsureList.text: Parenthetical elements interrupt sentences to add information that meets audience needs or supports the writer’s purpose.
unsureList.best: Parenthetical elements—though not essential to understanding what they are describing—interrupt sentences to provide additional information that may address an audience’s needs and/or advance a writer’s purpose.

changes.from: Perspective reflects how narrators, characters, or speakers understand circumstances through background, personality, biases, and relationships.

changes.from: Narrators and speakers tell accounts and establish a relationship between the text and its readers.
changes.to: Narrators or speakers relate accounts to readers and establish a relationship between the text and the reader.

changes.from: Repeated words or phrases can emphasize ideas or associations.
changes.to: Wordsorphrasesmayberepeatedtoemphasizeideas or associations.

changes.from: Readers’ understanding of a character’s viewpoint can depend on the narrator’s or speaker’s viewpoint.
changes.to: Readers’ understanding of a character’s perspective may depend on the perspective of the narrator or speaker.

changes.from: Episodes, encounters, and scenes can introduce and develop a narrative’s plot.
changes.to: Events include episodes, encounters, and scenes in a narrative that can introduce and develop a plot.

changes.from: Conflict is tension between competing values within a character or opposing outside forces.
changes.to: Conflictistensionbetweencompetingvalueseither within a character, known as internal or psychological conflict,orwithoutsideforcesthatobstructacharacter insomeway,knownasexternalconflict.

changes.from: Narrators’, characters’, and speakers’ backgrounds and perspectives shape the tone they convey.
changes.to: The narrators’, characters’, or speakers’ backgrounds and perspectives shape the tone they convey about subjects or events in the text.

changes.from: Body paragraphs develop reasoning by using evidence and commentary to connect claims with the thesis.
changes.to: The body paragraphs of a written argument develop the reasoning and justify claims using evidence and providing commentary that links the evidence to the overall thesis.

changes.from: Words with multiple meanings or connotations can add nuance and complexity to interpretations.
changes.to: Words with multiple meanings or connotations add nuance or complexity that can contribute to interpretations of a text. 5.B Explainthefunctionofspecific words and phrases in a text.

changes.from: Descriptive words contribute to sensory imagery.
changes.to: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, contribute to sensory imagery.

changes.from: Differences between characters’ private thoughts and behavior reveal tensions between their private and publicly expressed values.
changes.to: Inconsistencies between the private thoughts of characters and their actual behavior reveal tensions and complexities between private and professed values.

changes.from: A narrator’s or speaker’s tone toward events or characters influences how readers interpret related ideas.
changes.to: The narrator’s or speaker’s tone toward events or charactersinatextinfluencesreaders’interpretationof the ideas associated with those things.

changes.from: Sentence syntax can emphasize details or ideas and communicate a narrator’s or speaker’s tone.

changes.from: A material object becomes a symbol when it represents an idea or concept.

changes.from: Character change often emerges from conflicts between values represented in the narrative.

changes.from: Changes in a character’s circumstances can cause changes in that character.

changes.from: Explain how specific words and phrases function in a text.
changes.to: Explain the function of specific words and phrases in a text. FIG

changes.from: A narrator or speaker may change through actions and interactions across the text.

unsureList.text: Relationships, surroundings, plot events, and textual ideas shape and reveal a character’s perspective.

unsureList.text: Setting identifies the time and place in which a text’s events occur.

unsureList.text: Plot and exposition emphasize characters, relationships, setting, and other elements central to narrative development.
unsureList.best: NAR-1.F First-personnarratorsareinvolvedinthenarrative; their relationship to the events of the plot and the other characters shapes their perspective.

unsureList.text: The speaker or narrator is not necessarily the text’s author.

changes.from: Identify streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes as freshwater biomes important for drinking water.
changes.to: Freshwater biomes include streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes. These freshwater biomes are a vital resource for drinking water.

changes.from: Explain steps and reservoir interactions in the hydrologic cycle.
changes.to: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the hydrologic cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Explain how living organisms acquire and transfer solar energy.
changes.to: Explain how solar energy is acquired and transferred by living organisms. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Describe food chains and food webs and identify members by trophic level.
changes.to: Describe food chains and food webs, and their constituent members by trophic level. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Biodiversity includes genetic diversity, species diversity, and habitat diversity.
changes.to: Biodiversity in an ecosystem includes genetic, species, and habitat diversity.

changes.from: Ecosystem services are provisioning, regulating, cultural, or supporting services.
changes.to: There are four categories of ecosystem services: provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting.

changes.from: Describe island biogeography.
changes.to: ERT-2.E Describe the role of island biogeography in evolution. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Island biogeography examines organisms’ distributions, ecological relationships, and community structures on islands.
changes.to: Island biogeography is the study of the ecological relationships and distribution of organisms on islands, and of these organisms’ community structures.

changes.from: Explain how populations respond to environmental changes.
changes.to: Explain how populations respond to changes in their environment. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: The two main succession types are primary succession and secondary succession.
changes.to: There are two main types of ecological succession: primary and secondary succession.

changes.from: Distinguish between generalist and specialist species.
changes.to: Identify differences between generalist and specialist species. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Explain survivorship curves.
changes.to: Explain survivorship curves. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Explain how resource availability affects population growth.
changes.to: Explain how resource availability affects population growth. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Environmental factors, especially resources and space, limit population growth.
changes.to: Population growth is limited by environmental factors, especially by the available resources and space.

changes.from: Explain factors affecting total fertility rate in human populations.
changes.to: Explain factors that affect total fertility rate in human populations. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Define demographic transition.
changes.to: Define the demographic transition. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Describe geological changes and events associated with convergent, divergent, and transform plate boundaries.
changes.to: Describe the geological changes and events that occur at convergent, divergent, and transform plate boundaries. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Convergent boundaries may produce mountains, island arcs, earthquakes, and volcanoes.
changes.to: Convergent boundaries can result in the creation of mountains, island arcs, earthquakes, and volcanoes.

changes.from: Divergent boundaries may produce seafloor spreading, rift valleys, volcanoes, and earthquakes.
changes.to: Divergent boundaries can result in seafloor spreading, rift valleys, volcanoes, and earthquakes.

changes.from: Describe Earth’s atmospheric structure and composition.
changes.to: Describe the structure and composition of the Earth’s atmosphere. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Describe environmental changes and effects caused by El Niño and La Niña events.
changes.to: Describe the environmental changes and effects that result from El Niño or La Niña events (El Niño–Southern Oscillation). ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Explain the tragedy of the commons concept.
changes.to: Explain the concept of the tragedy of the commons. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Describe changes in agricultural practices.
changes.to: Describe changes in agricultural practices. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Improve soil fertility through crop rotation, green manure, and limestone.
changes.to: Strategies to improve soil fertility include crop rotation and the addition of green manure and limestone.

changes.from: Distinguish between renewable and nonrenewable energy sources.
changes.to: Identify differences between nonrenewable and renewable energy sources. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Fossil fuels are the world’s most widely used energy sources.
changes.to: The most widely used sources of energy globally are fossil fuels.

changes.from: Lignite, bituminous, and anthracite are coal types shaped by heat, pressure, and burial depth.
changes.to: Three types of coal used for fuel are lignite, bituminous, and anthracite. Heat, pressure, and depth of burial contribute to the development of various coal types and their qualities.

changes.from: Natural gas is mostly methane and is the cleanest fossil fuel.
changes.to: Natural gas, the cleanest of the fossil fuels, is mostly methane.

changes.from: Tar sands contain clay, sand, water, and bitumen and can yield crude oil.
changes.to: Crude oil can be recovered from tar sands, which are a combination of clay, sand, water, and bitumen.

changes.from: Describe nuclear energy use in electricity generation.
changes.to: Describe the use of nuclear energy in power generation. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Describe environmental effects of biomass use for power generation.
changes.to: Describe the effects of the use of biomass in power generation on the environment. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Active solar systems mechanically collect and store solar heat in liquid.
changes.to: Active solar energy systems use solar energy to heat a liquid through mechanical and electric equipment to collect and store the energy captured from the sun.

changes.from: Describe environmental effects of geothermal power generation.
changes.to: Describe the effects of the use of geothermal energy in power generation on the environment.

changes.from: Carbon monoxide is an indoor asphyxiant pollutant.
changes.to: Carbon monoxide is an indoor air pollutant that is classified as an asphyxiant.

changes.from: Indoor particulate pollutants include asbestos, dust, and smoke.
changes.to: Indoor air pollutants that are classified as particulates include asbestos, dust, and smoke.

changes.from: Natural indoor pollutants include radon, mold, and dust.
changes.to: Common natural source indoor air pollutants include radon, mold, and dust.

changes.from: Describe health and environmental effects of indoor air pollutants.
changes.to: Describe the effects of indoor air pollutants.

changes.from: Explain how air pollution can be reduced at its source.
changes.to: Explain how air pollutants can be reduced at the source. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Wet and dry scrubbers remove gases and particulates from industrial exhaust.
changes.to: Wet and dry scrubbers are air pollution control devices that remove particulates and/or gases from industrial exhaust streams.

changes.from: Natural and human sources of nitrogen and sulfur oxides produce acid rain and deposition.
changes.to: Acid rain and deposition is due to nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides from anthropogenic and natural sources in the atmosphere.

changes.from: Describe human activities that create noise pollution and its effects.
changes.to: Describe human activities that result in noise pollution and its effects. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Noise pollution is sufficiently loud sound that can cause physiological stress and hearing loss.
changes.to: Noise pollution is sound at levels high enough to cause physiological stress and hearing loss.

changes.from: Distinguish between point and nonpoint pollution sources.
changes.to: Identify differences between point and nonpoint sources of pollution. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: A point source is one identifiable pollutant source, such as a smokestack or discharge pipe.
changes.to: A point source refers to a single, identifiable source of a pollutant, such as a smokestack or waste discharge pipe.

changes.from: Ocean warming, sediment runoff, and destructive fishing damage coral reefs.
changes.to: Coral reefs have been suffering damage due to a variety of factors, including increasing ocean temperature, sediment runoff, and destructive fishing practices.

changes.from: Aquatic bacteria convert elemental mercury into highly toxic methylmercury.
changes.to: When elemental sources of mercury enter aquatic environments, bacteria in the water convert it to highly toxic methylmercury. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

changes.from: Describe human impacts on wetlands and mangroves.
changes.to: Describe the impacts of human activity on wetlands and mangroves. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Wetlands are areas whose soil is covered by water part or all of the time.
changes.to: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil, either part or all of the time.

changes.from: Wetlands provide water purification, flood protection, filtration, and habitat.
changes.to: Wetlands provide a variety of ecological services, including water purification, flood protection, water filtration, and habitat.

changes.from: Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients enrich a water body.
changes.to: Eutrophication occurs when a body of water is enriched in nutrients.

changes.from: Describe the effects of bioaccumulation and biomagnification.
changes.to: Describe the effects of bioaccumulation and biomagnification. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Incineration reduces waste volume but releases air pollutants.
changes.to: Solid waste can also be disposed of through incineration, where waste is burned at high temperatures. This method significantly reduces the volume of solid waste but releases air pollutants.

changes.from: Untreated sewage in streams and rivers can cause dysentery.
changes.to: Dysentery is caused by untreated sewage in streams and rivers.

changes.from: Infected mosquitoes transmit West Nile virus to humans through bites.
changes.to: West Nile virus is transmitted to humans via bites from infected mosquitoes.

changes.from: MERS is a viral respiratory illness transmitted from animals to humans.
changes.to: Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) is a viral respiratory illness that is transferred from animals to humans.

changes.from: Major greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, nitrous oxide, and CFCs.
changes.to: The principal greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, nitrous oxide, and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

changes.from: Temperature and rainfall changes can reduce soil viability and increase erosion.
changes.to: Climate change can affect soil through changes in temperature and rainfall, which can impact soil’s viability and potentially increase erosion.

changes.from: Explain the causes and effects of ocean warming.
changes.to: Explain the causes and effects of ocean warming. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING STB-4 Local and regional human activities can have impacts at the global level. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Explain the causes and effects of ocean acidification.
changes.to: Explain the causes and effects of ocean acidification. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING STB-4 Local and regional human activities can have impacts at the global level. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

changes.from: Competition for territory, food, mates, and habitat can contribute to endangerment and extinction.
changes.to: Species in a given ecosystem compete for resources like territory, food, mates, and habitat, and this competition may lead to endangerment or extinction.

unsureList.text: Describe where terrestrial biomes occur globally and summarize their main environmental characteristics.
unsureList.best: Describe the global distribution and principal environmental aspects of terrestrial biomes. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Identify major terrestrial biomes, including taiga, forests, rainforest, shrubland, grassland, savanna, desert, and tundra.
unsureList.best: Major terrestrial biomes include taiga, temperate rainforests, temperate seasonal forests, tropical rainforests, shrubland, temperate grassland, savanna, desert, and tundra.

unsureList.text: Explain that biome plant and animal communities reflect adaptations to their climate.
unsureList.best: A biome contains characteristic communities of plants and animals that result from, and are adapted to, its climate.

unsureList.text: Explain how climate, geography, latitude, altitude, nutrients, and soil affect terrestrial resource distribution.
unsureList.best: The global distribution of nonmineral terrestrial natural resources, such as water and trees for lumber, varies because of some combination of climate, geography, latitude and altitude, nutrient availability, and soil.

unsureList.text: Explain that biome locations change over time and may shift with global climate change.
unsureList.best: The worldwide distribution of biomes is dynamic; the distribution has changed in the past and may again shift as a result of global climate changes. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ERT-1 Ecosystems are the result of biotic and abiotic interactions. AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 37

unsureList.text: Explain how resource availability affects interactions among species.
unsureList.best: Explain how the availability of resources influences species interactions. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Explain how resource partitioning reduces competition within or between species.
unsureList.best: ERT-1.A Explain how the availability of resources influences species interactions. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Define symbiosis as a long-term close relationship and identify mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism.
unsureList.best: Symbiosis is a close and long-term interaction between two species in an ecosystem. Types of symbiosis include mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism.

unsureList.text: Identify predators as organisms that consume prey in predator-prey relationships.
unsureList.best: In a predator-prey relationship, the predator is an organism that eats another organism (the prey).

unsureList.text: Describe the global distribution and key environmental features of aquatic biomes.
unsureList.best: Describe the global distribution and principal environmental aspects of aquatic biomes. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Identify marine biomes and explain how algae contribute oxygen and remove atmospheric carbon dioxide.
unsureList.best: Marine biomes include oceans, coral reefs, marshland, and estuaries. Algae in marine biomes supply a large portion of the Earth’s oxygen, and also take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

unsureList.text: Explain how salinity, depth, turbidity, nutrients, and temperature affect marine resource distribution.
unsureList.best: The global distribution of nonmineral marine natural resources, such as different types of fish, varies because of some combination of salinity, depth, turbidity, nutrient availability, and temperature. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ERT-1 Ecosystems are the result of biotic and abiotic interactions.
