unsureList.text: Explain carbon-cycle steps and interactions among its reservoirs.
unsureList.best: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the carbon cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Describe carbon movement between sources and sinks.
unsureList.best: The carbon cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element carbon between sources and sinks.

unsureList.text: Compare carbon reservoirs that retain compounds for long versus short periods.
unsureList.best: Some of the reservoirs in which carbon compounds occur in the carbon cycle hold those compounds for long periods of time, while some hold them for relatively short periods of time.

unsureList.text: Explain how photosynthesis and cellular respiration cycle carbon through living organisms.
unsureList.best: Carbon cycles between photosynthesis and cellular respiration in living things.

unsureList.text: Explain how decomposition stores carbon and fossil-fuel combustion rapidly releases it as carbon dioxide.
unsureList.best: Plant and animal decomposition have led to the storage of carbon over millions of years. The burning of fossil fuels quickly moves that stored carbon into atmospheric carbon, in the form of carbon dioxide. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ERT-1 Ecosystems are the result of biotic and abiotic interactions. Required Course Content AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 39

unsureList.text: Explain nitrogen-cycle steps and interactions among reservoirs.
unsureList.best: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the nitrogen cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Describe nitrogen movement through fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, and denitrification.
unsureList.best: The nitrogen cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element nitrogen between sources and sinks. It involves several steps, including nitrogen fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, and denitrification. Microorganisms in the soil play an important role in many of these steps.

unsureList.text: Explain how soil bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia and biologically available ammonium.
unsureList.best: In nitrogen fixation, atmospheric nitrogen (N ) is converted by certain types of soil bacteria

unsureList.text: Explain how nitrogen fixation limits soil nitrogen availability and primary production.
unsureList.best: The availability of nitrogen compounds in the soil is limited by the rate of nitrogen fixation. In many ecosystems, the availability of nitrogen compounds limits primary production by plants and other producers.

unsureList.text: Identify the atmosphere as nitrogen’s largest reservoir and note that most reservoirs retain nitrogen briefly.
unsureList.best: ERT-1.E Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the nitrogen cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Explain phosphorus-cycle steps and interactions among reservoirs.
unsureList.best: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the phosphorus cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Describe phosphorus movement between sources and sinks.
unsureList.best: The phosphorus cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element phosphorus between sources and sinks.

unsureList.text: Identify rocks and ocean sediments as major phosphorus reservoirs and note its lack of a significant atmospheric phase.
unsureList.best: The major reservoirs of phosphorus in the phosphorus cycle are rock and ocean sediments that contain phosphorus-bearing minerals. The phosphorus cycle lacks a significant atmospheric component.

unsureList.text: Explain why slow weathering makes phosphorus scarce and often limiting for producers.
unsureList.best: Phosphorus is relatively scarce in ecosystems because rocks weather slowly. As a result, phosphorus is often a limiting nutrient for plants and other producers, particularly in freshwater and some terrestrial ecosystems. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ERT-1 Ecosystems are the result of biotic and abiotic interactions. AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 41

unsureList.text: Describe solar-powered movement of water among reservoirs and its solid, liquid, and gaseous phases.
unsureList.best: The hydrologic cycle, which is powered by the sun, is the movement of water in its various solid, liquid, and gaseous phases between sources and sinks.

unsureList.text: Identify oceans as the largest surface reservoir, with ice caps and groundwater as smaller reservoirs.
unsureList.best: ERT-1.G Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the hydrologic cycle. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Define primary productivity as the rate of converting sunlight into organic compounds through photosynthesis.
unsureList.best: Primary productivity is the rate at which solar energy (sunlight) is converted into organic compounds via photosynthesis over a unit of time.

unsureList.text: Define gross primary productivity as total photosynthetic activity in an area.
unsureList.best: Gross primary productivity is the total rate of photosynthesis in a given area.

unsureList.text: Define net primary productivity as energy stored after subtracting respiratory losses.
unsureList.best: Net primary productivity is the rate of energy storage by photosynthesizers in a given area, after subtracting the energy lost to respiration.

unsureList.text: Express productivity using energy per area per time, such as kcal/m²/year.
unsureList.best: Productivity is measured in units of energy per unit area per unit time (e.g., kcal/m2 /yr).

unsureList.text: Explain how water-depth light penetration affects aquatic photosynthesis and drives adaptations.
unsureList.best: Most red light is absorbed in the upper 1m of water, and blue light only penetrates deeper than 100m in the clearest water. This affects photosynthesis in aquatic ecosystems, whose photosynthesizers have adapted mechanisms to address the lack of visible light. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ENG-1 Energy can be converted from one form to another. AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 43

unsureList.text: Explain energy flow and matter cycling through trophic levels.
unsureList.best: Explain how energy flows and matter cycles through trophic levels. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Describe energy transfer from the sun to producers and then to higher trophic levels.
unsureList.best: ENG-1.C.2 The loss of energy that occurs when energy moves from lower to higher trophic levels can be explained through the laws of thermodynamics. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ENG-1 Energy can be converted from one form to another. AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 45

unsureList.text: Explain ecosystems’ dependence on continuous high-quality energy and matter transfer through biogeochemical cycles.
unsureList.best: All ecosystems depend on a continuous inflow of high-quality energy in order to maintain their structure and function of transferring matter between the environment and organisms via biogeochemical cycles.

unsureList.text: Explain that biogeochemical cycles sustain life while conserving matter.
unsureList.best: Biogeochemical cycles are essential for life and each cycle demonstrates the conservation of matter.

unsureList.text: Determine how energy declines as it moves through ecosystems.
unsureList.best: Determine how the energy decreases as it flows through ecosystems. ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Apply the approximate 10% rule to energy transfers between adjacent trophic levels.
unsureList.best: The 10% rule approximates that in the transfer of energy from one trophic level to the next, only about 10% of the energy is passed on.

unsureList.text: Explain trophic-level energy losses using the laws of thermodynamics.
unsureList.best: The loss of energy that occurs when energy moves from lower to higher trophic levels can be explained through the laws of thermodynamics. ENDURINGUNDERSTANDING ENG-1 Energy can be converted from one form to another. AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | 45

unsureList.text: Explain energy and matter flow from producers through consumers, decomposers, and detritivores.
unsureList.best: A food chain depicts the flow of energy and matter from producers (autotrophs) to primary consumers (herbivores) and secondary and tertiary consumers (omnivores and carnivores). Detritivores and decomposers play an essential role in food chains and food webs by returning nutrients to the soil. A food web is a model of an interlocking pattern of food chains that depicts the flow of energy and matter in two or more food chains.

unsureList.text: Explain how adding or removing species can create positive or negative feedback effects within food webs.
unsureList.best: Positive and negative feedback loops can each play a role in food webs. When one species is removed from or added to a specific food web, the rest of the food web can be affected. unsureList.text: Explain genetic, species, and habitat diversity and why each matters to ecosystems.

unsureList.text: Hunting, narrow diets, invasive competitors, and specialized habitats can threaten species with extinction.

unsureList.text: Adaptable or mobile species are generally less vulnerable to extinction after environmental change.
unsureList.best: Not all species will be in danger of extinction when exposed to the same changes in their ecosystem. Species that are able to adapt to changes in their environment or that are able to move to a new environment are less likely to face extinction.

unsureList.text: Selective pressures alter organism behavior and fitness within an environment.

unsureList.text: Fragmentation divides large habitats into isolated areas through roads, development, agriculture, pipelines, and logging.

unsureList.text: The harmful fragmentation threshold differs among species sharing an ecosystem.

unsureList.text: Climate change causes habitat loss through altered temperature, precipitation, and sea levels.

unsureList.text: Protected areas, habitat corridors, sustainable land use, and habitat restoration can reduce biodiversity loss.

unsureList.text: Explain how infantry, firearms, cannon and fortifications, paid for by taxes and bureaucracy, tilted power to resource-rich states.
unsureList.best: Advances in military technology led to new forms of warfare, including greater reliance on infantry, firearms, mobile cannon, and more elaborate fortifications, all financed by heavier taxation and requiring a larger bureaucracy. New military techniques and institutions (i.e., the military revolution) tipped the balance of power toward states able to marshal sufficient resources for the new military environment. Course Framework V.1 | AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how absolute monarchs limited noble governance but kept aristocratic privilege.
unsureList.best: Absolute monarchies limited the nobility’s participation in governance but preserved the aristocracy’s social position and legal privileges.

unsureList.text: Describe how Louis XIV and Colbert extended the central state's control in France.
unsureList.best: Louis XIV and his finance minister, Jean- Baptiste Colbert, extended the administrative, financial, military, and religious control of the central state over the French population.

unsureList.text: Describe how Peter the Great and Catherine the Great westernised and expanded Russia.
unsureList.best: Peter the Great “westernized” the Russian state and society, transforming political, religious, and cultural institutions; Catherine the Great continued this process. Course Framework V.1 | 87 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how science built on observation, experiment and maths challenged classical views of the cosmos, nature and body.
unsureList.best: New ideas in science based on observation, experimentation, and mathematics challenged classical views of the cosmos, nature, and the human body, although existing traditions of knowledge and the universe continued. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 105 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment raised the role of reason in culture, though not without challenge.
unsureList.best: The spread of Scientific Revolution concepts and practices and the Enlightenment’s application of these concepts and practices to political, social, and ethical issues led to an increased but not unchallenged emphasis on reason in European culture.

unsureList.text: Describe how Enlightenment ideas such as empiricism and rationalism challenged social order, government and faith.
unsureList.best: Enlightenment thought, which focused on concepts such as empiricism, skepticism, human reason, rationalism, and classical sources of knowledge, challenged the prevailing patterns of thought with respect to social order, institutions of government, and the role of faith.

unsureList.text: Explain how new public venues and print media spread Enlightenment ideas.
unsureList.best: New public venues and print media popularized Enlightenment ideas.

unsureList.text: Explain how rational study of religion led to natural religion and calls for toleration.
unsureList.best: During the Enlightenment, the rational analysis of religious practices led to natural religion and the demand for religious toleration.

unsureList.text: Explain how population, environment, medicine and technology shaped daily life.
unsureList.best: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by demographic, environmental, medical, and technological changes.

unsureList.text: Describe how family and private life reflected new population patterns and commercial wealth.
unsureList.best: By the 18th century, family and private life reflected new demographic patterns and the effects of the commercial revolution. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 4: Learning Objective I Explain how and why the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment challenged the existing European order and understanding of the world. Course Framework V.1 | 106 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how Copernicus, Galileo and Newton questioned ancient authority and built a sun-centred view of the cosmos.
unsureList.best: New ideas and methods in astronomy led individuals, including Copernicus, Galileo, and Newton, to question the authority of the ancients and traditional knowledge, and to develop a heliocentric view of the cosmos.

unsureList.text: Explain how Harvey and other physicians presented the body as an integrated system, challenging Galen's humoral theory.
unsureList.best: Anatomical and medical discoveries by physicians, including William Harvey, presented the body as an integrated system, challenging the traditional humoral theory of the body and of disease espoused by Galen.

unsureList.text: Explain how Bacon and Descartes defined inductive and deductive reasoning and promoted experiment and mathematics.
unsureList.best: Francis Bacon and René Descartes defined inductive and deductive reasoning and promoted experimentation and the use of mathematics, which would ultimately shape the scientific method.

unsureList.text: Explain why alchemy and astrology kept appealing and why many still saw spiritual forces ruling the cosmos.
unsureList.best: Alchemy and astrology continued to appeal to elites and some natural philosophers, in part because they shared with the new science the notion of a predictable and knowable universe. At the same time, many people continued to believe that the cosmos was governed by spiritual forces. Course Framework V.1 | 97 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe how Voltaire, Diderot and others applied scientific principles to society and institutions.
unsureList.best: Intellectuals, including Voltaire and Diderot, began to apply the principles of the Scientific Revolution to society and human institutions.

unsureList.text: Explain how Locke and Rousseau built political models on natural rights and the social contract.
unsureList.best: Locke and Rousseau developed new political models based on the concept of natural rights and the social contract.

unsureList.text: Explain the tension between Enlightenment equality and arguments, like Rousseau's, excluding women from politics.
unsureList.best: Despite the principles of equality espoused by the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, intellectuals such as Rousseau offered controversial arguments for the exclusion of women from political life. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 98 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe how salons and other institutions explored and spread Enlightenment culture.
unsureList.best: A variety of institutions, including salons, explored and disseminated Enlightenment culture.

unsureList.text: Explain how Locke saw society as self-interested individuals and the state as based on consent, not divine right.
unsureList.best: Political theories, including John Locke’s, conceived of society as composed of individuals driven by self-interest and argued that the state originated in the consent of the governed (i.e., a social contract) rather than in divine right or tradition.

unsureList.text: Explain how Adam Smith and others challenged mercantilism with free trade and free markets.
unsureList.best: Mercantilist theory and practice were challenged by new economic ideas, including Adam Smith’s, which espoused free trade and a free market.

unsureList.text: Explain how religion came to be seen as a private rather than public matter.
unsureList.best: KC-2.3.III.A Political theories, including John Locke’s, conceived of society as composed of individuals driven by self-interest and argued that the state originated in the consent of the governed (i.e., a social contract) rather than in divine right or tradition.

unsureList.text: Explain how food supply and population moved from periodic famine to steady growth by the 1700s.
unsureList.best: In the 17th century, small landholdings, low-productivity agricultural practices, poor transportation, and adverse weather limited and disrupted the food supply, causing periodic famines. By the 18th century, the balance between population and the food supply stabilized, resulting in steady population growth.

unsureList.text: Explain how better farming and transport raised food supply and cut demographic crises.
unsureList.best: KC-2.4.I In the 17th century, small landholdings, low-productivity agricultural practices, poor transportation, and adverse weather limited and disrupted the food supply, causing periodic famines. By the 18th century, the balance between population and the food supply stabilized, resulting in steady population growth.

unsureList.text: Explain how plague faded and inoculation reduced smallpox deaths.
unsureList.best: In the 18th century, plague disappeared as a major epidemic disease, and inoculation reduced smallpox mortality.

unsureList.text: Explain how population growth was limited by the European marriage pattern and birth control despite more illegitimate births.
unsureList.best: Although the rate of illegitimate births increased in the 18th century, population growth was limited by the European marriage pattern, and in some areas by various birth control methods. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 100 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how falling child mortality and wealth led families to invest in children, privacy and comfort.
unsureList.best: As infant and child mortality decreased, and commercial wealth increased, families dedicated more space and resources to children and child-rearing, as well as private life and comfort.

unsureList.text: Explain how cities drew rural migrants, transforming urban life and creating new problems.
unsureList.best: Cities offered economic opportunities, which attracted increasing migration from rural areas, transforming urban life and creating challenges for the new urbanites and their families.

unsureList.text: Explain how the Agricultural Revolution freed workers who migrated to cities.
unsureList.best: The Agricultural Revolution produced more food using fewer workers; as a result, people migrated from rural areas to the cities in search of work.

unsureList.text: Explain how urban growth eroded communal values and strained city governments.
unsureList.best: The growth of cities eroded traditional communal values, and city governments strained to provide protection and a healthy environment.

unsureList.text: Explain how concentrated urban poverty raised awareness of social problems and increased policing of marginal groups.
unsureList.best: The concentration of the poor in cities led to a greater awareness of poverty, crime, and prostitution as social problems, and prompted increased efforts to police marginal groups. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 4: Learning Objective E Explain the factors contributing to and the consequences of demographic changes from 1648 to 1815. Course Framework V.1 | 101 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how varied printed material, despite censorship, built a literate public and public opinion.
unsureList.best: Despite censorship, increasingly numerous and varied printed materials served a growing literate public and led to the development of public opinion.

unsureList.text: Explain how science, literature and popular culture exposed Europeans to non-European peoples and challenged social norms.
unsureList.best: Natural sciences, literature, and popular culture increasingly exposed Europeans to representations of peoples outside Europe and, on occasion, challenges to accepted social norms. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 102 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the arts shifted from religious and royal themes to private life and the public good.
unsureList.best: The arts moved from the celebration of religious themes and royal power to an emphasis on private life and the public good.

unsureList.text: Describe how Baroque art and music until about 1750 promoted faith and royal power.
unsureList.best: KC-2.3.V The arts moved from the celebration of religious themes and royal power to an emphasis on private life and the public good.

unsureList.text: Explain how 18th-century art reflected bourgeois values and how Neoclassicism expressed citizenship ideals.
unsureList.best: KC-2.4.II The consumer revolution of the 18th century was shaped by a new concern for privacy, encouraged the purchase of new goods for homes, and created new venues for leisure activities. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 4: Learning Objective F Explain how European cultural and intellectual life was maintained and changed throughout the period from 1648 to 1815. Course Framework V.1 | 103 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the consumer revolution brought privacy, new household goods and new leisure venues.
unsureList.best: The consumer revolution of the 18th century was shaped by a new concern for privacy, encouraged the purchase of new goods for homes, and created new venues for leisure activities. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 4: Learning Objective F Explain how European cultural and intellectual life was maintained and changed throughout the period from 1648 to 1815. Course Framework V.1 | 103 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe how some eastern and central European states experimented with enlightened absolutism.
unsureList.best: In the 18th century, a number of states in eastern and central Europe experimented with enlightened absolutism.

unsureList.text: Explain how most western and central governments granted toleration to Christian minorities, and some civil equality to Jews, by 1800.
unsureList.best: By 1800, most governments in western and central Europe had extended toleration to Christian minorities and, in some states, civil equality to Jews. THEMATICFOCUS National and European Identity NEI Definitions and perceptions of regional, cultural, national, and European identity have developed and been challenged over time, with varied and often profound effects on the political, social, and cultural order in Europe. unsureList.text: Explain how Westphalia's limits on the Empire let Prussia rise and the Habsburgs turn eastward.
unsureList.best: As a result of the Holy Roman Empire’s limitation of sovereignty in the Peace of Westphalia, Prussia rose to power, and the Habsburgs, centered in Austria, shifted their empire eastward. Course Framework V.1 | 104 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the French Revolution fundamentally challenged Europe's political and social order.
unsureList.best: The French Revolution posed a fundamental challenge to Europe’s existing political and social order.

unsureList.text: Explain how Napoleon spread French control in the name of revolutionary ideals and provoked nationalist reaction.
unsureList.best: Claiming to defend the ideals of the French Revolution, Napoleon Bonaparte imposed French control over much of the European continent, which eventually provoked a nationalistic reaction.

unsureList.text: Explain how commercial rivalries shaped diplomacy and war in early modern Europe.
unsureList.best: Commercial rivalries influenced diplomacy and warfare among European states in the early modern era.

unsureList.text: Explain how a revival of emotion and feeling challenged Enlightenment values.
unsureList.best: While Enlightenment values dominated the world of European ideas and culture, they were challenged by the revival of public expression of emotions and feeling.

unsureList.text: Describe how European sea powers competed for Atlantic influence in the 1700s.
unsureList.best: European sea powers vied for Atlantic influence throughout the 18th century.

unsureList.text: Explain how Asian rivalries ended in British rule in India and Dutch control of the East Indies.
unsureList.best: Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British rivalries in Asia culminated in British domination in India and Dutch control of the East Indies. Course Framework V.1 | 114 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the Britain-France rivalry produced world wars and put Britain ahead of France.
unsureList.best: Rivalry between Britain and France resulted in world wars fought both in Europe and in the colonies, with Britain supplanting France as the greatest European power. Course Framework V.1 | 115 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how long-term causes, Enlightenment ideas and fiscal crisis produced the French Revolution.
unsureList.best: The French Revolution resulted from a combination of long-term social and political causes, as well as Enlightenment ideas, exacerbated by short-term fiscal and economic crises.

unsureList.text: Describe the liberal phase: constitutional monarchy, wider participation, a nationalised Church and no hereditary privilege.
unsureList.best: The first, or liberal, phase of the French Revolution established a constitutional monarchy, increased popular participation, nationalized the Catholic Church, and abolished hereditary privileges.

unsureList.text: Describe the Jacobin republic under Robespierre: the Terror, price controls and de-Christianisation.
unsureList.best: After the execution of Louis XVI, the radical Jacobin republic led by Robespierre responded to opposition at home and war abroad by instituting the Reign of Terror, fixing prices and wages, and pursuing a policy of de-Christianization.

unsureList.text: Explain how mass-conscripted revolutionary armies carried French changes to the rest of Europe.
unsureList.best: Revolutionary armies, raised by mass conscription, sought to bring the changes initiated in France to the rest of Europe. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 116 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how women joined the early revolution but were soon excluded from citizenship.
unsureList.best: Women enthusiastically participated in the early phases of the revolution; however, while there were brief improvements in the legal status of women, citizenship in the republic was soon restricted to men. Course Framework V.1 | 117 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how revolutionary ideals inspired the Haitian revolt led by Toussaint L'Ouverture.
unsureList.best: Revolutionary ideals inspired a revolt of enslaved people led by Toussaint L’Ouverture in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which became the independent nation of Haiti in 1804.

unsureList.text: Contrast those inspired by equality and rights with critics of the revolution's violence.
unsureList.best: While many were inspired by the revolution’s emphasis on equality and human rights, others condemned its violence and disregard for traditional authority. Course Framework V.1 | 118 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe Napoleon's lasting domestic reforms alongside curbed rights and manipulated popular feeling.
unsureList.best: As first consul and emperor, Napoleon undertook a number of enduring domestic reforms while often curtailing some rights and manipulating popular impulses behind a façade of representative institutions.

unsureList.text: Explain how new tactics let Napoleon control much of Europe and spread revolutionary ideals.
unsureList.best: KC-2.1.V.D After the defeat of Napoleon by a coalition of European powers, the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815) attempted to restore the balance of power in Europe and contain the danger of revolutionary or nationalistic upheavals in the future. Course Framework V.1 | 120 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how Napoleon's empire stirred nationalist responses across Europe.
unsureList.best: Napoleon’s expanding empire created nationalist responses throughout Europe. Course Framework V.1 | 119 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the Congress of Vienna sought to restore the balance of power and contain revolution and nationalism.
unsureList.best: After the defeat of Napoleon by a coalition of European powers, the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815) attempted to restore the balance of power in Europe and contain the danger of revolutionary or nationalistic upheavals in the future. Course Framework V.1 | 120 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how Rousseau questioned sole reliance on reason and stressed emotion in moral improvement.
unsureList.best: Rousseau questioned the exclusive reliance on reason and emphasized the role of emotions in the moral improvement of self and society.

unsureList.text: Explain how Romanticism emerged as a challenge to Enlightenment rationality.
unsureList.best: Romanticism emerged as a challenge to Enlightenment rationality.

unsureList.text: Describe the religious revival, such as Methodism under John Wesley, that fit the Romantic Movement.
unsureList.best: Consistent with the Romantic Movement, religious revival occurred in Europe and included notable movements such as Methodism, founded by John Wesley.

unsureList.text: Explain how revolution and war showed the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism.
unsureList.best: Revolution, war, and rebellion demonstrated the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism. TOPIC5.8 Romanticism SUGGESTEDSKILL Contextualization 4.B Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context. unsureList.text: Explain how the Industrial Revolution spread from Britain to the continent, with states playing a bigger promoting role.
unsureList.best: The Industrial Revolution spread from Great Britain to the continent, where the state played a greater role in promoting industry.

unsureList.text: Describe how Britain led through mechanised textiles, iron and steel, and new transport in a favourable political and social climate.
unsureList.best: Great Britain established its industrial dominance through the mechanization of textile production, iron and steel production, and new transportation systems in conjunction with uniquely favorable political and social climates.

unsureList.text: Explain how industrialisation took root on the continent, sometimes with state sponsorship.
unsureList.best: Following the British example, industrialization took root in continental Europe, sometimes with state sponsorship. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 143 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how daily life was shaped by industrialisation according to a region's level of development.
unsureList.best: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by industrialization, depending on the level of industrial development in a particular location.

unsureList.text: Explain how industrialisation produced new classes in industrial regions.
unsureList.best: Industrialization promoted the development of new classes in the industrial regions of Europe.

unsureList.text: Explain how rapid population growth and urbanisation caused social dislocation.
unsureList.best: Europe experienced rapid population growth and urbanization, leading to social dislocations.

unsureList.text: Explain how industrialisation changed family structure and relations for bourgeois and working-class families.
unsureList.best: Over time, the Industrial Revolution altered the family structure and relations for bourgeois and working-class families.

unsureList.text: Explain how political revolutions and industrial complications triggered ideological, governmental and collective responses.
unsureList.best: Political revolutions and the complications resulting from industrialization triggered a range of ideological, governmental, and collective responses.

unsureList.text: Explain how ideologies took root as responses to industrial and political revolutions.
unsureList.best: Ideologies developed and took root throughout society as a response to industrial and political revolutions.

unsureList.text: Explain how governments, sometimes under pressure from organisations, responded to industrial problems.
unsureList.best: Governments, at times based on the pressure of political or social organizations, responded to problems created or exacerbated by industrialization. Course Framework V.1 | 131 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how Britain's coal, iron ore and other raw materials supported industrial growth.
unsureList.best: Britain’s ready supplies of coal, iron ore, and other essential raw materials promoted industrial growth.

unsureList.text: Explain how engineers, inventors and capitalists, working through private initiative, helped Britain lead industrialisation.
unsureList.best: Economic institutions and human capital such as engineers, inventors, and capitalists helped Britain lead the process of industrialization, largely through private initiative.

unsureList.text: Explain how Britain's parliament promoted industry because commercial interests were represented in it.
unsureList.best: Britain’s parliamentary government promoted commercial and industrial interests because those interests were represented in Parliament.

unsureList.text: Describe France's slower, state-supported industrialisation that disturbed traditional production less than Britain's.
unsureList.best: KC-3.1.I Great Britain established its industrial dominance through the mechanization of textile production, iron and steel production, and new transportation systems in conjunction with uniquely favorable political and social climates.

unsureList.text: Explain why eastern and southern Europe lagged: geography, resources, landed elites, serfdom and weak sponsorship.
unsureList.best: A combination of factors, including geography, lack of resources, the dominance of traditional landed elites, the persistence of serfdom in some areas, and inadequate government sponsorship, accounted for eastern and southern Europe’s lag in industrial development.

unsureList.text: Explain how old farming and landholding patterns left some areas behind, with famine, debt and land shortages.
unsureList.best: Because of the continued existence of more primitive agricultural practices and land-owning patterns, some areas of Europe lagged in industrialization while facing famine, debt, and land shortages. Course Framework V.1 | 133 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe how from about 1870 to 1914 industry spread to more areas and grew in scale and complexity.
unsureList.best: During the second industrial revolution (c. 1870–1914), more areas of Europe experienced industrial activity, and industrial processes increased in scale and complexity.

unsureList.text: Explain how mechanisation and the factory system became the dominant production mode by 1914.
unsureList.best: Mechanization and the factory system became the predominant modes of production by 1914.

unsureList.text: Explain how railways and new communications integrated national economies and created a global economic network.
unsureList.best: Newtechnologiesandmeansofcommunication and transportation—including railroads— resulted in more fully integrated national economies, a higher level of urbanization, and a truly global economic network.

unsureList.text: Explain how late-19th-century business cycles led firms and governments to manage markets with monopolies, banking and tariffs.
unsureList.best: Volatile business cycles in the last quarter of the 19th century led corporations and governments to try to manage the market through a variety of methods, including monopolies, banking practices, and tariffs.

unsureList.text: Explain how better harvests and industrialisation raised population, life expectancy and infant survival.
unsureList.best: Along with better harvests caused in part by the commercialization of agriculture, industrialization promoted population growth, longer life expectancy, and lowered infant mortality.

unsureList.text: Explain how the second industrial revolution fed a heightened consumerism.
unsureList.best: A heightened consumerism developed as a result of the second industrial revolution.

unsureList.text: Explain how mass production and marketing increased supply and demand for new goods and leisure.
unsureList.best: Industrialization and mass marketing increased both the production and demand for a new range of consumer goods— including clothing, processed foods, and labor-saving devices—and created more leisure opportunities.

unsureList.text: Explain how efficient transport and innovations created industries, spread goods, and raised quality of life.
unsureList.best: New, efficient methods of transportation and other innovations created new industries, improved the distribution of goods, increased consumerism, and enhanced quality of life. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 6: Learning Objective C Explain how innovations and advances in technology during the Industrial Revolutions led to economic and social change. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 134 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how labour divisions in industrial areas created self-conscious classes, including proletariat and bourgeoisie.
unsureList.best: In industrialized areas of Europe (i.e., western and northern Europe), socioeconomic changes created divisions of labor that led to the development of self-conscious classes, including the proletariat and the bourgeoisie.

unsureList.text: Explain how agricultural elites stayed dominant in less industrialised areas into the 20th century.
unsureList.best: In some of the less industrialized areas of Europe, the dominance of agricultural elites continued into the 20th century.

unsureList.text: Explain how associations, mutual aid societies and unions built class identity.
unsureList.best: Class identity developed and was reinforced through participation in philanthropic, political, and social associations among the middle classes, and in mutual aid societies and trade unions among the working classes.

unsureList.text: Explain how rural-to-urban migration crowded cities and weakened rural communities.
unsureList.best: With migration from rural to urban areas in industrialized regions, cities experienced overcrowding, while affected rural areas suffered declines in available labor as well as weakened communities. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 136 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how wages, labour laws, welfare, diet and birth control improved working-class life by century's end.
unsureList.best: By the end of the century, higher wages, laws restricting the labor of children and women, social welfare programs, improved diet, and increased access to birth control affected the quality of life for the working class.

unsureList.text: Explain how companionate marriage spread from the middle class to the working class.
unsureList.best: Economic motivations for marriage, while still important for all classes, diminished as the middle-class notion of companionate marriage began to be adopted by the working classes.

unsureList.text: Describe leisure centred on family and small groups, with new activities and spaces.
unsureList.best: Leisure time centered increasingly on the family or small groups, concurrent with the development of activities and spaces to use that time. Course Framework V.1 | 137 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how conservatism defended traditional authority on the view that human nature is not perfectible.
unsureList.best: Conservatives developed a new ideology in support of traditional political and religious authorities, which was based on the idea that human nature was not perfectible.

unsureList.text: Explain how the Concert of Europe tried to preserve the status quo through collective action and conservatism.
unsureList.best: KC-3.4.I.D The revolutions of 1848, triggered by economic hardship and discontent with the political status quo, challenged conservative politicians and governments and led to the breakdown of the Concert of Europe.

unsureList.text: Explain how the 1848 revolutions, sparked by hardship and discontent, broke down the Concert of Europe.
unsureList.best: The revolutions of 1848, triggered by economic hardship and discontent with the political status quo, challenged conservative politicians and governments and led to the breakdown of the Concert of Europe.

unsureList.best: Required Course Content THEMATICFOCUS States and Other Institutions of Power SOP European states and nations developed governmental and civil institutions from 1450 to the present to organize society and consolidate political power, with a variety of social, cultural, and economic effects. unsureList.text: Describe liberalism's focus on sovereignty, rights and self-interest, and debate over who should take part in governing.
unsureList.best: Liberals emphasized popular sovereignty, individual rights, and enlightened self-interest but debated the extent to which all groups in society should actively participate in its governance.

unsureList.text: Describe radicals' and republicans' demands for universal male suffrage and, for some, women's rights.
unsureList.best: Radicals in Britain and republicans on the continent demanded universal male suffrage and full citizenship without regard to wealth and property ownership; some argued that such rights should be extended to women.

unsureList.text: Explain how socialists demanded redistribution of wealth, moving from utopian ideas to a Marxist critique of capitalism.
unsureList.best: KC-3.3.I.B Radicals in Britain and republicans on the continent demanded universal male suffrage and full citizenship without regard to wealth and property ownership; some argued that such rights should be extended to women.

unsureList.text: Explain how Marx's scientific socialism analysed capitalism and historical change systematically and deterministically.
unsureList.best: Industrialization and Its Effects UNIT

unsureList.text: Describe the anarchist view that all government is unnecessary and should give way to voluntary cooperation.
unsureList.best: KC-3.3.I.A Liberals emphasized popular sovereignty, individual rights, and enlightened self-interest but debated the extent to which all groups in society should actively participate in its governance.

unsureList.text: Explain how political movements and social groups responded to industrial problems.
unsureList.best: Political movements and social organizations responded to problems of industrialization.

unsureList.text: Explain how mass-based parties became vehicles for reform.
unsureList.best: Mass-based political parties emerged as sophisticated vehicles for social, economic, and political reform.

unsureList.text: Describe how workers' unions and movements pushed for reform and grew into political parties.
unsureList.best: Workers established labor unions and movements promoting social and economic reforms that also developed into political parties.

unsureList.text: Describe feminists' campaigns for women's legal, economic and political rights and better working conditions.

unsureList.text: Explain how economic collapse and total war caused internal conflict and a clash among democracy, communism and fascism.

unsureList.text: Explain how 20th-century movements questioned objective knowledge, reason and religion's moral role.

unsureList.text: Explain how science and technology brought both material benefits and immense destruction.

unsureList.text: Contrast the century's war and genocide with its large gains in living standards.

unsureList.best: The Bolshevik takeover prompted a protracted civil war between communist forces and their opponents, who were aided by foreign powers.

unsureList.best: The League of Nations, created to prevent future wars, was weakened from the outset by the nonparticipation of major powers, including the U.S., Germany, and the Soviet Union.

unsureList.text: Explain how weak international trade and monetary practice caused the Great Depression, which undermined democracies and spurred radicalism.
unsureList.best: The Great Depression, caused by weaknesses in international trade and monetary theories and practices, undermined Western European democracies and fomented radical political responses throughout Europe.

unsureList.text: Explain how war debt, tariffs, overproduction, weak currencies and speculation weakened economies.
unsureList.best: World War I debt, nationalistic tariff policies, overproduction, depreciated currencies, disrupted trade patterns, and speculation created weaknesses in economies worldwide.

unsureList.text: Explain how the 1929 crash and the end of American capital flows caused financial collapse in Europe.
unsureList.best: Dependence on post-World War I American investment capital led to financial collapse when, following the 1929 stock market crash, the United States cut off capital flows to Europe.

unsureList.text: Explain how Western democracies failed to beat the Depression and were weakened by extremists.
unsureList.best: Despite attempts to rethink economic theories and policies and forge political alliances, Western democracies failed to overcome the Great Depression and were weakened by extremist movements. unsureList.text: Explain how fascist dictatorships used technology and propaganda, leader cults and glorified war to attract the disillusioned.
unsureList.best: Fascist dictatorships used modern technology and propaganda that rejected democratic institutions, promoted charismatic leaders, and glorified war and nationalism to attract the disillusioned.

unsureList.text: Explain how Mussolini and Hitler gained power by exploiting bitterness, terror and weak democracies.
unsureList.best: Mussolini and Hitler rose to power by exploiting postwar bitterness and economic instability, using terror, and manipulating the fledgling and unpopular democracies in their countries. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 178 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how Franco's fascist-backed victory in Spain served as a testing ground for World War II.

unsureList.text: Explain how authoritarian dictatorships replaced failed democracies in interwar central and eastern Europe.

unsureList.text: Explain how Blitzkrieg and Japan's attacks gave the Axis early victories.

unsureList.best: American and British industrial, scientific, and technological power, cooperative military efforts under the strong leadership of individuals such as Winston Churchill, the resistance of civilians, and the all-out military commitment of the USSR contributed critically to the Allied victories.

unsureList.text: Explain how military technology enabled industrialised war, genocide, nuclear proliferation and nuclear risk.

unsureList.text: Explain how Nazi racism and anti-Semitism, with help from collaborators, led to the Holocaust.

unsureList.text: Describe the losses of World War II: a generation of men, European Jewry and other targeted groups, mass migration and weakened class hierarchies.

unsureList.text: Explain how war anxiety led to a plurality of intellectual frameworks.

unsureList.text: Explain why Europeans before World War I trusted science and technology despite new theories and psychology.

unsureList.text: Explain how the challenge to Newtonian physics undermined faith in objective knowledge while enabling nuclear power.

unsureList.text: Explain how World War I created a lost generation, disillusionment, changed women's lives and democratised society.
unsureList.best: World War I created a “lost generation” and fostered disillusionment and cynicism, while it transformed the lives of women, and democratized societies.

unsureList.text: Explain how family and work duties, economic change and feminism defined women's lives.
unsureList.best: The lives of women were defined by family and work responsibilities, economic changes, and feminism.

unsureList.text: Explain how feminists in the west and government policy in the east won women the vote, education and professional careers.
unsureList.best: In Western Europe through the efforts of feminists, and in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union through government policy, women finally gained the vote, greater educational opportunities, and access to professional careers, even while continuing to face social inequalities.

unsureList.text: Explain how new forms of marriage, partnership, motherhood, divorce and reproduction widened women's personal options.
unsureList.best: New modes of marriage, partnership, motherhood,divorce,andreproductiongave women more options in their personal lives.

unsureList.text: Explain how women won high political office and more seats in legislatures.
unsureList.best: Women attained high political office and increased their representation in legislative bodies in many nations. Course Framework V.1 | 202 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how the postwar baby boom, often encouraged by governments, followed economic recovery.
unsureList.best: With economic recovery after World War II, the birth rate increased dramatically (the baby boom), often promoted by government policies.

unsureList.text: Explain how decolonisation proceeded across the century with varied cooperation, interference or resistance from imperial states.
unsureList.best: The process of decolonization occurred over the course of the century with varying degrees of cooperation, interference, or resistance from European imperialist states.

unsureList.text: Explain how Wilson's self-determination principle raised expectations in the non-European world after World War I.
unsureList.best: At the end of World War I, U.S. President Woodrow Wilson’s principle of national self-determination raised expectations in the non-European world for new policies and freedoms.

unsureList.text: Explain why independence for many African and Asian territories was delayed to the mid- and late 1900s.
unsureList.best: Required Course Content THEMATICFOCUS Interaction of Europe and the World INT Motivated by a variety of factors, Europe’s interaction with the world led to political, economic, social, and cultural exchanges that influenced both European and non-European societies. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 9: Learning Objective I Explain the various ways in which colonial groups around the world sought independence from colonizers in the 20th and 21st centuries. HISTORICALDEVELOPMENTS

unsureList.text: Explain how European states set aside nationalist rivalries for economic and political integration.
unsureList.best: European states began to set aside nationalist rivalries in favor of economic and political integration, forming a series of transnational unions that grew in size and scope over the second half of the 20th century.

unsureList.text: Trace how the Coal and Steel Community grew into the EEC and EU and a shared European identity.
unsureList.best: THEMATICFOCUS National and European Identity NEI Definitions and perceptions of regional, cultural, national, and European identity have developed and been challenged over time, with varied and often profound effects on the political, social, and cultural order in Europe. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE Unit 9: Learning Objective K Explain how the European Union affected national and European identity throughout the period following World War II to the present. HISTORICALDEVELOPMENTS

unsureList.text: Explain how EU members balance national sovereignty against membership duties.
unsureList.best: EU member nations continue to balance questions of national sovereignty with the responsibilities of membership in an economic and political union. Course Framework V.1 | 205 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how immigration changed Europe's religious makeup and sparked debate over religion in public life.
unsureList.best: Increased immigration into Europe altered Europe’s religious makeup, causing debate and conflict over the role of religion in social and political life.

unsureList.text: Explain how postwar migrant workers later faced anti-immigrant agitation and extreme nationalist parties after the 1970s downturn.
unsureList.best: Because of the economic growth of the 1950s and 1960s, migrant workers from southern Europe, Asia, and Africa immigrated to western and central Europe; however, after the economic downturn of the 1970s, these workers and their families often became targets of anti-immigrant agitation and extreme nationalist political parties. Course Framework V.1 | 206 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how medical advances extended life but raised social and moral questions without consensus.
unsureList.best: Medical theories and technologies extended life but posed social and moral questions that eluded consensus and crossed religious, political, and philosophical perspectives. SUGGESTEDSKILL Making Connections 5.B Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process. unsureList.text: Explain how imports of US technology and popular culture brought both enthusiasm and criticism.
unsureList.best: Increased imports of U.S. technology and popular culture after World War II generated both enthusiasm and criticism.

unsureList.text: Explain how new communication and transport technology multiplied connections and drove globalisation.
unsureList.best: New communication and transportation technologies multiplied the connections across space and time, transforming daily life and contributing to the proliferation of ideas and to globalization.

unsureList.text: Explain how Green parties challenged consumerism, urged sustainability and warned about globalisation.
unsureList.best: Green parties in Western and Central Europe challenged consumerism, urged sustainable development, and, by the late 20th century, cautioned against globalization. Course Framework V.1 | 208 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how war and depression undermined faith in science and reason, giving rise to existentialism and postmodernism.
unsureList.best: The effects of world war and economic depression undermined this confidence in science and human reason, giving impetus to existentialism and producing postmodernism in the post-1945 period.

unsureList.text: Explain how organised religion stayed part of European life despite conflict, secularism and rapid change.
unsureList.best: Organized religion continued to play a role in European social and cultural life despite the challenges of military and ideological conflict, modern secularism, and rapid social changes.

unsureList.text: Explain how the Second Vatican Council redefined Catholic doctrine and began redefining relations with other religions.
unsureList.best: Reform in the Catholic Church found expression in the Second Vatican Council, which redefined the church’s doctrine and practices and started to redefine its relations with other religious communities. continued on next page Course Framework V.1 | 209 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Explain how 20th-century arts were defined by experiment, self-expression, subjectivity and rising US influence.
unsureList.best: During the 20th century, the arts were defined by experimentation, self-expression, subjectivity, and the increasing influence of the United States in both elite and popular culture.

unsureList.text: Describe how new visual arts, architecture and music shifted aesthetic standards and satirised Western values.
unsureList.best: New movements in the visual arts, architecture, and music radically shifted existing aesthetic standards, explored subconscious and subjective states, and satirized Western society and its values.

unsureList.text: Explain how writers challenged literary conventions and Western values and tackled controversial issues.
unsureList.best: Throughout the century, a number of writers challenged traditional literary conventions, questioned Western values, and addressed controversial social and political issues.

unsureList.text: Explain how mass production and efficiency raised incomes and created a consumer culture with new household comforts.
unsureList.best: Mass production, new food technologies, and industrial efficiency increased disposable income and created a consumer culture in which greater domestic comforts such as electricity, indoor plumbing, plastics, and synthetic fibers became available.

unsureList.text: Describe women's, gay and lesbian, and other movements seeking expanded civil rights, with mixed success and opposition.
unsureList.best: Various movements, including women’s movements, political and social movements, gay and lesbian movements, and others, worked for expanded civil rights, in some cases obtaining the goals they sought, and in others facing strong opposition.

unsureList.text: Explain how intellectuals and youth reacted against bourgeois materialism, notably in the 1968 revolts.
unsureList.best: Intellectuals and youth reacted against perceived bourgeois materialism and decadence, most significantly with the revolts of 1968. Course Framework V.1 | 210 AP European History Course and Exam Description Return to Table of Contents © 2026 College Board

unsureList.text: Define Latin words and phrases, including the core vocabulary list.
unsureList.best: GRAM-1.B A noun in the nominative case can show the subject of a verb. SKILLCATEGORY1 Read and comprehend Latin prose.

unsureList.text: Work out the meaning of Latin words and phrases from their context.
unsureList.best: 1.A Identify the meaning of Latin words and phrases. 1.B Describe how grammar contributes to the meaning and function of Latin words and phrases in context 1.C Summarize Latin texts in English. 1.D Translate Latin texts into English.

unsureList.text: Explain that Latin nouns have gender, number and case set by their declension endings.
unsureList.best: Latin nouns have a gender, number, and case. The number and case of a noun are indicated bythenoun’sspecificendings,whichare dictatedbywhatgroup—calledadeclension— thenounbelongsto.Declensionssometimes, but not always, identify the noun’s gender as well.

unsureList.text: Recognize the nominative as the subject of a verb.
unsureList.best: A noun in the nominative case can show the subject of a verb.

unsureList.text: Recognize that both words joined by a linking verb are usually nominative.
unsureList.best: When a verb connects two ideas, both are usually in the nominative case. GENITIVE

unsureList.text: Recognize the genitive as showing possession.
unsureList.best: GRAM-1.C When a verb connects two ideas, both are usually in the nominative case. GENITIVE

unsureList.text: Recognize the genitive of description, whole (partitive) and objective use.
unsureList.best: GRAM-1.P Course Return to Table of Cont © 2025 College Boar ents d The nouns causa and gratia in the ablative case can follow nouns in the genitive case. In this use, both are translated as “for the sake of.” Framework V.1 | 16 AP Latin Course and Exam Description

unsureList.text: Recognize the dative as person to or for whom something is done.
unsureList.best: Nouns in the dative case show the person to whom, for whom, or to whose advantage the action is being done. These nouns can be used with verbs of speaking, giving, and showing and can be translated as “to ____” or “for ____.”

unsureList.text: Recognize the dative of purpose and the double dative.
unsureList.best: A noun in the dative case (e.g., usui) can show purpose, often paired with a dative of reference in a double dative construction.

unsureList.text: Recognize the dative of possession with sum and lack with desum.
unsureList.best: A noun in the dative case can be used with a form of sum to show possession or desum to show lack of possession.

unsureList.text: Recognize the accusative as direct object.
unsureList.best: A noun in the accusative case can be the direct object of a verb; it is the noun receiving the action of a verb.

unsureList.text: Recognize the accusative showing duration of time.
unsureList.best: GRAM-1.I A noun in the accusative case can be the direct object of a verb; it is the noun receiving the action of a verb.

unsureList.text: Recognize ablative means, agent, manner, place, time and separation.
unsureList.best: Nouns in the ablative case have a variety of functions. These nouns most commonly show the means by which an action is done, by whom an action is done, the manner in which an action is done, where or when an action takes place, or the separation between people or things.

unsureList.text: Recognize the ablative of respect ("in regard to").
unsureList.best: A noun in the ablative case, translated as “in ____,” “in respect to ____,” or “in regard to ____,” can show in what respect a statement may be true.

unsureList.text: Recognize the ablative of description with an adjective.
unsureList.best: The ablative case with an adjective can show description of a noun and is often translated “with ____” or “of ____” (e.g., vir animo bono: a man with a good mind).

unsureList.text: Recognize the ablative of comparison after comparatives ("than").
unsureList.best: GRAM-1.L A noun in the ablative case, translated as “in ____,” “in respect to ____,” or “in regard to ____,” can show in what respect a statement may be true.

unsureList.text: Recognize causa and gratia in the ablative after a genitive as "for the sake of".
unsureList.best: The nouns causa and gratia in the ablative case can follow nouns in the genitive case. In this use, both are translated as “for the sake of.”

unsureList.text: Recognize the ablative absolute as time or circumstance of an action.
unsureList.best: A noun and participle in the ablative case form an ablative absolute and can show the time or circumstance of an action. Rarely, the participle can be replaced by a second noun.

unsureList.text: Recognize the locative and place-to/place-from constructions for city names.
unsureList.best: LEARNING OBJECTIVE ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE GRAM-1 Describe how Latin nouns function in context and contribute to the meaning of the text. (continued) LOCATIVE

unsureList.text: Recognize the vocative as direct address.
unsureList.best: LEARNING OBJECTIVE ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE GRAM-1 Describe how Latin nouns function in context and contribute to the meaning of the text. (continued) LOCATIVE

unsureList.text: Explain that stem and ending give a verb's person, number, tense, voice and mood, including irregular and omitted sum.
unsureList.best: The person, number, tense, voice, and mood of a verb are indicated by a combination of its stem and ending. The specific endings are dictatedbywhatgroup—calledaconjugation— the verb belongs to. Irregular verbs (e.g., sum, esse) do not follow the expected patterns of a conjugation. Additionally, forms of sum, esse aresometimesomittedandmustbe inferred from context.

unsureList.text: Recognize the indicative mood for statements of fact.
unsureList.best: The indicative mood of verbs is used for statements of fact or reality.

unsureList.text: Identify and translate the six indicative tenses.
unsureList.best: There are six tenses of verbs in the indicative mood: present (____[s], is/are ____ing), imperfect (was/were ____ing, used to ____), future (will ____), perfect (____ed, has/have ____ed, did ____), pluperfect (had ____ed), and future perfect (will have ____ed).

unsureList.text: Translate ut with an indicative verb as "like", "as" or "when".
unsureList.best: When ut introduces a clause with an indicative verb the ut is translated “like,” “as,” or “when.”

unsureList.text: Recognize the many uses of the subjunctive and how a main-clause subjunctive is translated.
unsureList.best: The subjunctive mood has many uses: commands, conditions, wishes, possibility, and dependent clauses. A subjunctive in the main clause can be translated as “may ____,” “might ____,” “would ____,” “should ____,” “let ____,” and “I wish that ____.”

unsureList.text: Recognize indirect questions.
unsureList.best: Clauses introduced by question words and having verbs in the subjunctive mood are called indirect questions.

unsureList.text: Recognize result clauses with ut and their signal words.
unsureList.best: GRAM-2.F Clauses introduced by question words and having verbs in the subjunctive mood are called indirect questions.

unsureList.text: Recognize purpose clauses and indirect commands.
unsureList.best: GRAM-2.J The imperative mood of verbs is used for commands. VOICE

unsureList.text: Recognize conditions introduced by si, nisi and ni, in either mood.
unsureList.best: Conditions in Latin are introduced by si (“if”), nisi (“if not”), and sometimes ni (“not”). The verb in either part of the condition may be in either the subjunctive or indicative mood. MOOD – IMPERATIVE

unsureList.text: Recognize the imperative for commands.
unsureList.best: The imperative mood of verbs is used for commands.

unsureList.text: Tell active from passive voice.
unsureList.best: GRAM-2.J The imperative mood of verbs is used for commands. VOICE

unsureList.text: Recognize deponent verbs: passive form, active meaning.
unsureList.best: Some verbs, called deponent verbs, have passive forms in Latin but are translated into Englishwithactivemeanings.Deponentverbs are often listed with three principal parts that look passive (e.g., orior, oriri, ortus sum).

unsureList.text: Recognize the infinitive used with verbs like possum, volo and licet.
unsureList.best: The infinitive is used with certain verbs (e.g., possum, volo, licet) and is often translated as “to _____.”

unsureList.text: Recognize indirect statement: accusative subject with infinitive.
unsureList.best: A verb of speaking, thinking, feeling, etc., can introduce an indirect statement, with an accusative case noun as its subject and an infinitive as its verb.

unsureList.text: Tell a gerund from a gerundive and translate each.
unsureList.best: A gerund is a noun formed from a verb (e.g., bellandi: of waging war). Like the gerund, a gerundive is an adjective formed from a verb, and it modifies a noun (e.g., ad eas res conficiendas: for preparing these things).

unsureList.text: Recognize the gerundive of obligation with a dative agent.
unsureList.best: A gerundive (often but not always with a form of the verb sum, esse) can show necessity or obligation. A dative case noun can be used to show the agent of the action in this passive construction.

unsureList.text: Recognize the supine in -um and -u.
unsureList.best: LEARNING OBJECTIVE ESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE GRAM-2 Describe how Latin verbs and verbals function in context and contribute to the meaning of the text. (continued) MOOD – SUBJUNCTIVE (CONT’D)

unsureList.text: Explain that participles are verbal adjectives agreeing with nouns, with tense and voice.
unsureList.best: Participles can also describe nouns and are verbal adjectives that modify nouns. Like adjectives, they agree with nouns in case, number, and gender. Like verbs, they have a tense and a voice, and they may have objects. SPECIAL VERBS

unsureList.text: Recognize verbs that take dative, ablative or genitive objects.
unsureList.best: GRAM-2.R Participles can also describe nouns and are verbal adjectives that modify nouns. Like adjectives, they agree with nouns in case, number, and gender. Like verbs, they have a tense and a voice, and they may have objects. SPECIAL VERBS

unsureList.text: Explain that adjectives agree with nouns in gender, number and case, and may be used as nouns.
unsureList.best: Adjectives describe nouns and agree in gender, number, and case with the nouns they are describing. Adjectives usually modify an explicitly stated noun but may also modify an implied noun, when the adjective is used substantively. Adjectives occur in only the first three declensions but may modify nouns in any declension. Like nouns, an adjective’s gender, number, and case are indicated by its specific ending.

unsureList.text: Recognize and translate superlative adjectives.
unsureList.best: Superlative adjectives show the highest degree of the word and are often translated “____est” or “very ____.” The superlative degree of an adjective is indicated by its stem.

unsureList.text: Recognize and translate comparative adjectives.
unsureList.best: Comparative adjectives show a comparison between two words and are often translated “____er,” “more ____,” or “rather ____.” The comparative degree of an adjective is indicated by its stem. PRONOUNS

unsureList.text: Explain that pronouns have gender, number and case.
unsureList.best: Like nouns, pronouns have a gender, number, and case, which are indicated by a specific form.

unsureList.text: Find a pronoun's antecedent, which it matches in number and gender.
unsureList.best: The antecedent of a pronoun is the noun it refers to and takes the place of. This antecedent may be named earlier or simply be understood in the context. A pronoun agrees in number and gender with its antecedent.

unsureList.text: Recognize relative clauses with qui, quae, quod and how their case is set.
unsureList.best: Relative clauses are introduced by the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod. Like other pronouns, the antecedent of the relative pronoun is the noun it refers back to and gives more information about. The relative pronoun agrees in number and gender with its antecedent, but its case is determined by its use in the relative clause.

unsureList.text: Recognize the relative pronoun used as a demonstrative.
unsureList.best: Course Return to Table of Cont © 2025 College Boar ents d The relative pronoun can be used in Latin as a demonstrative pronoun and can be translated in English as “this,” “that,” “these,” or “those,” instead of “which” or “who.” Framework V.1 | 19 AP Latin Course and Exam Description

unsureList.text: Recognize adverbs, including comparative and superlative forms.
unsureList.best: An adverb can modify a verb, adjective, or other adverb. The comparative adverb ends in -ius,whilethesuperlativeadverboftenendsin-e.

unsureList.text: Recognize prepositional phrases with ablative or accusative.
unsureList.best: Prepositional phrases consist of a preposition and a noun, most often in the ablative or accusative cases.

unsureList.text: Translate cum clauses as "when", "since" or "although".
unsureList.best: When cum introduces a clause, it may be translated “when,” “since,” or “although,” among other acceptable translations. SKILL1.D Translate Latin texts into English. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE TRAN-1 Provide a translation of a text from Latin to English using idiomatic English.

unsureList.text: Recognize questions marked by interrogative words or -ne.
unsureList.best: Questions in Latin are typically introduced by interrogative words or the suffix -ne placed on the first or most important word of the question. SKILL1.D Translate Latin texts into English. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE TRAN-1 Provide a translation of a text from Latin to English using idiomatic English.

unsureList.text: Describe how authors use repetition for rhetorical or poetic effect.
unsureList.best: An author may repeat words or phrases for a variety of rhetorical or poetic effects. This can be done to stress the importance of an idea, to make a statement more memorable, or to give the text a more rhythmic, and at times musical, effect.

unsureList.text: Describe chiasmus (a-b-b-a) and its emphasis.
unsureList.best: Chiasmus is a rhetorical figure in which two corresponding pairs are arranged notfollowingaregularorderbutininvertedorder(a-b-b-a).Chiasmuscreates emphasis in speech, calling the reader’s or listener’s attention to that point.

unsureList.text: Describe interlocking word order (synchysis, a-b-a-b).
unsureList.best: To create an unexpected or emphatic moment in a text, an author may change the natural word order by using interlocking word order, also known as synchysis, withelementsplacedinana-b-a-bformat.

unsureList.text: Describe enjambment and its suspense.
unsureList.best: To create suspense or emphasis, an author may choose to delay the final word of a phrase, clause, or sentence to the beginning of the following poetic line. This delay is called enjambment.

unsureList.text: Describe similes as explicit comparisons that make images vivid.
unsureList.best: Repeated for review A simile is a rhetorical figure, in which an explicit comparison is made between two things, usually using “like” or “as” as connecting words. Similes tend to be used in descriptive passages and help make images more vivid or clear to the reader or listener. STYL-4 Describefeaturesofmeterin Latin poetry.

unsureList.text: Describe how epic poets echo predecessors, as Vergil drew on Homer.
unsureList.best: Epicpoetrywasahighlystylized,long-establishedgenreofpoetryintheancient world. In order to claim their place in that tradition, epic poets would use the same elements that their predecessors had, while adding their own personal contribution. For example, Vergil drew inspiration for the Aeneid from Greek epics, namely Homer’s Odyssey and Iliad.

unsureList.text: Describe the epic's structure: proem, invocation to the Muses, in medias res.
unsureList.best: An epic poem in the Greek and Roman tradition was a long narrative in verse, which started with a proem (a preface or prologue) and an invocation to the muses, followed by the start of the plot in medias res. SKILLCATEGORY2 Describe the style and context of Book 1, lines 1–33. 118 AP Latin Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Describe the gods' role in moving epic plots forward.
unsureList.best: In traditional epic poetry, the gods (which can be personified forces of nature) are always involved in and sometimes responsible for moving the narrative forward. SKILLCATEGORY2 Describe the style of Book 4, lines 74–89 and 165–197. 138 AP Latin Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Describe the epic hero, divine help and hindrance, and descent to the underworld.
unsureList.best: An epic poem usually follows the deeds of a hero who is helped and hindered by divine interventions and on many occasions must descend to the underworld to complete his or her quest. SKILLCATEGORY2 Describe the style and context of Book 6, lines 450–476, 788–800, and 847–853. 144 AP Latin Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Name other Latin genres: epigram, history, love poetry, didactic, drama, oratory, novels.
unsureList.best: Other genres of Latin literature include epigrams, historiography, love poems, didactic poetry, drama (tragedy and comedy), dialogues, oratory, ancient novels, and modern novellas. SKILL2.B DescribehistoricalandculturalcontextsofLatintexts. unsureList.text: Describe Vergil's life, works and lasting influence.
unsureList.best: Vergil (70–19 BCE) composed some of the most famous poems in Latin literature: the Eclogues (or Bucolics), the Georgics, and the Aeneid. His works were well known in his lifetime by most educated Romans, and they have had a lasting influence on Western literature.
