unsureList.text: Link LRAS to the PPC as maximum sustainable capacity.
unsureList.best: The LRAS curve corresponds to the production possibilities curve (PPC) because they both represent maximum sustainable capacity. Maximum sustainable capacity is the total output an economic system will produce over a set period of time if all resources are fully employed.

unsureList.text: Explain why LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.
unsureList.best: TheLRAScurveisverticalatthefull-employmentlevelof output because in the long run wages and prices fully adjust.

unsureList.best: Explain (using graphs as appropriate)theshort-run andlong-runequilibriumprice level and output level.

unsureList.text: Locate short-run equilibrium where AD meets SRAS.
unsureList.best: Short-runequilibriumoccurswhenthe aggregate quantity of output demanded and the aggregate quantity of output supplied are equal—i.e., at the intersection of the AD and SRAS curves.

unsureList.text: Locate long-run equilibrium where AD and SRAS meet on LRAS.
unsureList.best: Long-runequilibriumoccurswhentheADand SRAS curves intersect on the LRAS—i.e., at the full-employmentlevelofrealoutput.

unsureList.text: Show short-run output above, at or below full employment as inflationary or recessionary gaps.

unsureList.text: Show a positive or negative AD shock moves output, employment and prices the same way.
unsureList.best: A positive (negative) shock in AD causes output, employment, and the price level to rise

unsureList.text: Show a positive or negative SRAS shock moves output and employment opposite to prices.

unsureList.text: Explain prices signal marginal costs and benefits, so price equals marginal cost when efficient.

unsureList.text: Explain competitive firms sell all output at the market price.

unsureList.text: Explain price-taking firms produce where marginal cost equals marginal revenue.

unsureList.text: Explain price equals marginal benefit and marginal cost, giving allocative efficiency.

unsureList.text: Explain short-run profits or losses lead to entry or exit toward long-run equilibrium.

unsureList.text: Explain firms equalize marginal product per dollar across inputs to minimize cost.

unsureList.text: Explain why gravity dominates at large scales: large systems are electrically neutral.

changes.from: Describe symptoms and causes of selected trauma and stressor-related disorders.
changes.to: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected traumaandstressor-related disorders.

changes.from: Describe symptoms and causes of selected feeding and eating disorders.
changes.to: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected feeding and eating disorders.

changes.from: Describe symptoms and causes of selected personality disorders.
changes.to: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected personality disorders.

changes.from: Describe ethical principles in treating psychological disorders.
changes.to: Describe ethical principles in the treatment of psychological disorders.

changes.from: Describe techniques used with psychological therapies.
changes.to: Describe techniques used with psychological therapies.

changes.from: Describe person-centered therapy: active listening and unconditional positive regard.
changes.to: Therapy from the humanistic perspective, commonlyreferredtoasperson-centered therapy, employs active listening and unconditional positive regard. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

changes.from: Explain how group therapy differs from individual therapy.
changes.to: Explain how group therapy isdifferentfromindividual therapy.

changes.from: Describe effective uses of hypnosis.
changes.to: Describeeffectiveusesof hypnosis.

unsureList.text: Explain how heredity and environment together shape behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain the relationship between heredity and environment in shaping behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Explain that heredity (nature) and environment (nurture) interact to shape behavior.
unsureList.best: 1.1.A Explain the relationship between heredity and environment in shaping behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe the evolutionary perspective on natural selection and behavior, and its misuse in eugenics.
unsureList.best: The evolutionary perspective explores how naturalselectionaffectstheexpressionof behavior and mental processes to increase survival and reproductive success. Some theorists have sought to apply principles of the evolutionary perspective in ways that discriminate against others (eugenics).

unsureList.text: Identify twin, family and adoption studies as methods for studying gene effects.
unsureList.best: 1.1.A.1.ii Environmental factors, or “nurture,” refers to the external factors that one experiences, such as family interactions or education. Exclusion Statement: Specific information about genetics (genotype, phenotype, DNA, chromosomes, and recessive and dominant gene expression) is beyond the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Differentiate the subsystems of the human nervous system and their functions.
unsureList.best: Differentiateamongthe subsystems of the human nervous system and their functions.

unsureList.text: Describe the peripheral nervous system, with autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic, involuntary) and somatic (voluntary) parts.
unsureList.best: 1.2.A.2.i The autonomic nervous system governs processes that are involuntary and includes the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems.

unsureList.text: Distinguish neurons from glial cells.
unsureList.best: 1.3.A Explain how the structures and functions of typical neurons in the central nervoussystemaffect behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe the spinal-cord reflex arc of sensory, motor and interneurons.
unsureList.best: Inthespinalcord,thereflexarcdemonstrates how neurons within the central and peripheral nervous systems work together to respond to stimuli. Three types of neurons work together inthespinalcordtocreateareflexarc:sensory neurons, motor neurons, and interneurons.

unsureList.text: Explain how neural transmission relates to behavior.
unsureList.best: Explain how the basic process of neural transmission is related to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Explain neural transmission: all-or-none principle, threshold, depolarization, resting potential, refractory period and reuptake, and disorders when disrupted.
unsureList.best: 1.3.B Explain how the basic process of neural transmission is related to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and GABA.
unsureList.best: UNIT

unsureList.text: Describe hormones such as adrenaline, leptin, ghrelin, melatonin and oxytocin.
unsureList.best: UNIT

unsureList.text: Explain how drugs act as agonists, antagonists or reuptake inhibitors.
unsureList.best: 1.3.C Explain how psychoactive drugsaffectbehaviorand mental processes.

unsureList.text: Compare stimulants, depressants, hallucinogens and opioids.
unsureList.best: 1.3.C.2.iv Opioids, such as heroin, typically act as pain relievers.

unsureList.text: Describe tolerance, addiction and withdrawal.
unsureList.best: Psychoactive drug use can lead to tolerance and/or addiction. Addiction can create significantwithdrawalsymptomsifthe psychoactive drugs are no longer consumed. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Identify the brain stem and medulla as controlling breathing and heart rate.
unsureList.best: The brain stem (including the medulla) generally controls basic functioning such as breathing and heart rate.

unsureList.text: Identify the reticular activating system and reward center as controlling alertness, movement, learning and emotion.
unsureList.best: The reticular activating system and the brain’s reward center generally control alertness, some voluntary movement, eye movement, and some types of learning, cognition, and emotion.

unsureList.text: Identify the cerebellum as controlling coordination, balance and procedural learning.
unsureList.best: The cerebellum generally controls coordination of muscle movement, balance, and some forms of procedural learning.

unsureList.text: Describe the cortex hemispheres, limbic system, corpus callosum and the occipital, temporal, parietal and frontal lobes.
unsureList.best: The cerebral cortex is divided into two hemispheres and includes the limbic system (thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, hippocampus, amygdala), corpus callosum, and the lobes of the cortex.

unsureList.text: Explain split-brain research and left-hemisphere language areas Broca's and Wernicke's, and aphasia.
unsureList.best: 1.4.A.5.i Areasofthebrainthataffectlanguageare typically located in the left hemisphere and include Broca’s area (responsible for speech production) and Wernicke’s area (responsible for speech comprehension). Damage to these parts of the brain can lead to aphasia.

unsureList.text: Define brain plasticity, rewiring that lets other areas assume damaged functions.
unsureList.best: Brain plasticity is the ability of the brain to rewire itself or modify or create new connections throughout development and generally allows for the function of a damaged partofthebraintobeassumedbyadifferent part of the brain.

unsureList.text: Name brain research methods: EEG, fMRI scans, case studies and lesioning.
unsureList.best: Research on the brain is done using scans (including EEG and fMRI), case studies, and surgical procedures (such as lesioning) to promoteunderstandingofhowthedifferent structures of the brain work and how the brain functions together as a whole. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe consciousness as varying awareness, with sleep and wakefulness as two types.
unsureList.best: Consciousness has varying levels of awareness of thoughts, feelings, behavior, and events in individuals’ internal and external worlds. Sleep and wakefulness are two types of consciousness.

unsureList.text: Describe circadian rhythm, a roughly 24-hour cycle disrupted by jet lag and shift work.
unsureList.best: The sleep/wake cycle is a circadian rhythm, whichinhumansisabouta24-hourcycle. Jet lag and shift work are disruptions of the circadian rhythm.

unsureList.text: Describe sleep stages by EEG pattern, NREM stages 1 to 3 and paradoxical REM sleep with dreaming and rebound.
unsureList.best: Thestagesofsleepareidentifiedbytheir specificEEGpatterns.

unsureList.text: Compare activation-synthesis and consolidation theories of dreams.
unsureList.best: Theories regarding the structure and function ofdreamsincludeactivation-synthesisand consolidation theory. Exclusion Statement: The psychoanalytic theory of dreams is outside of the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Describe memory consolidation and restoration theories of why we sleep.
unsureList.best: Memory consolidation and restoration are current theories about why sleep occurs. These theories suggest that sleep is useful fororganizingandconsolidatingmemoriesor restoring depleted resources used throughout a given day.

unsureList.text: Describe sleep disorders such as insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea and somnambulism and their effects.
unsureList.best: 1.5.A.5 Memory consolidation and restoration are current theories about why sleep occurs. These theories suggest that sleep is useful fororganizingandconsolidatingmemoriesor restoring depleted resources used throughout a given day.

unsureList.text: Define sensation as detecting and transducing stimuli, with the absolute threshold at 50 percent detection.
unsureList.best: Sensation is the process of detecting information from the environment that meets a certain threshold and transducing stimuli into neurochemical messages for processing (perception) in the brain. The absolute threshold occurs when a stimulus can be detected at least 50% of the time.

unsureList.text: Explain just-noticeable difference, sensory adaptation and Weber's law.
unsureList.best: Detection of change in stimuli or diminished sensitivity to stimuli can be explained by thejust-noticeabledifferenceandsensory adaptation. Weber’s law describes the degree towhichstimulineedtobedifferentforthe differencetobedetected.

unsureList.text: Describe sensory interaction and synesthesia.
unsureList.best: The sensory systems constantly work together in a process called sensory interaction. Synesthesia is an experience of sensation in which one system of sensation is experienced through another.

unsureList.text: Explain how the visual system relates to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how the structures and functions of the visual sensory system relate to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe the retina, the blind spot and the brain filling in gaps.
unsureList.best: 1.6.B.5 Damage to parts of the brain responsible for vision (mainly the occipital lobes) can result in disorders such as prosopagnosia (face blindness) and blindsight. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain accommodation by the lens and nearsightedness or farsightedness.
unsureList.best: Visual stimuli are focused onto the retina by the lens via a process called accommodation. When this process is altered, nearsightedness or farsightedness can result.

unsureList.text: Describe rods, which detect shape and movement in low light.
unsureList.best: Cells that lie in the periphery of the eye and detect shapes and movement, but not color, are called rods. These cells are mainly activatedinlow-lightenvironments.Thesecells play a role in light and dark adaptation.

unsureList.text: Explain color vision with trichromatic and opponent-process theories, cones, afterimages and color deficiency.
unsureList.best: Color vision is explained by both the trichromatictheoryandtheopponent-process theory.

unsureList.text: Describe vision disorders from brain damage, such as prosopagnosia and blindsight.
unsureList.best: Damage to parts of the brain responsible for vision (mainly the occipital lobes) can result in disorders such as prosopagnosia (face blindness) and blindsight. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain how the auditory system relates to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how the structures and functions of the auditory sensory system relate to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Relate sound pitch and loudness to wave frequency and amplitude.
unsureList.best: Sound occurs through the movement of air moleculesatdifferentwavelengths(called pitch) and amplitudes (called loudness).

unsureList.text: Compare place, volley and frequency theories of pitch.
unsureList.best: Theories that help explain pitch perception include place theory, volley theory, and frequency theory.

unsureList.text: Describe sound localization.
unsureList.best: Soundlocalizationdescribeshowweidentify where sounds in our environment are coming from.

unsureList.text: Distinguish conduction and sensorineural hearing loss.
unsureList.best: Hearingdifficultiescanresultfromagingand various kinds of damage to auditory structures. Types of hearing loss include conduction deafness and sensorineural deafness.

unsureList.text: Explain how the chemical senses relate to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how the structures and functions of the chemical sensory systems relate to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe olfaction, its bypass of the thalamus, and pheromones.
unsureList.best: Structures in the nose and brain process and/ or transduce olfactory stimuli. Smell is the onlysensenotprocessedfirstinthethalamus of the brain. Pheromones produce chemical messages for the olfactory system.

unsureList.text: Explain taste receptors and supertasters, medium tasters and nontasters.
unsureList.best: Structures in the tongue, mouth, and brain process and/or transduce basic tastes. The number of taste receptors on the tongue is related to how sensitive people are to tastes, classifying them as supertasters, medium tasters, or nontasters.

unsureList.text: Explain how smell and taste interact.
unsureList.best: The chemical senses interact to create the sensation of taste. Without the sense of smell, taste sensations are either muted or not experienced.

unsureList.text: Explain how the touch system relates to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how the structures and functions of the touch sensory system relate to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe skin and brain processing of touch, and hot as warm plus cold receptor activation.
unsureList.best: Structures within the skin and brain process and/or transduce touch stimuli. The sensation of “hot” is produced by the activation of warm and cold receptors in the skin.

unsureList.text: Describe gate control theory and phantom limb sensation.
unsureList.best: Pain is processed both in the body and in the brain. Gate control theory is one attempt to describe the complexities of pain. Phantom limb sensation occurs when people who have lost limbs report sensation or pain where the limb used to be.

unsureList.text: Explain how the vestibular and kinesthetic senses relate to behavior.
unsureList.best: Explain how the structures and functions that maintain balance (vestibular) and body movement (kinesthetic) relate to behavior and mental processes. AP Psychology Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Describe the vestibular sense of balance via the semicircular canals.
unsureList.best: The vestibular sense controls balance and is primarily detected by the semicircular canals and structures in the brain.

unsureList.text: Describe kinesthesis as sense of body movement.
unsureList.best: Kinesthesis the sense of one’s body movement. Kinesthesis allows the body to move in coordinated ways without having to look at the various parts of the body as it moves.

unsureList.text: Contrast bottom-up and top-down processing.
unsureList.best: Perceptionisinfluencedbywhetherone primarily relies on external sensory information (bottom-upprocessing)orinternalprior expectations(top-downprocessing).

unsureList.text: Identify schemas and perceptual sets as internal perception filters.
unsureList.best: Schemas and perceptual sets are internal factorsthatfilterperceptionsoftheworld.

unsureList.text: Identify context, experience and culture as external perception filters.
unsureList.best: 2.1.A Explain how internal and externalfactorsinfluence perception.

unsureList.text: Apply Gestalt principles: closure, figure-ground, proximity and similarity.
unsureList.best: Perceptual principles proposed by Gestalt psychology(closure,figureandground, proximity, and similarity) help explain how humansorganizetheirperceptualworld.

unsureList.text: Explain attention, selective attention such as the cocktail party effect, and change blindness.
unsureList.best: 2.1.A.5.i Some experiences of attention can be selective, such as with the cocktail party effect,wherepeopleattendtomentions oftheirnamesorspecifictopicsinloudor distracting environments.

unsureList.text: Explain how visual perception produces correct or incorrect interpretations.
unsureList.best: Explain how visual perceptual processes produce correct or incorrect interpretations of stimuli. AP Psychology Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Explain binocular depth cues: retinal disparity and convergence.
unsureList.best: Binocular depth cues of retinal disparity (the differencebetweentheimagesprojectingonto the retina) and convergence (the merging of theretinalimagesbythebrain)utilizeimages from each eye to provide perception of depth.

unsureList.text: Explain monocular depth cues such as relative size, texture gradient, linear perspective and interposition.
unsureList.best: Monocular depth cues (relative clarity, relative size,texturegradient,linearperspective,and interposition)givetheillusionofdepthonflat ortwo-dimensionalsurfaces. Exclusion Statement: The AP Psychology Exam will only address the listed monocular depth cues in EK 2.1.B.2.

unsureList.text: Explain perceptual constancies.
unsureList.best: Visual perceptual constancies maintain the perception of an object even when the images oftheobjectinthevisualfieldchange.

unsureList.text: Explain apparent movement.
unsureList.best: Apparent movement can be visually perceived even when objects are not actually moving.

unsureList.text: Describe concepts and prototypes as the basis of thought.
unsureList.best: Concepts form the basis of thought. Prototypes are the ideal example for any given concept.

unsureList.text: Contrast assimilation and accommodation in forming schemas.
unsureList.best: People form and modify schemas, or frameworks for thinking, through assimilation (taking in new information but not changing the schema in light of it) and accommodation (taking in new information and changing the schema to incorporate the new information).

unsureList.text: Define algorithms as trying all possible solutions.
unsureList.best: Algorithms address problems by attempting all possible solutions until the correct one is found.

unsureList.text: Explain heuristics and the representativeness and availability heuristics.
unsureList.best: 2.2.A Explain how psychological concepts and theories account for thinking, problem-solving,judgment, anddecision-making.

unsureList.text: Explain mental set, priming and framing in decisions.
unsureList.best: Decisionmakingcanbeinfluencedbyprior experiences that were successful (mental set) or circumstances surrounding a decision (priming and framing).

unsureList.text: Identify gambler's and sunk-cost fallacies.
unsureList.best: UNIT

unsureList.text: Define executive functions as planning and goal-directed cognitive control.
unsureList.best: Executive functions are cognitive processes thatallowindividualstogenerate,organize, plan,andcarryoutgoal-directedbehaviorsand experience critical thinking.

unsureList.text: Describe creativity, divergent versus convergent thinking, and functional fixedness.
unsureList.best: Creativity is a way of thinking that includes generating novel ideas and engaging in divergent (versus convergent) thinking. Creative thinking is hindered by functional fixedness. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Distinguish explicit (episodic, semantic), implicit (procedural) and prospective memory.
unsureList.best: 2.3.A.1.i Explicit memory is a type of memory that is more easily described or explained to others. Types of explicit memory include episodic and semantic.

unsureList.text: Describe long-term potentiation as strengthening synapses through use.
unsureList.best: Long-termpotentiation,aprocessbywhich synaptic connections between neurons become stronger with frequent activation, is a biological process for memory.

unsureList.text: Describe the working memory model: central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad.
unsureList.best: 2.3.A.5 The levels of processing model proposes that memory is encoded on three levels from shallowest to deepest: structural, phonemic, and semantic. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe the multi-store model: sensory, short-term and long-term memory with automatic and effortful processing.
unsureList.best: Themulti-storemodelproposesthree interacting systems (sensory memory [including iconic and echoic memory], short-termmemory,andlong-termmemory) that information must pass through to be remembered. This model focuses on the impactofautomaticandeffortfulprocessing on memory encoding, storage, and retrieval.

unsureList.text: Describe the levels of processing model: structural, phonemic and semantic.
unsureList.best: The levels of processing model proposes that memory is encoded on three levels from shallowest to deepest: structural, phonemic, and semantic. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain that how information is encoded affects storage and retrieval.
unsureList.best: 2.5.A Explain how memory storage processes retain information in memory.

unsureList.text: Use mnemonic devices such as method of loci.
unsureList.best: Mnemonic devices, such as method of loci, are processes that aid in encoding information into workingandlong-termmemory.

unsureList.text: Improve encoding by chunking, categories and hierarchies.
unsureList.best: Encoding can be improved by the process of grouping information together into meaningful chunks (“chunking”), categories, or hierarchies.

unsureList.text: Explain the spacing effect, massed versus distributed practice.
unsureList.best: Thespacingeffectisaprocessthatcan causesignificantdifferencesinencodingand memory consolidation depending on whether the information is encoded all at once (massed practice) or distributed over time (distributed practice).

unsureList.text: Explain the serial position effect, primacy and recency.
unsureList.best: 2.5.A Explain how memory storage processes retain information in memory.

unsureList.text: Contrast maintenance and elaborative rehearsal.
unsureList.best: Storage may be prolonged by rehearsing information over time (maintenance rehearsal). Rehearsing information over time in ways that promote meaning (elaborative rehearsal) helps with memory retention.

unsureList.text: Describe highly superior autobiographical memory and self-relevant memories.
unsureList.best: Some people demonstrate highly superior autobiographical memory which may indicate that there are biological processes for superior memory storage. Autobiographical memory may also explain why memories connected to our own lives or selves are more memorable.

unsureList.text: Describe storage problems: amnesia types, Alzheimer's disease and infantile amnesia.
unsureList.best: 2.5.A Explain how memory storage processes retain information in memory.

unsureList.text: Contrast recall with recognition.
unsureList.best: The process of memory retrieval occurs through recall (remembering without cues) or recognition (which relies on retrieval cues).

unsureList.text: Explain context-, mood-congruent and state-dependent memory.
unsureList.best: The process of memory retrieval can be enhanced when people are in the same environmentalspace(context-dependent memory),mood(mood-congruentmemory),or physicalstate(state-dependentmemory)as they were when they encoded the information to be retrieved.

unsureList.text: Explain retrieval practice, the testing effect and metacognition.
unsureList.best: 2.6.A Explain how memory retrieval processes get information out of memory.

unsureList.text: Describe the forgetting curve: rapid forgetting that levels off.
unsureList.best: The forgetting curve shows that time is a significantfactorinforgetting.Forgetting occurs rapidly after initial learning and levels offovertime.

unsureList.text: Explain encoding failure, proactive and retroactive interference, and tip-of-the-tongue retrieval failure.
unsureList.best: Manymemoriesaredifficulttoretrievedue to encoding failure, interference (proactive or retroactive),orinadequateretrieval(i.e.,tip-of- the-tonguephenomenon).

unsureList.text: Describe repression as forgetting to defend the ego.
unsureList.best: Psychodynamic theorists believe that information or memories can be forgotten to defend the ego from distress (repression).

unsureList.text: Explain the misinformation effect, source amnesia and constructive memory.
unsureList.best: 2.7.A Explain possible reasons why memory failure or errors may occur.

unsureList.text: Explain the debate over general intelligence g versus multiple abilities, and bias in measuring it.
unsureList.best: Throughout history, consensus about how to defineandmeasureintelligencecontinues to be elusive and can be subject to bias. Researchers debate whether intelligence is a general ability (called g) or is comprised of multiple abilities.

unsureList.text: Explain how intelligence is measured.
unsureList.best: Explain how intelligence is measured.

unsureList.text: Describe IQ as mental age over chronological age and its educational uses.
unsureList.best: Early formal intelligence tests yielded an intelligence quotient (IQ), which divided mental age by chronological age. In modern times, IQ scores are often used to identify students for educational services. ExclusionStatement:Labelingordescribing cognitiveabilitiesanddisabilitiesareoutside thescopeoftheAPPsychologyExam.

unsureList.text: Define standardization, validity (construct, predictive) and reliability (test-retest, split-half).
unsureList.best: 2.8.B.2.ii A test is considered valid if it measures what it is designed to measure. Types of validity include construct and predictive.

unsureList.text: Explain socio-culturally responsive assessments and stereotype threat and lift.
unsureList.best: Researchers strive to develop assessments of intelligencethataresocio-culturallyresponsive to reduce stereotype threat and potential inequity that may occur due to stereotype lift. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain the Flynn effect as rising IQ scores from societal factors.
unsureList.best: IQ scores across much of the world have generallyincreasedovertime(FlynnEffect) due to societal factors, such as higher socioeconomic status and access to better health care and better nutrition.

unsureList.text: Explain that IQ varies more within than between groups and that bias and inequity affect scores.
unsureList.best: IQ scores tend to vary more within a group than between groups. Personal and sociocultural biases can impact the interpretation of individual IQ scores and the score’s relationship with other outcomes. Poverty, discrimination, and educational inequities cannegativelyinfluenceintelligencescores of individuals and societal groups around the world.

unsureList.text: Describe how IQ scores have been used to limit access to jobs, military ranks, schools and immigration.
unsureList.best: Scores from intelligence tests have been used to limit access to jobs, military ranks, educational institutions, and immigration to the US.

unsureList.text: Contrast achievement tests with aptitude tests.
unsureList.best: Some academic tests attempt to measure what someone knows (achievement tests) or predict how someone will perform in the future (aptitude tests).

unsureList.text: Contrast fixed and growth mindsets and their effect on achievement.
unsureList.best: People’s beliefs about whether intelligence is fixedfrombirth(fixedmindset)ormalleable duetoexperience(growthmindset)canaffect academic achievement.

unsureList.text: Name developmental themes: stability and change, nature and nurture, continuous and discontinuous stages.
unsureList.best: Developmental psychology is concerned with both chronological order of development and/ or thematic issues in development across the lifespan. Thematic issues of interest to developmental psychologists include stability and change, nature and nurture, and continuous and discontinuous stages of development.

unsureList.text: Describe how cross-sectional and longitudinal designs inform understanding of development.
unsureList.best: 3.1.A Explain how enduring themes inform developmental psychology.

unsureList.text: Identify teratogens, illness, genetic and hormonal factors that shape prenatal milestones.
unsureList.best: Teratogens, maternal illness, genetic mutations, hormonal, and environmental factorscaninfluencethemajorphysicaland psychological milestones that occur during prenatal development. Exclusion Statement: The stages of prenatal development (zygote, embryo, and fetus) are outside the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Explain how physical development in infancy and childhood applies to behavior.
unsureList.best: Explain how physical development in infancy and childhood apply to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe fine and gross motor milestones that follow a similar order with varying timing.
unsureList.best: Physical development in infancy and childhood happens in generally the same order, but the timing of the development can vary. Thedevelopmentoffineandgrossmotor coordination is among the major physical andpsychologicalmilestonesthatdefine infancy and childhood. These physical skills develop as children mature, allowing children to develop critical skills needed to become more independent.

unsureList.text: Identify infant reflexes such as rooting as milestones.
unsureList.best: Infantspossessreflexes,liketherooting reflex,thatindicateon-trackphysicaland psychological milestone development.

unsureList.text: Explain what the visual cliff shows about infant depth perception.
unsureList.best: 3.2.A Explain how physical development before birth applies to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Explain critical and sensitive periods, such as for language, and imprinting.
unsureList.best: Research suggests that critical or sensitive periods in infancy and childhood have strong developmentaleffects,especiallyforskills suchaslanguage.Somenon-humananimals willimprintonthefirstobjecttheyencounter as a means of survival. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe the growth spurt, puberty and primary and secondary sex characteristics.
unsureList.best: The main physical and psychological milestones that occur in adolescence are the adolescent growth spurt and puberty, in which reproductive ability develops. Adolescents develop primary and secondary sex characteristics during this time, such as menarche and spermarche.

unsureList.text: Explain how physical development in adulthood applies to behavior.
unsureList.best: Explain how physical development in adulthood applies to behavior and mental processes. AP Psychology Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 |

unsureList.text: Describe adult declines in reproductive ability, mobility, reaction time and sensory acuity.
unsureList.best: Adulthood spans most of the lifespan and is characterizedbyagenerallevelingoffandthen a varying decline in reproductive ability (i.e., menopause),mobility,flexibility,reactiontime, and visual and auditory sensory acuity.

unsureList.text: Describe how sex and gender influence socialization and other aspects of development.
unsureList.best: Describe how sex and gender influencesocialization and other aspects of development. SUGGESTEDSKILLS 2.C Evaluate the appropriate use of research design elements in non-experimental methodologies. unsureList.text: Describe Piaget's stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational.
unsureList.best: 3.4.A.1.iii The concrete operational stage occurs from early through late childhood. Children in this stage can generally correct the cognitive errors made in the preoperational stage and understand the world in logical, realistic, and straightforward ways, but struggle to think systematically.

unsureList.text: Describe Vygotsky's social learning, scaffolding and zone of proximal development.
unsureList.best: According to Vygotsky, children are social learners who learn through interacting with andscaffoldingbyotherpeoplewithin sociocultural contexts. Ideally, learning occurs whilethepersonisintheirzoneofproximal development.

unsureList.text: Contrast adult crystallized and fluid intelligence, and dementia.
unsureList.best: Adults experience changes in cognitive capabilities as they progress through the lifespan.Crystallizedintelligenceremains relativelystablethroughadulthoodwhilefluid intelligence tends to wane as people age. Cognitivedisordersthataffectadultsinclude dementia. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe language as rule-governed, generative symbols: phonemes, morphemes, semantics, grammar and syntax.
unsureList.best: Language is a shared (mutually agreed upon) system of arbitrary symbols (often expressed as and combined into phonemes, morphemes, andsemantics)thatarerule-governed(via grammar and syntax) and generative to produceaninfinityofideas. Exclusion Statement: Pragmatics of language are outside the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Describe language stages from cooing and babbling to telegraphic speech, and overgeneralization errors.
unsureList.best: 3.5.B Explain how language develops in humans.

unsureList.text: Describe Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems: micro, meso, exo, macro and chronosystem.
unsureList.best: The ecological systems theory explores howthesocialenvironmentinfluences development.Thefivesystemsinthistheory are as follows: § Microsystem (groups that have direct contact with the individual) § Mesosystem (the relationships between groups in the microsystem) § Exosystem (indirect factors in an individual’s life) § Macrosystem(culturaleventsthataffect the individuals and others around them) § Chronosystem (the individual’s current stage of life).

unsureList.text: Compare authoritarian, authoritative and permissive parenting and cultural differences.
unsureList.best: Researchhasidentifieddifferentparenting styles of caregivers, including authoritarian, authoritative, and permissive. Cultural differencesexistinthewaystheseparenting stylesaffectoutcomesincaregiversand children.

unsureList.text: Describe secure and insecure attachment styles, separation anxiety and comfort-versus-food research.
unsureList.best: 3.6.A.3.i Separation anxiety occurs when children express heightened anxiety or fear when away from a caregiver or in the presence of a stranger.

unsureList.text: Describe peer relationships from childhood play to adolescent imaginary audience and personal fable.
unsureList.best: 3.6.A.4.ii Adolescents gradually rely more on peer relationships as they age. As adolescents interact with peers, they demonstrate a type of egocentrism that is often demonstrated via the imaginary audience and the personal fable.

unsureList.text: Describe adult social development: the social clock, emerging adulthood and adult attachment.
unsureList.best: 3.6.A.5.i Culture plays a role in determining when adulthood begins and when major life events occur (social clock). Some cultures allow for a time of emerging adulthood as a transition from adolescence to adulthood.

unsureList.text: Describe Erikson's eight psychosocial stages.
unsureList.best: UNIT

unsureList.text: Explain adverse childhood experiences and their sociocultural variation.
unsureList.best: The experience of adverse childhood experiences(ACEs)haseffectson relationships people form throughout the lifespan.Socioculturaldifferencesexistinwhat isconsideredanACEandhowACEsaffect outcomes people may experience.

unsureList.text: Describe identity development: achievement, diffusion, foreclosure and moratorium, and possible selves.
unsureList.best: Adolescents develop a sense of identity for who they will be as an adult through theprocessesofachievement,diffusion, foreclosure, and moratorium. Identity development also includes processes for developing identities such as racial/ethnic identity, gender identity, sexual orientation, religious identity, occupational identity, and familial identity, often through considering possible selves. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain how classical conditioning applies to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how classical conditioning applies to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe the behaviorist focus on observable behavior and conditioning.
unsureList.best: The behavioral perspective evolved from theories about learning via conditioning. Behaviorists have traditionally focused on observable behavior to the exclusion of mental processes.

unsureList.text: Explain classical conditioning: UCS, UCR, CS, CR, timing, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination and higher-order conditioning.
unsureList.best: 3.7.A.2.v ACScanbeusedasaUCSinhigher-order conditioning. Exclusion Statement: Delayed conditioning, trace conditioning, simultaneous conditioning, and backward conditioning are outside the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Explain conditioned emotional responses and counterconditioning therapy.
unsureList.best: Research has demonstrated that emotional responses can be classically conditioned. Thesefindingsformthebasisoftherapeutic interventions for many mental disorders, such as counterconditioning. Exclusion Statement: The expectancy theory is outside the scope of the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Explain taste aversion, one-trial learning and biological preparedness.
unsureList.best: Development and Learning ESSENTIALKNOWLEDGE

unsureList.text: Define habituation.
unsureList.best: Habituation occurs when organisms grow accustomed to and exhibit a diminished response to a repeated or enduring stimulus. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain the law of effect: reinforcement and punishment shape repeated behavior.
unsureList.best: Operant conditioning focuses on associating consequences (reinforcement and punishment) withbehaviors.TheLawofEffectstatesthat behaviors with reinforcing consequences are more likely to be repeated while behaviors with punishing consequences are not as likely to be repeated.

unsureList.text: Distinguish positive and negative reinforcement and punishment, and primary and secondary reinforcers.
unsureList.best: Reinforcement and punishment can be positive or negative. Reinforcers can be primary or secondary. Reinforcement discrimination and generalizationhavebeendemonstratedin studies of operant conditioning.

unsureList.text: Explain shaping by successive approximations and instinctive drift.
unsureList.best: Reinforcement can be used to shape behavior (“shaping”) gradually through rewarding successive approximations of the desired behavior. Research with animals shows that only certain behaviors can be shaped through reinforcement (known as instinctive drift).

unsureList.text: Explain superstitious behavior and learned helplessness.
unsureList.best: 3.8.A Explain how operant conditioning applies to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Compare continuous and partial reinforcement schedules, fixed and variable, interval and ratio.
unsureList.best: 3.8.A.5.ii The partial reinforcement schedules focus on whether reinforcement is delivered on atime-basedschedule(fixed-orvariable- interval) or for the number of behaviors performed(fixed-orvariable-ratio). LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Explain social learning theory, observation, vicarious conditioning and modeling.
unsureList.best: Social learning theory proposes that learning can occur by observation and does not have to involve personal experience with a consequence (vicarious conditioning). Learning can occur by copying the behavior of models. The more similar a model is, the more likely the behavior is to be learned.

unsureList.text: Define insight learning.
unsureList.best: Insight learning occurs when the solution to a problem occurs without any association, consequence, or model being present.

unsureList.text: Define latent learning and cognitive maps.
unsureList.best: 3.9.B Explain how cognitive factors in learning apply to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Distinguish dispositional from situational attributions.
unsureList.best: Attributions are how people explain behavior and mental processes of themselves and others. Dispositional attributions relate to internal qualities of others (such as intelligence or personality) while situational attributions relate to external circumstances that are experienced.

unsureList.text: Explain upward and downward social comparison and relative deprivation.
unsureList.best: Social comparison is a type of person perception that occurs when people evaluate themselves based on comparisons to other members of society or social circles. unsureList.best: Implicit attitudes are those that individuals hold but may be unaware of or may not acknowledge. Research has focused on how implicitattitudesreflectnegativeevaluations ofothers,asdemonstratedbythejust-world phenomenon,out-grouphomogeneitybias,in- group bias, or ethnocentrism.

unsureList.text: Explain belief perseverance and confirmation bias.
unsureList.best: Belief perseverance occurs when a belief persists even if evidence suggests it is not accurate. People experiencing belief perseverancemayengageinconfirmation bias, thereby clinging to an attitude or belief regardless of the evidence for or against it.

unsureList.best: 4.2.B Explain how belief perseverance and cognitive dissonance apply to attitude formation and change.

unsureList.text: Distinguish normative and informational social influence.
unsureList.best: Socialinfluencetheoryproposesthatsocial pressure to behave or think in certain ways can be normative or informational.

unsureList.text: Explain individualism, collectivism and multiculturalism.
unsureList.best: Cultural phenomena such as individualism, collectivism,andmulticulturalismcaninfluence how one perceives and behaves towards oneself and others.

unsureList.best: Beingamemberofagroupcaninfluence how one behaves or experiences mental processesviagrouppolarization,groupthink, diffusionofresponsibility,socialloafing,and deindividuation.

unsureList.text: Define social facilitation.
unsureList.best: Performing a mental or physical behavior in front of a group can lead to social facilitation.

unsureList.text: Explain the bystander effect.
unsureList.best: Thebystandereffectdemonstratesthat situational and attentional variables predict whether someone is likely to help another person.

unsureList.text: Explain that unconscious processes drive personality.
unsureList.best: According to the psychodynamic theory of personality, unconscious processes drive personality. Exclusion Statement: The stage theory of psychosexual development is out of scope for the AP Psychology Exam.

unsureList.text: Identify ego defense mechanisms such as denial, projection, regression and sublimation.
unsureList.best: Ego defense mechanisms (denial, displacement,projection,rationalization, reaction formation, regression, repression, and sublimation) serve to protect the ego unconsciously from threats.

unsureList.text: Describe projective tests.
unsureList.best: Psychodynamic personality psychologists assess personality using projective tests that are designed to probe the preconscious and unconscious mind.

unsureList.text: Explain how humanistic theory defines and assesses personality.
unsureList.best: Explain how the humanistic theoryofpersonalitydefines and assesses personality.

unsureList.text: Explain unconditional regard and the self-actualizing tendency.
unsureList.best: 4.4.A Explain how the psychodynamic theory of personalitydefinesand assesses personality.

unsureList.text: Explain reciprocal determinism, self-concept, self-efficacy and self-esteem.
unsureList.best: Accordingtosocial-cognitivetheory,reciprocal determinism shapes personality. Reciprocal determinismexploresself-concept(howone views themselves and in relation to others) andhowself-efficacyandself-esteemboth contributetoself-concept.

unsureList.text: Describe traits as enduring characteristics.
unsureList.best: Trait theories of personality conclude that personality involves a set of enduring characteristics that lead to typical responses to stimuli.

unsureList.text: Contrast intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in self-determination and incentive theory.
unsureList.best: Self-determinationtheoryproposesthat people are motivated by intrinsic (internal) or extrinsic (external) motivations. Incentive theory explores the role of rewards (an extrinsic motivation) in motivating behavior.

unsureList.text: Explain instincts in animals but not humans.
unsureList.best: Manynon-humananimalsaremotivatedby instincts(innate,typicallyfixedpatternsof behavior in animals in response to certain stimuli). Humans do not seem to demonstrate instinctual behavior or mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe Lewin's approach and avoidance motivational conflicts.
unsureList.best: Lewin’smotivationalconflictstheoryproposes thatchoicescreateconflictsonemustresolve asthebasisofmotivation.Thetypeofconflicts facedincludeapproach-approach,approach- avoidance,andavoidance-avoidance.

unsureList.best: 4.6.B.1.i Hormones, such as ghrelin and leptin (regulated by the hypothalamus via the pituitary gland), regulate feelings of hunger and satiety.

unsureList.text: Discuss universality of emotions like anger, disgust, sadness, happiness, surprise and fear.
unsureList.best: Research has explored whether the expression of emotions is universally common. Some emotions that may be commonly experienced across cultures include anger, disgust, sadness, happiness, surprise, and fear. Research on the universality of emotions shows mixed results.

unsureList.text: Explain cultural display rules and elicitors.
unsureList.best: Display rules and elicitors for emotional expressioncandifferamongcultures. Display rules and elicitors may regulate how peoplefromdifferentgenders,ages,or socioeconomic classes within a culture can display and interpret emotions.

unsureList.text: Explain how stress applies to behavior and mental processes.
unsureList.best: Explain how stress applies to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Link stress to hypertension, headaches, immune suppression and disease susceptibility.
unsureList.best: Stress is a factor in heightened susceptibility to disorders and disease. Stress has been linked to physiological issues such as hypertension, headaches, and immune suppression.

unsureList.text: Distinguish eustress from distress, trauma from daily hassles, and ACEs as stressors.
unsureList.best: Stressors can be viewed as motivating (eustress) or debilitating (distress). Stressors can be experienced as traumatic or as daily hassles that can build up over time. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are sources of stressthatcanaffectapersonthroughoutthe lifespan.

unsureList.text: Describe the tend-and-befriend response to stress.
unsureList.best: 5.1.D Explain how the ways that people cope with stress applies to behavior and mental processes.

unsureList.text: Describe problem-focused coping.
unsureList.best: Problem-focusedcopinginvolvesseeing stress as a problem to be solved and working solutions until a solution is found.

unsureList.text: Describe emotion-focused coping such as breathing, meditation or medication.
unsureList.best: Emotion-focusedcopinginvolvesmanaging emotional reactions to stress as a means of coping.Strategiesthatareemotion-focused may include deep breathing, meditation, or taking medication aimed at reducing stressful emotional responses.

unsureList.text: Describe positive psychology's focus on well-being, resilience and positive emotions.
unsureList.best: Positive psychology seeks to identify factors thatleadtowell-being,resilience,positive emotions, and psychological health.

unsureList.text: Explain that gratitude raises subjective well-being.
unsureList.best: Expressing gratitude, a positive subjective experience,increasessubjectivewell-being.

unsureList.text: Use dysfunction, distress and deviation from norms to identify disorders.
unsureList.best: Level of dysfunction, perception of distress, and deviation from the social norm are all factors used to identify psychological disorders.

unsureList.text: Weigh the positive and negative consequences of diagnosis, including stigma and bias.
unsureList.best: Diagnosing or classifying psychological disorders has positive and negative consequences depending on the nature of the disorder, the individual being diagnosed, and the presence of cultural/societal norms, stigma, racism, sexism, ageism, and discrimination.

unsureList.text: Explain that diagnosis needs training and tools such as the DSM and ICD.
unsureList.best: Diagnosing psychological disorders requires specializedtrainingandtheuseofevidence- based diagnostic tools. unsureList.best: 5.3.A Describe the approaches usedtodefinebehaviors and mental processes as psychological disorders.

unsureList.text: Explain the behavioral perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The behavioral perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive learned associations between or among responses to stimuli.

unsureList.text: Explain the psychodynamic perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The psychodynamic perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on unconscious thoughts and experiences, often developed during childhood.

unsureList.text: Explain the humanistic perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The humanistic perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on a lack of socialsupportandbeingunabletofulfillone’s potential.

unsureList.text: Explain the cognitive perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The cognitive perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive thoughts, beliefs, attitudes, or emotions.

unsureList.text: Explain the evolutionary perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The evolutionary perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on behaviors and mental processes that reduce the likelihood of survival.

unsureList.text: Explain the sociocultural perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The sociocultural perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive social and cultural relationships and dynamics.

unsureList.text: Explain the biological perspective on disorders.
unsureList.best: The biological perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on physiological or genetic issues. LEARNINGOBJECTIVE

unsureList.text: Describe the biopsychosocial model.
unsureList.best: The biopsychosocial model assumes that any psychological problem potentially involves a combination of biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors.

unsureList.text: Describe the diathesis-stress model.
unsureList.best: Thediathesis-stressmodelassumesthat psychological disorders develop due to a genetic vulnerability (diathesis) in combination with stressful life experiences (stress).

unsureList.text: Describe ADHD and autism spectrum disorder as neurodevelopmental disorders.
unsureList.best: Neurodevelopmental disorders are a group of disorders with onset occurring during the developmental period. Symptoms of neurodevelopmental disorders focus on whether the person is exhibiting behaviors appropriate for their age or maturity range. Selected disorders in scope for AP Psychology in this category are attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

unsureList.best: Possiblecausesofschizophreniasuggest a genetic or biological link, such as prenatal virus exposure or imbalances with certain neurotransmitters (dopamine hypothesis).

unsureList.text: Describe major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder.
unsureList.best: Depressivedisordersarecharacterizedbythe presence of sad, empty, or irritable mood along withphysicalandcognitivechangesthataffect a person’s ability to function. Selected disorders in scope for AP Psychology in this category are major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder.

unsureList.text: Describe Bipolar I and II with mania, depression and cycling.
unsureList.best: Bipolardisordersarecharacterizedbyperiods of mania and periods of depression. Bipolar cycling involves experiencing periods of depression and mania in alternating periods that can last various amounts of time. Selected disorders in scope for AP Psychology in this category are Bipolar I disorder and Bipolar II disorder.

unsureList.text: Describe cognitive restructuring, fear hierarchies and the cognitive triad.
unsureList.best: Cognitive therapies may employ cognitive restructuring or fear hierarchies to combat maladaptive thinking. Cognitive therapy proposes that people should focus on the cognitivetriad—negativethoughtsabout oneself, the world, and the future.

unsureList.best: Applied behavior analysis involves applying principles of conditioning to address mental disorders and developmental disabilities. Exposure therapies (such as systematic desensitization),aversiontherapies,andtoken economies all employ principles of applied behavior analysis. Biofeedback uses principles of conditioning to help clients regulate body systems (such as the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems) that contribute to feelings of anxiety or depression.

unsureList.text: Describe cognitive-behavioral therapies such as DBT and REBT.
unsureList.best: Cognitive-behavioraltherapies,suchas dialecticalbehaviortherapyandrational- emotive behavior therapy, combine techniques from the cognitive and behavioral perspectives to treat mental and behavioral disorders.

unsureList.text: Explain that hypnosis helps with pain and anxiety but not accurate memory retrieval.
unsureList.best: Hypnosishasshowneffectivenessintreating pain and anxiety. Research does not support the use of hypnosis to retrieve accurate memories or regress in age.

unsureList.text: Describe interventions derived from the biological perspective.
unsureList.best: Describe interventions derived from the biological perspective. AP Psychology Course and Exam Description Course Framework V.1 | Return to Table of Contents © 2024 College Board Return to Table of Contents © 2024 College Board

unsureList.text: Describe psychoactive medications, targeted neurotransmitters and side effects like tardive dyskinesia.
unsureList.best: Psychoactive medications, such as antidepressants, antianxiety drugs, lithium, or antipsychotic medications, interact with specificneurotransmittersinthecentral nervous system to address possible biochemical causes of mental disorders. Psychoactive medications can have side effectssuchastardivedyskinesia(amovement disorder related to the regulation of dopamine in the nervous system).

unsureList.text: Describe psychosurgery, TMS and electroconvulsive therapy, and lobotomy history.
unsureList.best: Surgical or invasive interventions include psychosurgery (which may involve lesioning), TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation), or electroconvulsive therapy. The lobotomy is a form of psychosurgery that was popular inthemid-20thcenturybutisrarely,ifever, performed today.

changes.from: Explain the purpose and significance of scholarly inquiry
changes.to: LO 1.1D: Articulating the purpose and significance of the scholarly inquiry.

changes.from: Scholars explore, explain and create
changes.to: EK 1.1D1: Scholars explore, explain, and create.

changes.from: Align methods of collection, analysis, innovation or interpretation with the question or goal
changes.to: EK 1.5B1: Methods for data collection, analysis, innovation, and/or interpretation should be aligned with the research question/project goal.

changes.from: Methods may be qualitative, quantitative, mixed, or artistic processes
changes.to: EK 1.5B2: Methods of inquiry may include research methods (e.g., qualitative, quantitative, or mixed) or artistic processes (e.g., generating, conceptualizing, testing, and then refining aesthetic approaches).

changes.from: Combine qualitative and quantitative data to triangulate trends and patterns
changes.to: EK 1.5B10: Scholars can combine qualitative and quantitative data/information to triangulate and corroborate trends, patterns, correlations, and/or themes.

changes.from: Show perseverance by setting goals, managing time and working independently
changes.to: LO 1.5C: Demonstrating perseverance through setting goals, managing time, and working independently on a long-term project.

changes.from: Plan methods and activities around deadlines, priorities, risks and others' availability
changes.to: EK 1.5C1: Scholars carefully plan methods of inquiry, analysis, and other feasible research activities, taking into account deadlines, priorities, risks, setbacks, and the availability of others.

changes.from: Laws and rules govern research on humans and animals, including institutional review board approval
changes.to: EK 1.5D2: There are laws, rules, and guidelines that govern the conduct of researchers, in particular when studies involve humans and animals. Accordingly, scholars gain approval to conduct research with humans through an institutional review board (IRB).

changes.from: Copyright and patent rules govern use of others' work and information
changes.to: EK 1.5D3: There are copyright and patent laws and guidelines that govern the use and reproduction of others’ instruments, work, personal information, and intellectual property.

changes.from: Read closely for main idea, tone, assumptions, context, perspective, reasoning and evidence
changes.to: EK 2.1A1: Reading critically means reading closely to identify the main idea, tone, assumptions, context, perspective, line of reasoning, and evidence used.

changes.from: Make meaning by annotating, note-taking, highlighting and reading aloud
changes.to: EK 2.1A3: Strategies active readers use to make meaning from texts include annotating, note-taking, highlighting, and reading aloud.

changes.from: Perspectives are shared through written, spoken, visual or performance texts and include attitude or tone
changes.to: EK 2.1A4: Perspectives are shared through written, spoken, visual, or performance texts. A perspective includes the writer’s attitude/ tone regarding the subject and is expressed through an argument.

changes.from: The main idea sits in the thesis, claim or conclusion, or is implied
changes.to: EK 2.1B1: The main idea of an argument is often expressed in the thesis statement, claim, or conclusion, or implied throughout a work.

changes.from: Artistic works convey a perspective; analyse context, subject, structure, style and aesthetic
changes.to: EK 2.1B2: Artistic works (e.g., painting, film, music, dance) convey a perspective. Analysis of a work’s context, subject, structure, style, and aesthetic is critical to understanding its aims.

changes.from: A line of reasoning is claims justified by evidence
changes.to: EK 2.2A1: Authors use reasons to support their arguments. The line of reasoning is composed of one or more claims justified through evidence.

changes.from: Writers may appeal to or manipulate readers through language, authority, qualifiers, fallacies and emphasis
changes.to: EK 2.2B4: Writers appeal to (or possibly manipulate) readers through a variety of strategies and techniques (e.g., language, authority, qualifiers, fallacies, emphasis).

changes.from: Evidence can show comparative, causal or correlational relationships and trends
changes.to: EK 2.2B5: Evidence may be used to identify and explain relationships (comparative, causal, or correlational) and/or patterns and trends.

changes.from: Conclusions are contextual and must be affirmed, qualified or refuted
changes.to: EK 2.2C3: Conclusions are contextual and their validity must be affirmed, qualified, or refuted.

changes.from: Arguments' consequences may be intended or unintended
changes.to: EK 2.3A1: The implications and consequences of arguments may be intended or unintended.

changes.from: Evaluate alternate, opposing or competing arguments by their implications and limitations
changes.to: LO 3.2A: Evaluating alternate, opposing, or competing perspectives or arguments, by considering their implications and limitations.

changes.from: Effective arguments use reason and evidence to convey a perspective stated in the thesis or conclusion
changes.to: EK 4.1A1: Effective arguments use reason and evidence to convey a perspective, point of view, or some version of the truth that is stated or implied in the thesis and/or conclusion.

changes.from: A line of reasoning is a clear logical path to a conclusion
changes.to: EK 4.1A5: The line of reasoning is a clear, logical path leading the audience through the reasons to a conclusion.

changes.from: Choose a process aligned with the inquiry or project goal
changes.to: EK 4.1A10: Whether developing an argument or conceptualizing an idea or work of art, scholars thoughtfully choose and implement a process aligned with the inquiry or project goal.

changes.from: An aesthetic rationale is a reasoned argument for formal and stylistic choices in an artwork
changes.to: EK 4.1A12: An aesthetic rationale is an argument in that it is a reasoned articulation of specific formal and stylistic choices made in the course of devising the artistic work.

changes.from: Each discipline has its own conventions for knowing, questioning and communicating
changes.to: EK 4.1B1: Each discipline has its own conventions and ways of knowing, questioning, and communicating.

changes.from: Compelling evidence is sufficient, accurate, relevant, current and credible
changes.to: EK 4.2A2: Evidence is used to support the claims and reasoning of an argument. Compelling evidence is sufficient, accurate, relevant, current, and credible to support the conclusion.

changes.from: Write insightful commentary that links evidence with claims
changes.to: LO 4.2B: Providing insightful and cogent commentary that links evidence with claims.

changes.from: Commentary connects evidence to the claim by interpretation or inference, patterns, trends and relationships
changes.to: EK 4.2B1: Commentary connects the chosen evidence to the claim through interpretation or inference, identifying patterns, describing trends, and/or explaining relationships (e.g., comparative, causal, correlational). EU 4.3: Responsible participation in the scholarly community requires acknowledging and respecting the prior findings and contributions of others.

changes.from: Accurate attribution enhances credibility
changes.to: EK 4.3A1: Accurate and ethical attribution enhances one’s credibility.

changes.from: Disciplines use specific style guides such as APA, MLA or Chicago
changes.to: EK 4.3A5: Academic disciplines use specific style guides for citing and attributing sources (e.g., APA, MLA, Chicago, AMA).

changes.from: Offer resolutions or solutions based on evidence, limitations and implications
changes.to: LO 4.5A: Offering resolutions, conclusions, and/or solutions based on evidence considering limitations and implications.

changes.from: Express tone through word choice, sentence structure and imagery
changes.to: EK 5.1B1: A writer expresses tone or attitude about a topic through word choice, sentence structure, and imagery.

changes.from: Spelling and grammar errors weaken credibility
changes.to: EK 5.1B4: Spelling and grammar errors detract from credibility.

changes.from: Adapt an argument to context, purpose and audience
changes.to: LO 5.1D: Adapting an argument for context, purpose, and/or audience.

changes.from: Defend inquiry choices and the final product with clarity and conviction
changes.to: LO 5.1F: Defending inquiry choices and final product with clarity, consistency, and conviction.

changes.from: Teams are built around tasks; low-risk teambuilding helps
changes.to: EK 5.2B1: Teams are built around tasks. Low-risk teambuilding activities and simulations enhance a team’s performance.

changes.from: Teams work best when they understand their diverse perspectives, talents and skills
changes.to: EK 5.2B2: Teams function at their best when they understand the diversity of their social–cultural perspectives, talents, and skills.

changes.from: Use interpersonal communication, consensus building, conflict resolution and negotiation
changes.to: EK 5.2B3: Teams function at their best when they practice effective interpersonal communication, consensus building, conflict resolution, and negotiation.

changes.from: Receive and consider peer review of your work
changes.to: LO 5.4B: Engaging in peer review to receive and consider responses to their work.

unsureList.text: Place a problem or issue in context and identify its complexities
unsureList.best: LO 1.1A: Contextualizing and identifying the complexities of a problem or issue.

unsureList.text: Others' perspectives prompt new questions; inquiry starts by narrowing interest, finding the problem and its origins, and situating it in a larger context
unsureList.best: EK 1.1A1: Examining the perspectives and ideas of others often leads to questions for further investigation. Inquiry begins with narrowing scope of interest, identifying a problem or issue and its origins within that scope, and situating the problem or issue in a larger context.

unsureList.text: Ask questions and seek answers reflecting multiple, divergent or contradictory perspectives
unsureList.best: LO 1.1B: Posing questions and seeking out answers that reflect multiple, divergent, or contradictory perspectives.

unsureList.text: Good research questions account for the complexity of the issue
unsureList.best: EK 1.1B1: Effective research questions lead to an examination taking into account the complexity of a problem or issue.

unsureList.text: Inquiry uses curiosity and imagination to explore approaches to complex issues
unsureList.best: EK 1.1B2: The inquiry process allows one to draw upon curiosity and imagination to engage with ideas or explore approaches to complex issues. unsureList.text: Identify a topic of inquiry

unsureList.text: Topics come from personal interest, passion for a field, wanting to understand more, or addressing a real-world issue

unsureList.text: Explore the knowledge base and perspectives, then adjust scope to the project's limits and resources

unsureList.text: Situate inquiry within the scholarly community it matters to
unsureList.best: EK 1.1D3: Scholarly inquiry should be situated within a broader understanding of the scholarly community and of importance and relevance to that community.

unsureList.best: LO 1.1E: Developing and revising a focused research question/project goal.

unsureList.text: Retrieve, question, organise and use prior knowledge about a topic

unsureList.text: Understanding comes from experience, sources, culture and assumptions, not just collecting information
unsureList.best: EK 1.2A1: Understanding comes not only through collection of information but also from a variety of other factors (e.g., experience, external sources, cultural context, assumptions).

unsureList.best: EK 1.2A2: A variety of strategies (e.g., brainstorming, concept mapping, prewriting, exploration of space, drafting) can be used to illustrate, organize, and connect ideas.

unsureList.text: Inquiry confirms or challenges existing understanding and assumptions
unsureList.best: EK 1.2A3: Inquiry confirms or challenges one’s existing understandings, assumptions, beliefs, and/or knowledge.

unsureList.text: Online databases and libraries hold secondary and some primary sources
unsureList.best: EK 1.3A2: Online databases (e.g., EBSCO, ProQuest, JSTOR, Google Scholar) and libraries catalog and house secondary and some primary sources.

unsureList.text: Source bibliographies can lead to more resources
unsureList.best: EK 1.3A4: Consulting the bibliographies of other sources may provide additional ideas or resources.

unsureList.text: Social media can be a source if its limitations are understood
unsureList.best: EK 1.3A5: Social media may be used as a potential source of information, but an understanding of its limitations is necessary to maintain credibility.

unsureList.text: Citation and reference software helps manage sources and bibliographies
unsureList.best: EK 1.3A6: Software (e.g., Microsoft Word, EndNote) and online tools (e.g., citation generators, WorldCat) are used by scholars to manage and catalog sources and produce bibliographies.

unsureList.best: EK 1.3A7: Software and online tools (e.g., SurveyMonkey, SPSS) can be used to survey participants and analyze large data sets. EU 1.4: The relevance and credibility of the source of information is determined by the context of its use.

unsureList.text: Evaluate the relevance and credibility of sources and data for the inquiry
unsureList.best: LO 1.4A: Evaluating the relevance and credibility of the source of information and data in relation to the inquiry.

unsureList.text: Research scope, purpose and source credibility affect the generalisability and reliability of conclusions

unsureList.text: Credible evidence comes from relevant, reliable, current and authoritative sources

unsureList.text: How a problem is framed guides the information and methods needed

unsureList.text: Design, plan and carry out a scholarly inquiry
unsureList.best: LO 1.5B: Designing, planning, and implementing a scholarly inquiry.

unsureList.best: EK 1.5B8: Descriptive or inferential statistics can be used to display and/or analyze data.

unsureList.text: Code and categorise data to find patterns or themes

unsureList.text: Seek expert guidance while staying self-sufficient

unsureList.text: Use ethical research practices

unsureList.text: Researchers have ethical and moral responsibilities
unsureList.best: EK 1.5D1: Scholars have ethical and moral responsibilities when they conduct research.

unsureList.text: Use suitable reading strategies and read critically for a purpose
unsureList.best: LO 2.1A: Employing appropriate reading strategies and reading critically for a specific purpose.

unsureList.best: EK 2.1A2: Strategies active readers use to preview and prioritize a written text include skimming, scanning, rereading, and questioning.

unsureList.text: Summarise and explain a text's main idea or aim without oversimplifying
unsureList.best: LO 2.1B: Summarizing and explaining a text’s main idea or aim while avoiding faulty generalizations and oversimplification.

unsureList.text: Explain and analyse the logic and line of reasoning of an argument
unsureList.best: LO 2.2A: Explaining and analyzing the logic and line of reasoning of an argument.

unsureList.text: Reasoning is organised by purpose, such as causality, definition or solution
unsureList.best: EK 2.2A2: An argument’s line of reasoning is organized based on the argument’s purpose (e.g., to show causality, to define, to propose a solution).

unsureList.text: Missing the complexity of an argument leads to oversimplification
unsureList.best: EK 2.2A4: A lack of understanding of the complexities of an argument (tone, implications, limitations, nuance, context) can lead to oversimplification and/or generalization.

unsureList.best: EK 2.2A5: Effective arguments acknowledge other arguments and/or respond to them with counterarguments (e.g., concession, refutation, rebuttal).

unsureList.text: Evaluate the relevance and credibility of evidence in context
unsureList.best: LO 2.2B: Evaluating the relevance and credibility of evidence used to support an argument, taking context into consideration.

unsureList.text: Context and situation relative to other arguments shape interpretation
unsureList.best: EK 2.2B1: An argument’s context (time and purpose) and situation (in relation to other arguments) inform its interpretation.

unsureList.text: Qualitative and quantitative evidence vary in validity
unsureList.best: EK 2.2B2: Writers use qualitative and/ or quantitative evidence (e.g., facts, data, observations, predictions, analogies, explanations, opinions) to support their claims. Evidence has varying degrees of validity.

unsureList.text: Authors choose evidence strategically
unsureList.best: EK 2.2B3: Authors strategically include evidence to support their claims.

unsureList.text: Credibility drops when authors ignore limitations, opposing views or their own biases
unsureList.best: EK 2.2B6: Credibility is compromised when authors fail to acknowledge and/or consider the limitations of their conclusions, opposing views or perspectives, and/or their own biases.

unsureList.text: Evaluate the validity of an argument
unsureList.best: LO 2.2C: Evaluating the validity of an argument.

unsureList.text: An argument is valid when reasoning and conclusion align logically
unsureList.best: EK 2.2C1: An argument is valid when there is logical alignment between the line of reasoning and the conclusion.

unsureList.text: Validity needs evidence aligned with conclusions and acknowledged limits
unsureList.best: EK 2.2C2: Validity is most often achieved when the presented evidence is aligned with the conclusions. unsureList.text: Evaluate and critique others' inquiries, studies, works and perspectives
unsureList.best: LO 2.2D: Evaluating and critiquing others’ inquiries, studies, artistic works, and/or perspectives.

unsureList.text: Judge studies on internal coherence and alignment of purpose, goals and methods
unsureList.best: EK 2.2D1: Scholars analyze and evaluate others’ studies and artistic works in terms of internal coherence and alignment of the purposes, goals, and methods of inquiry. EU 2.3: Arguments have implications and consequences.

unsureList.text: Connect an argument to broader issues through the implications of its claim
unsureList.best: LO 2.3A: Connecting an argument to broader issues by examining the implications of the author’s claim.

unsureList.text: Evaluate potential resolutions or solutions raised by an argument
unsureList.best: LO 2.3B: Evaluating potential resolutions, conclusions, or solutions to problems or issues raised by an argument.

unsureList.text: Arguments can change behaviour and have real-world impact
unsureList.best: EK 2.3B1: Arguments are significant and have real-world impact because they can influence behavior (e.g., call one to action, suggest logical next steps).

unsureList.text: Identify, compare and interpret multiple perspectives or arguments on an issue
unsureList.best: LO 3.1A: Identifying, comparing, and interpreting multiple perspectives on or arguments about an issue.

unsureList.text: Perspective is shaped by background, assumptions, worldview and outside sources
unsureList.best: EK 3.1A1: An individual’s perspective is influenced by his or her background (e.g., experiences, culture, education), assumptions, and worldview, as well as by external sources.

unsureList.text: Perspectives may concur, complement or compete
unsureList.best: EK 3.1A2: Perspectives are not always oppositional; they may be concurring, complementary, or competing.

unsureList.text: Some perspectives are ambiguous, so interpretation may not give a definite answer

unsureList.text: Arguments may appeal to emotion, values, bias, assumptions and logic

unsureList.text: Consider how your own biases and assumptions influence judgment

unsureList.text: Build a well-reasoned argument that accounts for the problem's complexity
unsureList.best: EK 4.3A3: Source material should be introduced, integrated, or embedded into the text of an argument.

unsureList.text: Carefully chosen, connected claims, reasons and evidence unify an argument
unsureList.best: EK 4.1A2: Effective arguments are supported and unified by carefully chosen and connected claims, reasons, and evidence.
