unsureList.text: Compare pictures of embryonic development across species to find relationships hidden in adult anatomy.

unsureList.text: Explain how genetic variation of traits makes some individuals more likely to survive and reproduce.

(MS-LS4-6) Crosscutting Concepts Patterns

unsureList.text: Model the role of gravity in motions within galaxies and the solar system.

unsureList.text: Prove trigonometric identities involving the six trigonometric functions.
unsureList.best: Use the formulas for the nth term and for the sum of the first n terms to solve problems involving arithmetic or geometric progressions. Problems may be in context. Formulas are given in the List of formulas.

unsureList.text: Solve arrangement and selection problems using permutations or combinations.
unsureList.best: both permutations and combinations, are not included.

unsureList.text: Use the general binomial term to find specified terms, including terms independent of a variable.

unsureList.text: Identify arithmetic and geometric progressions and distinguish between them.

unsureList.text: Use nth-term and finite-sum formulas to solve arithmetic and geometric progression problems.
unsureList.best: Use the formulas for the nth term and for the sum of the first n terms to solve problems involving arithmetic or geometric progressions. Problems may be in context. Formulas are given in the List of formulas.

unsureList.text: Understand and correctly use different forms of vector notation.

unsureList.best: Know and use position vectors and unit vectors. For example: The unit vector in the same direction as a is a a.

unsureList.text: Understand the concept of a derived function, including an informal understanding of limits.

unsureList.best: Why choose this syllabus? Key benefits Cambridge IGCSE is the world’s most popular international qualification for 14 to 16 year olds, although it can be taken by students of other ages. It is tried, tested and trusted. Students can choose from 70 subjects in any combination – it is taught by over 5000 schools in 150 countries. Our programmes promote a thorough knowledge and understanding of a subject and help to develop the skills learners need for their next steps in education or employment. Cambridge IGCSE Information and Communication Technology provides learners with the ability to use a broad range of ICT skills and encourages knowledge and understanding of the development of ICT systems, networks and their safe use. This course provides learners with the ability to understand the rapid change of ICT in a technology-based world and the impact ICT has on the world. Learners in a modern ICT based world need to have the ability to gather, process and manipulate data; this course helps learners to fulfil this. Our approach in Cambridge IGCSE Information and Communication Technology encourages learners to be: confident, in applying knowledge and understanding of ICT technologies and using skills to solve ICT problems, both as individuals and working with others responsible, for themselves, responsive to and respectful of others with particular consideration to physical safety and eSafety reflective, in their ability to learn and develop ICT skills innovative, in the way that they use ICT-based solutions to solve problems and identify alternative solutions to solve problems engaged, socially, in the work that they undertake and to interrogate unfamiliar situations to provide ICT-based solutions. An explanation of how to distinguish between a maximum point and a minimum point may be required. Unless specified otherwise, any valid method is allowed.

unsureList.text: Integrate sums of powers of x, including 1/x and 1/(ax+b).
unsureList.best: Integrate sums of terms in powers of x, including x

unsureList.text: Integrate (ax+b)^n, sin, cos, sec^2 and exponential forms of ax+b.
unsureList.best: sin (ax + b)

unsureList.text: Evaluate definite integrals and find plane areas.
unsureList.best: a sum of two areas.

unsureList.text: Use differentiation and integration for displacement, velocity and acceleration in straight-line motion.

unsureList.text: Draw and use displacement, distance, velocity, speed and acceleration time graphs.

changes.from: Measure liquid volume with a measuring cylinder and solid volume by displacement.

changes.from: Measure time intervals with clocks and digital timers.
changes.to: Describe how to measure a variety of time intervals using clocks and digital timers

changes.from: Find an average small distance or short time by measuring many, such as a pendulum period.
changes.to: Determine an average value for a small distance and for a short interval of time by measuring multiples (including the period of oscillation of a pendulum)

changes.from: Name common scalar quantities: distance, speed, time, mass, energy, temperature.
changes.to: Know that the following quantities are scalars: distance, speed, time, mass, energy and temperature

changes.from: Calculate average speed from total distance and total time.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation average speed = total distance travelled total time taken

changes.from: Define acceleration and use a = change in velocity / time.

changes.from: State that mass measures the quantity of matter in an object.

changes.to: State that the mass of an object resists change from its state of rest or motion (inertia)

changes.from: Compare weights and masses with a beam or equal-arm balance.

changes.from: Measure weight with a force meter.
changes.to: Describe how to measure weight using a force meter

changes.from: State that a gravitational field is a region where a mass feels a force.

changes.from: Define thinking, braking and stopping distance.

changes.to: Explain applications and consequences of thermal expansion in the context of common examples, including the liquid-in-glass thermometer

changes.from: Convert between kelvin and Celsius.

changes.to: Describe experiments to distinguish between good and bad emitters of infrared radiation

changes.to: Describe experiments to distinguish between good and bad absorbers of infrared radiation

changes.from: Define and use normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction.
changes.to: Define and use the terms normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction

changes.to: Describe an experiment to show refraction of light by transparent blocks of different shapes

changes.to: Describe experiments to show internal reflection and total internal reflection

changes.to: Define and use the terms focal length, principal axis and principal focus (focal point)

changes.to: Draw ray diagrams to illustrate the formation of real and virtual images of an object by a converging lens and know that a real image is formed by converging rays and a virtual image is formed by diverging rays

changes.to: Describe the use of a single lens as a magnifying glass

changes.from: Know the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and wavelength.
changes.to: Know the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and in order of wavelength

changes.from: Describe sound produced by vibrating sources.
changes.to: Describe the production of sound by vibrating sources

changes.to: Describe the longitudinal nature of sound waves and describe compressions and rarefactions

changes.to: Explain why sound waves cannot travel in a vacuum and describe an experiment to demonstrate this

changes.to: Describe how changes in amplitude and frequency affect the loudness and pitch of sound waves

changes.to: Describe an echo as the reflection of sound waves

changes.from: Describe simple experiments showing sound reflection.
changes.to: Describe simple experiments to show the reflection of sound waves

changes.to: Know that, in general, sound travels faster in solids than in liquids and faster in liquids than in gases

changes.to: Describe the uses of ultrasound in cleaning, prenatal and other medical scanning, and in sonar (including calculation of depth or distance from time and wave speed)

changes.from: Describe forces between poles and between magnets and magnetic materials.
changes.to: Describe the forces between magnetic poles and between magnets and magnetic materials, including the use of the terms north pole (N pole), south pole (S pole), attraction and repulsion, magnetised and unmagnetised

changes.to: Draw the pattern and direction of the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet

changes.to: Describe an electric field as a region in which an electric charge experiences a force

changes.to: Describe an experiment to distinguish between electrical conductors and insulators

changes.to: Recall and use a simple electron model to explain the difference between electrical conductors and insulators

changes.to: Describe electrical conduction in metals in terms of the movement of free electrons

changes.to: Know that current is measured in amps (amperes) and that the amp is given by coulomb per second (C/s)

changes.from: Describe analogue and digital ammeters with different ranges.

changes.to: Describe the action of a variable potential divider

changes.from: State the advantages of connecting lamps in parallel.
changes.to: State the advantages of connecting lamps in parallel in a lighting circuit

changes.from: Use P = IV.

changes.from: Use E = IVt.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation energy = current × voltage × time E = IVt

changes.to: Explain the use and operation of trip switches and fuses and choose appropriate fuse ratings and trip switch settings

changes.from: Explain why fuses and circuit breakers go in the live wire.
changes.to: Explain why fuses and circuit breakers are connected into the live wire

changes.from: Describe an experiment showing electromagnetic induction.
changes.to: Describe an experiment to demonstrate electromagnetic induction

changes.to: Describe a simple form of a.c. generator (rotating coil or rotating magnet) and the use of slip rings and brushes where needed

changes.from: Use the relative directions of force, field and current.
changes.to: Recall and use the relative directions of force, magnetic field and current

changes.to: Describe the operation of an electric motor, including the action of a split-ring commutator and brushes

changes.from: Describe the structure and principle of an iron-cored transformer.
changes.to: Describe the structure and explain the principle of operation of a simple iron-cored transformer

changes.from: Use primary, secondary, step-up and step-down.

unsureList.best: Describe the formation of ethanoic acid by the oxidation of ethanol: (a) with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)

unsureList.text: Deduce addition polymer structures from alkenes and the reverse.
unsureList.best: Deduce the structure or repeat unit of an addition polymer from a given alkene and vice versa

unsureList.text: Deduce condensation polymer structures: polyamides and polyesters.
unsureList.best: Deduce the structure or repeat unit of a condensation polymer from given monomers and vice versa, limited to: (a) polyamides from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine (b) polyesters from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol

unsureList.text: Describe how plastic properties affect disposal.
unsureList.best: Describe how the properties of plastics have implications for their disposal

unsureList.text: Describe the environmental challenges of plastics.
unsureList.best: Describe the environmental challenges caused by plastics, limited to: (b) accumulation in oceans

unsureList.text: Describe and draw nylon and PET.
unsureList.best: Describe and draw the structure of: (a) nylon, a polyamide C O C O C C O O N H N H N H N H C O

unsureList.text: State that PET can be recycled to monomers.
unsureList.best: State that PET can be converted back into monomers and re-polymerised

unsureList.text: Describe proteins as natural polyamides made of amino acids.
unsureList.best: Describe proteins as natural polyamides and that they are formed from amino acid monomers with the general structure: H O H O H N H C C R where R represents different types of side-chain

unsureList.text: Name apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume.
unsureList.best: Name appropriate apparatus for the measurement of time, temperature, mass and volume, including: (f) measuring cylinders

unsureList.text: Describe solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue and filtrate.
unsureList.best: Describe a: (d)  saturated solution as a solution containing the maximum concentration of a solute dissolved in the solvent at a specified temperature

unsureList.text: Describe an acid-base titration using a burette, pipette and indicator.
unsureList.best: Describe an acid–base titration to include the use of a: (a) burette (b) volumetric pipette (c) suitable indicator

unsureList.text: Interpret chromatograms to identify unknowns and pure or impure substances.
unsureList.best: Interpret simple chromatograms to identify: (b) pure and impure substances

unsureList.text: Describe tests for the anions carbonate, halides, nitrate, sulfate and sulfite.
unsureList.best: Describe tests to identify the anions: (d) sulfate, SO4 2–, by acidifying with dilute nitric acid then adding aqueous barium nitrate

unsureList.text: Describe tests for cations using sodium hydroxide and ammonia.
unsureList.best: Describe tests using aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to identify the aqueous cations: (a) aluminium, Al3+

unsureList.text: Describe tests for ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur dioxide.
unsureList.best: Describe tests to identify the gases: (a) ammonia, NH3, using damp red litmus paper (b) carbon dioxide, CO2, using limewater (c) chlorine, Cl2, using damp litmus paper (d) hydrogen, H2, using a lighted splint (e) oxygen, O2, using a glowing splint (f) sulfur dioxide, SO2, using acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)

changes.from: Describe a bacterial cell: ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmids, cytoplasm, membrane and wall.
changes.to: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell, limited to: ribosomes, circular deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and plasmids, cytoplasm, cell membrane and cell wall

changes.from: Use the terms cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism correctly with examples.
changes.to: Understand the terms cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism as illustrated by examples covered in the syllabus

changes.from: State and use the formula magnification = image size divided by actual size.
changes.to: State and use the formula magnification = image size actual size

changes.from: Describe a species as organisms able to breed and produce fertile offspring.
changes.to: Describe a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring

changes.from: State the main features that place organisms in the animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote or protoctist kingdom.
changes.to: State the main features used to place all organisms into one of the five kingdoms: Animal, Plant, Fungus, Prokaryote, Protoctist

changes.from: State the features of vertebrate groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and arthropod groups (myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans).
changes.to: State the main features used to place organisms into groups within the animal kingdom, limited to: (a) the main groups of vertebrates: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish (b) the main groups of arthropods: myriapods, insects, arachnids, crustaceans

changes.from: State the main features of viruses: a protein coat and genetic material.
changes.to: State the main features of viruses, limited to protein coat and genetic material

changes.from: Understand that viruses can only replicate inside living cells.
changes.to: Understand that viruses can only replicate in living cells

changes.from: Describe water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
changes.to: Describe the role of water as a solvent in organisms with reference to digestion, excretion and transport

changes.from: Understand that random kinetic energy of molecules and ions powers diffusion and osmosis.
changes.to: Understand that the energy for diffusion and osmosis comes from the kinetic energy of random movement of molecules and ions

changes.from: Investigate how surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance affect diffusion.
changes.to: Investigate the factors that influence diffusion, limited to: surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance

changes.from: Understand osmosis as net water movement from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
changes.to: Understand osmosis as the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane

changes.from: Understand that water pressure inside cells pushes on the cell wall and supports plants.
changes.to: Understand that plants are supported by the pressure of water inside the cells pressing outwards on the cell wall

changes.from: Describe osmosis effects on plant and animal tissues, and the role of the water potential gradient in water uptake and loss.
changes.to: Describe the effects of osmosis on plant and animal tissues and explain the importance of water potential gradient and osmosis in the uptake and loss of water

changes.from: Investigate plant tissues in different concentrations, using turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effects on plant tissues of immersing them in solutions of different concentrations, using the terms turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid

changes.from: Investigate osmosis with materials such as dialysis tubing.
changes.to: Investigate osmosis using materials such as dialysis tubing

changes.from: Understand active transport as movement against a concentration gradient through the membrane using energy from respiration.
changes.to: Understand active transport as the movement of molecules or ions into or out of a cell through the cell membrane, from a region of their lower concentration to a region of their higher concentration (i.e. against a concentration gradient), using energy released during respiration

changes.from: Explain why active transport matters for ion uptake by root hair cells.
changes.to: Explain the importance of active transport in ion uptake by root hair cells

changes.from: List the chemical elements in carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and DNA.
changes.to: List the chemical elements that make up: (a) carbohydrates (b) lipids (fats and oils) (c) proteins (d) DNA

changes.from: State that large molecules are built from smaller ones: starch, cellulose, glycogen from glucose; proteins from amino acids; lipids from fatty acids and glycerol; DNA from nucleotides.
changes.to: State that large molecules are made from smaller molecules, limited to: starch, cellulose and glycogen from glucose; proteins from amino acids; lipids from fatty acids and glycerol; DNA from nucleotides

changes.from: Describe enzymes as protein biological catalysts involved in all metabolic reactions.
changes.to: Describe enzymes as proteins that function as biological catalysts and are involved in all metabolic reactions

changes.from: Explain enzyme action using substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex and product.
changes.to: Explain enzyme action with reference to the substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex, and product

changes.from: Investigate and describe how temperature and pH change enzyme activity.
changes.to: Investigate and describe the effects of temperature and pH on enzyme activity

changes.from: Understand photosynthesis as making carbohydrates from raw materials using light energy.
changes.to: Understand that photosynthesis is the process by which plants make carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light

changes.from: State that chlorophyll converts light energy into chemical energy for making glucose and other carbohydrates.
changes.to: State that chlorophyll transfers light energy into chemical energy for the formation of glucose and other carbohydrates

changes.from: Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide, using suitable controls.
changes.to: Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, using appropriate controls

changes.from: Describe and explain how light, carbon dioxide and temperature change the rate of photosynthesis.
changes.to: Describe and explain the effect of varying light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis

changes.from: Identify and explain limiting factors of photosynthesis in different conditions.
changes.to: Identify and explain the limiting factors of photosynthesis in different environmental conditions

changes.from: Relate root hair cell structure to water and ion uptake.
changes.to: Relate the structure of root hair cells to their function of water and ion uptake

changes.from: Outline the water route through root hair cells, cortex, xylem and mesophyll cells.
changes.to: Outline the pathway taken by water through the root, stem and leaf, limited to: root hair cells, root cortex cells, xylem and mesophyll cells

changes.from: Use a stain to investigate the water pathway in a cut stem.
changes.to: Investigate, using a suitable stain, the pathway of water in a cut stem

changes.from: Understand that water evaporates from mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out through the stomata.
changes.to: Understand that water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells into air spaces and then diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata as water vapour

changes.from: Explain how wind, temperature, humidity and light affect transpiration rate, and how wilting happens.
changes.to: Explain: (a)  the effects of wind speed, and the variation of temperature, humidity and light intensity on transpiration rate (b) how wilting occurs

changes.from: Describe translocation as phloem movement of sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks.
changes.to: Describe translocation as the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from parts of plants that produce or release them (sources) to parts of plants that use or store them (sinks)

changes.from: State that xylem carries water and mineral ions and gives support.
changes.to: State the functions of xylem as transport of water and mineral ions, and support

changes.from: List sources and dietary importance of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium, iron, fibre and water.
changes.to: List the principal sources of, and describe the dietary importance of, carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins (C and D only), mineral salts (calcium and iron only), fibre (roughage) and water

changes.from: Name deficiency diseases and symptoms: scurvy, rickets (vitamin D and calcium) and anaemia.
changes.to: Name the diseases and describe the symptoms resulting from deficiencies of vitamin C (scurvy), vitamin D (rickets), calcium (rickets) and iron (anaemia)

changes.from: Understand what a balanced diet is.
changes.to: Understand the concept of a balanced diet

changes.from: Explain why most foods must be digested before absorption.
changes.to: Explain why most foods must be digested before they can be absorbed

changes.from: Describe physical digestion as breaking food into smaller pieces without chemical change.
changes.to: Describe physical digestion as the breakdown of food into smaller pieces without chemical change to the food molecules

changes.from: Describe chemical digestion as breaking large molecules into small ones.
changes.to: Describe chemical digestion as the breakdown of large molecules into small molecules

changes.from: State that physical digestion increases surface area for enzymes.
changes.to: State that physical digestion increases the surface area of food for the action of enzymes in chemical digestion

changes.from: Identify incisors, canines, premolars and molars.
changes.to: Identify the types of human teeth (incisors, canines, premolars and molars)

changes.from: Describe tooth structure: enamel, dentine, pulp, nerves and cement, set in the gum.
changes.to: Describe the structure of human teeth, limited to: enamel, dentine, pulp, nerves and cement, and understand that teeth are embedded in the gum

changes.from: Describe hydrochloric acid in the stomach as killing swallowed bacteria.
changes.to: Describe the function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach as killing ingested bacteria

changes.from: Understand that stomach and duodenum proteases work best at different pH levels.
changes.to: Understand that the different proteases present in the stomach and the duodenum work best at different pH levels

changes.from: State that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
changes.to: State that the small intestine is the region where nutrients are absorbed

changes.from: Understand absorption as movement of nutrients from the intestine into the blood, by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
changes.to: Understand that absorption (by diffusion, osmosis and active transport) is the movement of nutrients from the intestines into cells lining the digestive system and then into the blood

changes.from: Understand that water is absorbed in the small intestine and colon, mostly in the small intestine.
changes.to: Understand that water is absorbed from the lumen of the small intestine and the colon, but that most absorption of water happens in the small intestine

changes.from: State that the hepatic portal vein carries most absorbed molecules and ions to the liver.
changes.to: State the function of the hepatic portal vein as the route taken to the liver by most of the molecules and ions absorbed from the ileum

changes.from: Describe human gas exchange surfaces: large area, thin, good blood and air supply.
changes.to: Describe the features of gas exchange surfaces in humans, limited to: large surface area, thin surface, good blood and air supply

changes.from: Identify the larynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and capillaries.
changes.to: Identify, on diagrams and images, the larynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and associated capillaries

changes.from: State the features and role of the alveoli as the exchange surface.
changes.to: State the characteristics of, and describe the role of, the exchange surface of the alveoli in gas exchange

changes.from: Identify ribs, intercostal muscles and the diaphragm.
changes.to: Identify, on diagrams and images, the ribs, internal and external intercostal muscles and the diaphragm

changes.from: State the uses of energy: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and keeping body temperature steady.
changes.to: State the uses of energy in living organisms including muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, the passage of electrical impulses along neurones and the maintenance of a constant body temperature

changes.from: Investigate and describe how temperature affects respiration in yeast.
changes.to: Investigate and describe the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast

changes.from: State the word and balanced chemical equations for aerobic respiration.
changes.to: State the word equation and balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration

changes.from: Describe anaerobic respiration as releasing little energy from glucose without oxygen.
changes.to: Describe anaerobic respiration as the release of a relatively small amount of energy by the breakdown of glucose without using oxygen

changes.from: Explain why lactic acid builds up in vigorous exercise, causing an oxygen debt (EPOC).
changes.to: Explain why lactic acid builds up in muscles and blood during vigorous exercise causing Excess Post‑exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) or an ‘oxygen debt’

changes.from: Describe the circulatory system as vessels, a pump and valves giving one-way blood flow.
changes.to: Describe the circulatory system as a system of blood vessels with a pump and valves to ensure one- way flow of blood

changes.from: Describe double circulation as blood passing through the heart twice per circuit.
changes.to: Describe a double circulation as a system in which blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit

changes.from: Understand that double circulation gives low pressure to the lungs and high pressure to the body.
changes.to: Understand that a double circulation provides a low pressure circulation to the lungs and a high pressure circulation to the body tissues

changes.from: Identify the heart's muscular wall, septum, ventricles, atria, valves and coronary arteries.
changes.to: Identify the structures of the mammalian heart, limited to: the muscular wall, the septum, the left and right ventricles and atria, atrioventricular and semilunar valves and coronary arteries

changes.from: State that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it.
changes.to: State that blood is pumped away from the heart in arteries and returns to the heart in veins

changes.from: State that heart activity is monitored by ECG, pulse rate and listening to valve sounds.
changes.to: State that the activity of the heart may be monitored by electrocardiogram (ECG), pulse rate and listening to sounds of valves closing

changes.from: Investigate and explain how physical activity changes heart rate.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effect of physical activity on heart rate

changes.from: Discuss how diet and exercise reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
changes.to: Discuss the role of diet and exercise in reducing the risk of coronary heart disease

changes.from: Describe and identify the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries: wall thickness, wall composition, lumen and valves.
changes.to: Describe, and identify on diagrams and photomicrographs, the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries, limited to: (a) relative thickness of wall (b) composition of wall (muscle and elastic tissue) (c) diameter of lumen (d) presence of valves

changes.from: Identify red cells and white cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes) on slides and images.
changes.to: Identify red and white blood cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes) as seen under the light microscope on prepared slides, and in diagrams and photomicrographs

changes.from: List the components of blood: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
changes.to: List the components of blood as red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma

changes.from: Describe how substances pass between capillary blood, tissue fluid and body cells.
changes.to: Describe the transfer of substances between blood in capillaries, tissue fluid and body cells

changes.from: Describe a transmissible disease as one whose pathogen passes from host to host.
changes.to: Describe a transmissible disease as a disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another

changes.from: Describe the body's barriers: skin, nose hairs, mucus and stomach acid.
changes.to: Describe the human body’s barriers to the entry of pathogens, limited to: skin, hairs in the nose, mucus, stomach acid

changes.from: Understand the mosquito as a disease vector.
changes.to: Understand the role of the mosquito as a vector of disease

changes.from: Explain that HIV is a viral pathogen.
changes.to: Explain that human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a viral pathogen

changes.from: Understand that HIV infection may lead to AIDS.
changes.to: Understand that HIV infection may lead to Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS)

changes.from: Describe ways HIV can be controlled.
changes.to: Describe the methods by which HIV may be controlled

changes.from: Explain how the cholera toxin causes chloride secretion, osmotic water loss, diarrhoea and dehydration.
changes.to: Explain that the cholera bacterium produces a toxin that causes secretion of chloride ions into the small intestine, causing osmotic movement of water into the gut, resulting in diarrhoea, dehydration and loss of ions from the blood

changes.from: Describe the effects of tobacco smoke (nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide) on health and on birth weight.
changes.to: Describe the effects of tobacco smoke and its major toxic components (nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide): strong association with bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer, heart disease, and the association between smoking during pregnancy and reduced birth weight of the baby

changes.from: Describe a drug as any substance that changes chemical reactions in the body.
changes.to: Describe a drug as any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body

changes.from: Describe antibiotics as treatment for bacterial infection.
changes.to: Describe the use of antibiotics for the treatment of bacterial infection

changes.from: State that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.
changes.to: State that antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses

changes.from: Explain how using antibiotics only when essential limits resistant bacteria, including MRSA.
changes.to: Explain how development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, including MRSA, can be minimised by using antibiotics only when essential

changes.from: Describe active immunity as defence by the body's own antibody production.
changes.to: Describe active immunity as defence against a pathogen by antibody production in the body

changes.from: State that each pathogen has its own antigens with specific shapes.
changes.to: State that each pathogen has its own antigens, which have specific shapes

changes.from: Describe antibodies as proteins that bind antigens, destroying pathogens or marking them for phagocytes.
changes.to: Describe antibodies as proteins that bind to antigens leading to direct destruction of pathogens, or marking of pathogens for destruction by phagocytes

changes.from: State that antibodies have shapes complementary to specific antigens.
changes.to: State that specific antibodies have complementary shapes which fit specific antigens

changes.from: Explain that active immunity comes from infection or vaccination.
changes.to: Explain that active immunity is gained after an infection by a pathogen, or by vaccination

changes.from: Outline vaccination: weakened pathogens or antigens, an immune response, and memory cells for long-term immunity.
changes.to: Outline the process of vaccination: (a) weakened pathogens or their antigens are given (b) the antigens stimulate an immune response by lymphocytes which produce antibodies (c) memory cells are produced that give long-term immunity

changes.from: Explain passive immunity as short-term defence from another person's antibodies, via the placenta and breast milk.
changes.to: Explain that passive immunity is a short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual, limited to: across the placenta and in breast milk

changes.from: Explain why breast-feeding matters for infants' passive immunity.
changes.to: Explain the importance of breast-feeding for the development of passive immunity in infants

changes.from: State that passive immunity produces no memory cells.
changes.to: State that memory cells are not produced in passive immunity

changes.from: State that carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs.
changes.to: State that carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration, which is excreted through the lungs

changes.from: State that urea is a toxic waste made in the liver from excess amino acids.
changes.to: State that urea is a toxic waste product produced in the liver from the breakdown of excess amino acids

changes.from: Identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra and state each function.
changes.to: Identify, on diagrams, the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra and state the function of each (the function of the kidney should be described simply as removing urea and excess salts and water from the blood as urine)

changes.from: Outline nephron structure: Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, tubules, loop of Henle and collecting duct.
changes.to: Outline the structure of a nephron and its associated blood vessels, limited to: Bowman’s capsule, glomerulus, tubules, loop of Henle and collecting duct

changes.from: State that the nervous system coordinates and regulates body functions.
changes.to: State that the nervous system (brain, spinal cord and nerves) coordinates and regulates body functions

changes.from: Describe a simple reflex arc: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector.
changes.to: Describe simple reflex arcs in terms of receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector (muscles and glands)

changes.from: Describe synapse structure: vesicles of neurotransmitter, the gap and receptor proteins.
changes.to: Describe the structure of a synapse, including the presence of vesicles containing neurotransmitter molecules, the synaptic gap and receptor proteins

changes.from: State that synapses make impulses travel in one direction only.
changes.to: State that synapses ensure that impulses travel in one direction only

changes.from: Describe sense organs as receptor cell groups responding to specific stimuli.
changes.to: Describe sense organs as groups of receptor cells responding to specific stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals

changes.from: Identify the structures of the eye, from cornea to blind spot.
changes.to: Identify, on a diagram, the structures of the eye, limited to: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments, retina, fovea, optic nerve and blind spot

changes.from: Explain the pupil reflex using circular and radial iris muscles.
changes.to: Explain the pupil reflex in terms of light intensity and antagonistic action of circular and radial muscles in the iris

changes.from: Explain accommodation for near and distant objects.
changes.to: Explain accommodation to view near and distant objects in terms of the contraction and relaxation of the ciliary muscles, tension in the suspensory ligaments, shape of the lens and refraction of light

changes.from: Describe a hormone as a chemical from a gland, carried in blood, that changes target organs.
changes.to: Describe a hormone as a chemical substance, produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs

changes.from: Compare nervous and hormonal control in speed and duration.
changes.to: Compare nervous and hormonal control, limited to speed of action and duration of effect

changes.from: Describe homeostasis as keeping the internal environment constant.
changes.to: Describe homeostasis as the maintenance of a constant internal environment

changes.from: Explain negative feedback around a set point.
changes.to: Explain the concept of control by negative feedback with reference to a set point

changes.from: Describe the role of insulation in keeping mammals' body temperature constant.
changes.to: Describe the role of insulation in maintaining a constant internal body temperature in mammals

changes.from: Describe the roles of the hypothalamus and skin temperature receptors.
changes.to: Describe the roles of the hypothalamus and of temperature receptors in the skin in maintaining a constant internal body temperature in mammals

changes.from: Describe how the liver, pancreas, insulin and glucagon control blood glucose.
changes.to: Describe the control of blood glucose concentration by the liver and pancreas and the roles of insulin and glucagon

changes.from: Describe signs and insulin treatment of Type 1 diabetes.
changes.to: Describe the signs of Type 1 diabetes (limited to increased blood glucose concentration and glucose in urine) and its treatment (administration of insulin)

changes.from: Describe mitosis as nuclear division giving genetically identical cells.
changes.to: Describe mitosis as nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells in which the chromosome number is maintained (details of stages are not required)

changes.from: Outline the roles of mitosis: growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction.
changes.to: Outline the role of mitosis in growth, repair of damaged tissues, replacement of dying cells and asexual reproduction

changes.from: Describe stem cells as unspecialised cells that divide and can then specialise.
changes.to: Describe stem cells as unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions

changes.from: State that meiosis produces gametes.
changes.to: State that meiosis is involved in the production of gametes

changes.from: Describe meiosis as a reduction division giving genetically different haploid cells.
changes.to: Describe meiosis as a reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid resulting in genetically different cells (details of stages are not required)

changes.from: Understand that cancers result from uncontrolled cell division.
changes.to: Understand that cancers form as a result of uncontrolled cell division

changes.from: Describe asexual reproduction as one parent producing identical offspring.
changes.to: Describe asexual reproduction as a process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent

changes.from: Describe sexual reproduction as fusion of haploid nuclei into a diploid zygote, giving varied offspring.
changes.to: Describe sexual reproduction as the process involving the fusion of haploid nuclei (fertilisation) to form a diploid zygote and the production of genetically different offspring

changes.from: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction.
changes.to: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction

changes.from: Compare insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers and their pollen.
changes.to: Compare the flower structure and the pollen from insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers

changes.from: Outline pollination and distinguish self-pollination from cross-pollination.
changes.to: Outline the process of pollination and distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination

changes.from: Describe pollen tube growth into the ovule and then fertilisation.
changes.to: Describe the growth of the pollen tube and its entry into the ovule followed by fertilisation (production of endosperm and details of development are not required)

changes.from: Investigate and describe seed structure: embryo (radicle, plumule, cotyledons) and testa.
changes.to: Investigate and describe the structure of a seed, limited to embryo (radicle, plumule and cotyledons) and testa

changes.from: Understand that seed and fruit dispersal colonises new areas and lowers competition.
changes.to: Understand that seed and fruit dispersal by wind and by animals is a means of colonising new areas and of reducing competition

changes.from: Relate features of wind-dispersed and animal-dispersed fruits to their functions.
changes.to: Relate the features of wind-dispersed fruits and animal-dispersed fruits to their functions

changes.from: Describe germination, including the role of enzymes.
changes.to: Describe the process of germination, including the role of enzymes

changes.from: Describe fertilisation as fusion of the nuclei of sperm and egg.
changes.to: Describe fertilisation as the fusion of the nuclei from a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg cell)

changes.from: Compare male and female gametes in size, structure, number and motility.
changes.to: Compare male and female gametes in terms of size, structure, numbers and motility

changes.from: Describe the roles of testosterone and oestrogen in puberty.
changes.to: Describe the roles of testosterone and oestrogen in the development and regulation of secondary sexual characteristics during puberty

changes.from: Describe the menstrual cycle: egg release and changes in the uterus lining.
changes.to: Describe the menstrual cycle in terms of development and release of an egg and changes in the lining of the uterus

changes.from: Explain how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone control the menstrual cycle.
changes.to: Explain the roles of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinising hormone (LH), oestrogen and progesterone in controlling the menstrual cycle

changes.from: Describe early zygote development to an embryo implanting in the uterus.
changes.to: Describe the early development of the zygote, limited to the formation of a ball of cells (embryo) that becomes implanted in the lining of the uterus

changes.from: State the functions of the amniotic sac and fluid.
changes.to: State the functions of the amniotic sac and the amniotic fluid

changes.from: State that some viruses can cross the placenta and affect the fetus.
changes.to: State that some viruses can pass across the placenta and affect the fetus

changes.from: Describe variation as differences between individuals of one species.
changes.to: Describe variation as differences between individuals of the same species

changes.from: Understand continuous variation as a range of phenotypes between two extremes.
changes.to: Understand that continuous variation results in a range of phenotypes between two extremes, including body length and body mass

changes.from: Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling protein production, including enzymes.
changes.to: Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins, including enzymes

changes.from: Use the terms dominant, recessive, phenotype, genotype, homozygous and heterozygous.
changes.to: Understand and use the terms: dominant, recessive, phenotype, genotype, homozygous and heterozygous

changes.from: Use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares to predict monohybrid crosses and 1:1 and 3:1 ratios.
changes.to: Use genetic diagrams, including Punnett squares, to predict the results of monohybrid crosses and calculate phenotypic ratios, limited to 1:1 and 3:1 ratios

changes.from: Explain why observed ratios often differ from expected ones, especially in small samples.
changes.to: Explain why observed ratios often differ from expected ratios, especially when there are small numbers of offspring

changes.from: Describe sex determination in humans (XX and XY).
changes.to: Describe the determination of sex in humans (XX and XY chromosomes)

changes.from: Describe gene mutation as a random change in DNA base sequence, using sickle cell anaemia.
changes.to: Describe a gene mutation as a random change in the base sequence of DNA, using sickle cell anaemia as an example

changes.from: Describe chromosome mutation as a change in chromosome number or structure, using Down's syndrome.
changes.to: Describe a chromosome mutation as a change in the chromosome number or structure, using Down’s syndrome as an example (47 chromosomes instead of 46)

changes.from: State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation create genetic variation.
changes.to: State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation are sources of genetic variation in populations

changes.from: Understand that ionising radiation and some chemicals raise mutation rates.
changes.to: Understand that ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation

changes.from: Describe how a population's inherited features evolve through natural selection.
changes.to: Describe how the inherited features of a population can evolve over time as a result of natural selection

changes.from: Describe antibiotic-resistant bacteria, including MRSA, as natural selection.
changes.to: Describe the development of strains of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, including MRSA, as an example of natural selection

changes.from: Describe the role of artificial selection in economically important plants and animals.
changes.to: Describe the role of artificial selection in the production of economically important plants and animals

changes.from: Explain the role of yeast in making bread and ethanol.
changes.to: Explain the role of yeast in the production of bread and ethanol

changes.from: Describe fermenters and the conditions controlled: temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients and waste.
changes.to: Describe how fermenters can be used for the large-scale production of useful products by bacteria and fungi, including the conditions that need to be controlled, limited to: temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrient supply and waste products

changes.from: Describe enzymes in washing powders, pectinase in juice and lactase in lactose-free milk.
changes.to: Describe the use of: (a) enzymes in biological washing powders (b) pectinase for fruit juice production (c) lactase for lactose-free milk

changes.from: Describe genetic modification as removing, changing or inserting individual genes.
changes.to: Describe genetic modification as changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes

changes.from: Discuss potential advantages and risks of modifying crop plants and bacteria.
changes.to: Discuss potential advantages and risks of genetic modification, limited to modifying crop plants and bacteria

changes.from: Understand that the Sun is the main energy source for most biological systems.
changes.to: Understand that the Sun is the principal source of energy input to most biological systems

changes.from: Explain why most life depends completely on photosynthesis.
changes.to: Explain why most forms of life are completely dependent on photosynthesis

changes.from: Describe energy flow through food chains and webs, ending in transfer to the environment.
changes.to: Describe the flow of energy through food chains and webs including energy from light and energy in living organisms and its eventual transfer to the environment

changes.from: Understand producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore and decomposer.
changes.to: Understand the terms producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore and decomposer

changes.from: Describe food webs as linked food chains and construct and interpret them.
changes.to: Describe food webs as networks of interconnected food chains and construct and interpret them

changes.from: Explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient.
changes.to: Explain why the transfer of energy from one trophic level to another is inefficient

changes.from: Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossil fuels and combustion.
changes.to: Describe the carbon cycle, limited to: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, formation of fossil fuels and combustion

changes.from: Describe a population as one species living in one area at one time.
changes.to: Describe a population as a group of organisms of one species, living in the same area, at the same time

changes.from: Describe a community as all the populations in an ecosystem.
changes.to: Describe a community as all of the populations of different species in an ecosystem

changes.from: Describe an ecosystem as a community and its environment interacting.
changes.to: Describe an ecosystem as a unit containing the community of organisms and their environment, interacting together

changes.from: Describe biodiversity as the number of different species in an area.
changes.to: Describe biodiversity as the number of different species that live in an area

changes.from: State the factors affecting population growth: food, competition, predation and disease.

changes.from: Understand that human population growth increases the demand for global resources.
changes.to: Understand that the growth of the human population is increasing the demand for global resources

changes.from: Outline the causes and consequences of deforestation.
changes.to: Outline the causes and describe the consequences of deforestation, limited to its effects on: biodiversity, extinction, loss of soil, flooding and concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

changes.from: Discuss reasons for conservation: biodiversity, reducing extinction and protecting vulnerable environments.
changes.to: Discuss reasons for conservation of species with reference to: (a) maintenance of biodiversity (b) reducing extinction (c) protecting vulnerable environments

changes.from: Explain how forests are conserved by education, protected areas, quotas and replanting.
changes.to: Explain how forests can be conserved using education, protected areas, quotas and replanting

changes.to: Explain how fish stocks can be conserved using education, closed seasons, protected areas, controlled net types and mesh size, quotas and monitoring

changes.from: Describe a sustainable resource as one produced as fast as it is removed.
changes.to: Describe a sustainable resource as one which is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment so that it does not run out
