unsureList.best: Identify the main regions of the digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum and ileum), pancreas, liver, gall bladder and large intestine (colon, rectum and anus)

unsureList.text: Describe the functions of the mouth, salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, ileum, colon, rectum and anus.
unsureList.best: Identify the main regions of the digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum and ileum), pancreas, liver, gall bladder and large intestine (colon, rectum and anus)

changes.from: Identify mitochondria, nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane in an animal cell on diagrams and micrographs.
changes.to: Identify on diagrams, photomicrographs or electron micrographs, the mitochondria, nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane in an animal cell

changes.from: Identify chloroplasts, sap vacuole and cellulose cell wall as well, in a plant cell.
changes.to: Identify on diagrams, photomicrographs or electron micrographs, the mitochondria, chloroplasts, nucleus, sap vacuole, cytoplasm, cell membrane and cellulose cell wall in a plant cell

changes.from: Describe water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
changes.to: Describe the role of water as a solvent in organisms with reference to digestion, excretion and transport

changes.from: Describe how surface area, temperature, gradient and distance affect diffusion rate.
changes.to: Describe how the rate of diffusion is affected by surface area, temperature, concentration gradients and distance

changes.from: Explain osmosis as net water movement from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
changes.to: Understand osmosis as the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane (calculations of water potential are not required)

changes.from: Describe osmosis effects on plant and animal tissues and its role in water uptake and loss.
changes.to: Describe the effects of osmosis on plant and animal tissues and explain the importance of water potential gradient and osmosis in the uptake and loss of water

changes.from: Investigate plant tissues in different solutions using turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effects on plant tissues of immersing them in solutions of different concentrations, using the terms turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid

changes.from: Explain enzyme action using substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex and product.
changes.to: Explain enzyme action with reference to the substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex, and product

changes.from: Explain enzyme specificity through the complementary shape of the active site.
changes.to: Explain the specificity of enzymes in terms of the complementary shape and fit of the active site with the substrate

changes.from: Explain photosynthesis as plants making carbohydrates from raw materials using light energy.
changes.to: Understand that photosynthesis is the process by which plants make carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light

changes.from: State the word and balanced equations for photosynthesis.
changes.to: State the word equation and balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis

changes.from: Investigate how light intensity affects photosynthesis rate in submerged aquatic plants.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effect of varying light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using submerged aquatic plants

changes.from: Explain how a large surface area and thin leaf suit photosynthesis.
changes.to: State that most leaves have a large surface area and are thin, and explain how these features are adaptations for photosynthesis

changes.from: Identify the leaf tissues (stomata, guard cells, mesophyll, air spaces, xylem, phloem, chloroplasts) and explain their adaptations.
changes.to: Identify and label the cuticle, cellular and tissue structures of a dicotyledonous leaf, as seen in diagrams or photomicrographs, and explain how these structures are adaptations for photosynthesis and gas exchange, limited to: (a) stomata and guard cells (b) spongy and palisade mesophyll cells (c) air spaces (d) vascular bundles (xylem and phloem) (e) distribution of chloroplasts

changes.from: Relate root hair cell structure to water and mineral uptake.
changes.to: Relate the structure of root hair cells to their function of water and mineral ion uptake

changes.from: Explain the importance of nitrate ions for amino acids and magnesium ions for chlorophyll.
changes.to: Explain the importance of: (a) nitrate ions for making amino acids, required for the production of proteins (b) magnesium ions for making chlorophyll

changes.from: Outline the water pathway through root, stem and leaf.
changes.to: Outline the pathway taken by water through the root, stem and leaf, limited to: root hair cells, root cortex cells, xylem and mesophyll cells

changes.from: Describe transpiration as evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion through stomata.
changes.to: Describe transpiration as the evaporation of water from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells into air spaces and then the diffusion of the water vapour out of the leaves through the stomata

changes.from: Describe translocation of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks.
changes.to: Describe translocation as the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from parts of plants that produce them (sources) to parts of plants that use or store them (sinks)

changes.from: List the elements in carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
changes.to: List the chemical elements that make up: (a) carbohydrates (b) lipids (fats and oils) (c) proteins

changes.from: State that starch, cellulose, glycogen, proteins and lipids are built from glucose, amino acids, glycerol and fatty acids.
changes.to: State that starch, cellulose and glycogen are made from glucose, proteins from amino acids and lipids from glycerol and fatty acids

changes.from: Describe and do tests for starch, glucose and maltose, protein and lipids.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do chemical tests for: (a) starch (iodine solution) (b) glucose and maltose (Benedict’s solution) (c) protein (biuret test) (d) lipids (ethanol emulsion test)

changes.from: List sources and dietary importance of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium, iron, fibre and water.
changes.to: List the principal sources of, and describe the dietary importance of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins (C and D only), mineral ions (calcium and iron only), fibre (roughage) and water

changes.from: Understand a balanced diet.
changes.to: Understand the concept of a balanced diet

changes.from: Describe Type 2 diabetes signs and its treatment by diet, exercise or insulin.
changes.to: Describe the signs of Type 2 diabetes (limited to increased blood glucose concentration and glucose in urine) and its treatment by diet, exercise and/or administration of insulin

changes.from: Describe the functions of mouth, salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, liver, pancreas, ileum, colon, rectum and anus.
changes.to: Identify the main regions of the digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum and ileum), pancreas, liver and large intestine (colon, rectum and anus)

changes.from: Describe hydrochloric acid killing bacteria in the stomach.
changes.to: Describe the function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach as killing ingested bacteria

changes.from: Explain that stomach and duodenum proteases work best at different pH.
changes.to: Understand that the different proteases present in the stomach and the duodenum work best at different pH levels

changes.from: Define assimilation as the uptake and use of nutrients from blood by cells.
changes.to: Understand that assimilation is the uptake and use by cells of nutrients from the blood

changes.from: State the hepatic portal vein carries absorbed nutrients to the liver.
changes.to: State the function of the hepatic portal vein as the route taken to the liver by most of the nutrients absorbed from the ileum

changes.from: Explain differences between inspired and expired air.
changes.to: State and explain the differences between inspired and expired air

changes.from: Identify the larynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and capillaries.
changes.to: Identify, on diagrams and images, the larynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and associated capillaries

changes.from: Investigate how physical activity changes breathing rate and depth.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effect of physical activity on the rate and depth of breathing

changes.from: State that carbon dioxide is a waste product excreted by the lungs.
changes.to: State that carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration, which is excreted through the lungs in humans

changes.from: Explain lactic acid build-up and oxygen debt in vigorous exercise.
changes.to: Explain why lactic acid builds up in muscles and blood during vigorous exercise causing an ‘oxygen debt’

changes.from: Describe the circulatory system as vessels, a pump and valves giving one-way flow.
changes.to: Describe the circulatory system as a system of blood vessels with a pump and valves to ensure one- way flow of blood

changes.from: Investigate how physical activity affects heart rate.
changes.to: Investigate and explain the effect of physical activity on heart rate

changes.from: Describe coronary heart disease as blocked coronary arteries and state its risk factors.
changes.to: Describe coronary heart disease in terms of the blockage of coronary arteries and state the possible risk factors including diet, sedentary lifestyle, stress, smoking, genetic predisposition, age and gender

changes.from: Name the main vessels to and from the heart, lungs and liver.
changes.to: Name the main blood vessels that carry blood to and from the heart, lungs and liver, limited to: aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, hepatic artery, hepatic vein and hepatic portal vein

changes.from: Identify red blood cells and white blood cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes).
changes.to: Identify red and white blood cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes) as seen in diagrams and photomicrographs

changes.from: Describe a drug as a substance that modifies chemical reactions in the body.
changes.to: Describe a drug as any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body

changes.from: Describe the effects of excessive alcohol.
changes.to: Describe the effects of excessive consumption of alcohol: reduced self-control, depressant, effect on reaction times, damage to liver and social implications

changes.from: State that the nervous system coordinates body functions.
changes.to: State that the nervous system (brain, spinal cord and nerves) coordinates and regulates body functions

changes.from: State that sensory receptors detect environmental changes.
changes.to: State that sensory receptors detect changes in the environment to which the body can respond via the nervous system

changes.from: Describe a reflex as a rapid automatic response.
changes.to: Describe a reflex action as a rapid and automatic response to a stimulus

changes.from: Describe a hormone as a chemical from a gland carried in blood to target organs.
changes.to: Describe a hormone as a chemical substance, e.g. insulin, produced by a gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs

changes.from: Understand that chromosomes contain DNA, which carries genetic information in genes.
changes.to: Understand that chromosomes contain DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), which carries genetic information in the form of genes

changes.from: State that a gene is a section of DNA coding for a protein, usually an enzyme.
changes.to: State that a gene is a specific section of DNA carrying the code needed to make a specific protein, which is usually an enzyme

changes.from: State that most cells are diploid and human cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes.
changes.to: State that most cells contain a diploid nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes and that human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes

changes.from: Describe mitosis as giving genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number.
changes.to: Describe mitosis as nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells in which the chromosome number is maintained (detail of stages are not required)

changes.from: Outline mitosis in growth, repair and replacement.
changes.to: Outline the role of mitosis in growth, repair of damaged tissues and replacement of dying cells

changes.from: State that meiosis makes gametes in testes and ovaries.
changes.to: State that meiosis is involved in the production of gametes and in humans occurs only in the testes and ovaries

changes.from: Compare male and female gametes.
changes.to: Compare male and female gametes in terms of size, structure, numbers and motility

changes.from: Describe how HIV is transmitted.
changes.to: Describe how the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is transmitted

changes.from: Understand HIV may lead to AIDS.
changes.to: Understand that HIV infection may lead to Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS)

changes.from: Describe methods of controlling HIV.
changes.to: Describe the methods by which HIV may be controlled

changes.from: Describe genetic modification as removing, inserting or changing genes.
changes.to: Describe genetic modification as changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, inserting or changing individual genes

changes.from: Understand that the human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria for insulin production.
changes.to: Understand that the gene that controls the production of human insulin is inserted into bacterial DNA for commercial production of insulin

changes.from: Describe energy flow through food chains to the environment.
changes.to: Describe the flow of energy through food chains including energy from light and energy in living organisms and its eventual transfer to the environment

changes.from: Explain why eating crop plants is more energy efficient than eating livestock.
changes.to: Explain why it is more energy efficient for humans to eat crop plants than to eat livestock that have been fed on crop plants

changes.from: Understand that population growth increases demand for resources.
changes.to: Understand that the growth of the human population is increasing the demand for global resources

changes.from: Describe the carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossil fuels and combustion.
changes.to: Describe the carbon cycle, limited to: (a) photosynthesis (b) respiration (c) feeding (d) decomposition and the role of decomposers (e) formation of fossil fuels (f) combustion

changes.from: Outline causes and consequences of deforestation.
changes.to: Outline the causes and describe the consequences of deforestation, limited to its effects on biodiversity, extinction, loss of soil, flooding and concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

changes.from: Describe their particle separation, arrangement and motion.
changes.to: Describe the structures of solids, liquids and gases in terms of particle separation, arrangement and motion

changes.from: Explain melting, boiling, evaporation, freezing and condensing with kinetic particle theory.
changes.to: Describe and explain changes of state (melting, boiling, evaporation, freezing and condensing) in terms of kinetic particle theory

changes.from: Describe paper chromatography to separate soluble substances.
changes.to: Describe how to use paper chromatography to separate mixtures of soluble substances, using a suitable solvent

changes.from: Describe the atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells.
changes.to: Describe the structure of the atom as a central nucleus containing neutrons and protons surrounded by electrons in shells

changes.from: Determine electronic configuration for elements 1 to 20.
changes.to: Determine the electronic configuration of elements with proton number 1 to 20, e.g. 2,8,3

changes.from: Describe cations and anions with noble gas configurations.
changes.to: Describe the formation of positive ions, known as cations, and negative ions, known as anions, with noble gas electronic configurations

changes.from: Describe the giant ionic lattice.
changes.to: Describe the giant lattice structure of ionic compounds as a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions

changes.from: State that an ionic bond is electrostatic attraction between opposite ions.
changes.to: State that an ionic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions

changes.from: State that a covalent bond is a shared electron pair giving noble gas configurations.
changes.to: State that a covalent bond is formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms leading to noble gas electronic configurations

changes.from: Describe covalent bonding in H2, Cl2, H2O, CH4, NH3, HCl, O2 and CO2 with dot-and-cross diagrams.
changes.to: Describe the formation of covalent bonds in simple molecules, including H2, Cl2, H2 O, CH4, NH3, HCl, O2 and CO2. Use dot-and-cross diagrams to show the electronic configurations in these and similar molecules.

changes.from: Explain low melting points and poor conductivity of simple molecular compounds.
changes.to: Describe and explain in terms of structure and bonding the properties of simple molecular compounds: (a) low melting points and boiling points in terms of weak intermolecular forces (specific types of intermolecular forces are not required) (b) poor electrical conductivity

changes.from: State formulae of the named elements and compounds.
changes.to: State the formulae of the elements and compounds named in the subject content

changes.from: Construct word and symbol equations with state symbols.
changes.to: Construct word equations and symbol equations to show how reactants form products, including state symbols

changes.from: Deduce symbol equations from given information.
changes.to: Deduce the symbol equation for a chemical reaction, given relevant information

changes.from: Calculate concentration in g/dm3.
changes.to: Calculate concentration as the mass of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, measured in g/dm3

changes.from: Prepare solutions of known concentration with pipettes, flasks and balances.
changes.to: Use volumetric pipettes, volumetric flasks and balances to prepare solutions of known concentration

changes.from: State that exothermic reactions warm the surroundings; neutralisation and combustion are exothermic.
changes.to: State that neutralisation and combustion are exothermic reactions

changes.from: State that endothermic reactions cool the surroundings; dissolving ammonium nitrate and cracking are endothermic.
changes.to: State that dissolving ammonium nitrate and cracking are endothermic reactions

changes.from: Explain that a catalyst is unchanged at the end.
changes.to: Explain that a catalyst is unchanged at the end of a reaction

changes.from: Describe, use and evaluate methods for measuring rate, such as gas formation.
changes.to: Describe, use and evaluate practical methods for investigating the rate of a reaction, including the formation of a gas

changes.from: Interpret rate data and graphs.
changes.to: Interpret data, including graphs, from rate of reaction experiments

changes.from: Define redox as simultaneous reduction and oxidation.
changes.to: Define redox reactions as involving simultaneous reduction and oxidation

changes.from: Identify redox reactions by oxygen gain and loss.
changes.to: Identify redox reactions as reactions involving gain and loss of oxygen

changes.from: Test for oxygen with a glowing splint.
changes.to: Describe and use a test to identify oxygen gas, O2, using a glowing splint

changes.from: State acids contain H+ and alkalis OH- ions.
changes.to: State that aqueous solutions of acids contain H+ ions and aqueous solutions of alkalis contain OH– ions

changes.from: State that bases are metal oxides or hydroxides and alkalis are soluble bases.
changes.to: State that bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals and that alkalis are soluble bases

changes.from: Describe acid reactions with some metals, bases and carbonates.
changes.to: Describe the characteristic properties of acids in terms of their reactions with: (a) some metals (b) bases (c) carbonates

changes.from: Describe base reactions with acids and ammonium salts.
changes.to: Describe the characteristic properties of bases in terms of their reactions with: (a) acids (b) ammonium salts

changes.from: State neutralisation occurs between acid and base, and acid with alkali gives water.
changes.to: State that a neutralisation reaction occurs between an acid and a base

changes.from: Describe separation using solvent, filtration and crystallisation.
changes.to: Describe and explain methods of separation and purification using: (a) a suitable solvent (b) filtration (c) crystallisation

changes.from: Explain group similarities by electronic configuration.
changes.to: Explain similarities in the chemical properties of elements in the same group of the Periodic Table in terms of their electronic configuration

changes.from: Use flame tests for Li+, Na+ and K+.
changes.to: Describe and use flame tests to identify Group I cations, limited to: (a) lithium, Li+, red (b) sodium, Na+, yellow (c) potassium, K+, lilac

changes.from: Predict properties of other Group I elements.
changes.to: Predict the properties of other elements in Group I, given information about the elements

changes.from: Describe halogens as diatomic non-metals with increasing density and decreasing reactivity down the group.
changes.to: Describe the Group VII halogens, chlorine, bromine and iodine, as diatomic non-metals with general trends down the group, limited to: (a) increasing density (b) decreasing reactivity

changes.from: Predict properties of other Group VII elements.
changes.to: Predict the properties of other elements in Group VII, given information about the elements

changes.from: Use sodium hydroxide and ammonia to identify Al3+, NH4+, Ca2+, Cr3+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and Zn2+.
changes.to: Do tests and use information provided on the reactions of aqueous cations with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to identify: (a) aluminium, Al3+ (b) ammonium, NH4 + (c) calcium, Ca2+ (d) chromium(III), Cr3+ (e) copper(II), Cu2+ (f) iron(II), Fe2+ (g) iron(III), Fe3+ (h) zinc, Zn2+

changes.from: State the reactivity series as metals in decreasing reactivity.
changes.to: State that the reactivity series is an arrangement of metals in decreasing order of their reactivity

changes.from: Explain aluminium's apparent unreactivity through its oxide layer.
changes.to: Explain the apparent unreactivity of aluminium in terms of its oxide layer

changes.from: Describe desalination.
changes.to: Describe desalination as a process to obtain drinking water from sea water

changes.from: State the composition of clean dry air.
changes.to: State the composition of clean, dry air as approximately 78% nitrogen, N2, 21% oxygen, O2, and the remainder as a mixture of noble gases and carbon dioxide, CO2

changes.from: Explain strategies to reduce global warming.
changes.to: State and explain strategies to reduce global warming, limited to increasing use of renewable energy, decreasing use of fossil fuels, limiting deforestation and reduction in livestock farming

changes.from: Name fossil fuels, methane in natural gas, and hydrocarbons.
changes.to: Name the fossil fuels: coal, natural gas and petroleum

changes.from: State that petroleum is a hydrocarbon mixture.
changes.to: State that petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons

changes.from: Describe fractional distillation of petroleum.
changes.to: Describe the separation of petroleum into useful fractions by fractional distillation

changes.from: Describe alkanes as generally unreactive except for combustion.
changes.to: Describe the properties of alkanes as being generally unreactive, except in terms of combustion

changes.from: State alkenes have a carbon double bond and are unsaturated.
changes.to: State that the bonding in alkenes includes a double carbon–carbon covalent bond and that alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons

changes.from: Test saturated versus unsaturated with aqueous bromine.
changes.to: Describe the test to distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons by their reaction with aqueous bromine

changes.from: Measure liquid volume with a measuring cylinder and solid volume by displacement.
changes.to: Describe how and be able to use a measuring cylinder to measure the volume of a liquid and to determine the volume of a solid by displacement

changes.from: Measure time intervals with clocks and digital timers.
changes.to: Describe how and be able to measure a variety of time intervals using clocks and digital timers

changes.from: Use average speed as total distance over total time.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation average speed = total distance travelled total time taken

changes.from: Define acceleration as change in speed per time and use a = change in v over t.
changes.to: Define acceleration as change in speed per unit time; recall and use the equation acceleration = change in speed time taken a = ∆v ∆t

changes.from: Define gravitational field strength as force per mass (g = W/m), equal to acceleration of free fall.
changes.to: Define gravitational field strength as force per unit mass; recall and use the equation gravitational field strength = weight mass g = W m and know that this is equivalent to the acceleration of free fall

changes.from: Define density as mass per volume and use rho = m/V.
changes.to: Define density as mass per unit volume; recall and use the equation density = mass volume ρ = m V

changes.from: Identify and use types of force: weight, friction, drag, tension, electrostatic, magnetic, thrust, contact.
changes.to: Identify and use different types of force, including weight (gravitational force), friction, drag, air resistance, tension (elastic force), electrostatic force, magnetic force, thrust (driving force) and contact force

changes.from: State that a force can change the direction or speed of an object.
changes.to: State that a force may change the motion of an object by changing its direction or speed

changes.from: Use F = ma.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation resultant force = mass × acceleration F = ma

changes.from: Sketch, plot and interpret load-extension graphs and describe the procedure.
changes.to: Sketch, plot and interpret load-extension graphs for an elastic solid and describe the associated experimental procedures

changes.from: Do an experiment to verify the principle of moments.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do an experiment to verify the principle of moments

changes.from: State the energy stores: kinetic, gravitational, chemical, elastic, nuclear, electrostatic and internal.
changes.to: State that energy may be stored as: kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic (strain), nuclear, electrostatic and internal (thermal)

changes.from: Use work done W = Fd.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force W = Fd

changes.from: Explain applications and consequences of thermal expansion, including the liquid-in-glass thermometer.
changes.to: Explain some of the applications and consequences of thermal expansion in the context of common examples, including the liquid-in-glass thermometer

changes.from: Do experiments to distinguish good and bad thermal conductors.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do experiments to distinguish between good and bad thermal conductors

changes.from: Explain convection through density changes and illustrate it.
changes.to: Explain convection in liquids and gases in terms of density changes and describe experiments to illustrate convection

changes.from: Distinguish good and bad emitters of infrared radiation experimentally.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do experiments to distinguish between good and bad emitters of infrared radiation

changes.from: Distinguish good and bad absorbers of infrared radiation experimentally.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do experiments to distinguish between good and bad absorbers of infrared radiation

changes.from: Describe wave motion in ropes, springs and water waves.
changes.to: Describe what is meant by wave motion as illustrated by vibrations in ropes and springs and by experiments using water waves

changes.from: Define normal, angle of incidence and angle of reflection.
changes.to: Define and use the terms normal, angle of incidence and angle of reflection

changes.from: Do experiments showing the law of reflection.
changes.to: Describe and be able to do experiments to illustrate the law of reflection

changes.from: Define normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction.
changes.to: Define and use the terms normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction

changes.from: Know the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum by frequency and wavelength.
changes.to: Know the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and in order of wavelength

changes.from: State positive and negative charges, coulombs, and that like charges repel and unlike attract.
changes.to: State that unlike charges attract and like charges repel

changes.from: State examples of conductors and insulators.
changes.to: State examples of electrical conductors and insulators

changes.from: Describe where electrostatic charge is a problem or useful.
changes.to: Describe examples where electrostatic charge is a problem, including lightning and aircraft refuelling

changes.from: Define current as charge per time and use I = Q/t.
changes.to: Define electric current as charge passing a point per unit time; recall and use the equation electric current = charge time I = Q t

changes.from: Describe conduction in metals by free electrons.
changes.to: Describe electrical conduction in metals in terms of the movement of free (delocalised) electrons

changes.from: Use ammeters with different ranges.
changes.to: Describe the use of and be able to use ammeters (analogue and digital) with different ranges

changes.from: Use voltmeters with different ranges.
changes.to: Describe the use of and be able to use voltmeters (analogue and digital) with different ranges

changes.from: Calculate total voltage of sources in series.
changes.to: Calculate the total voltage available from several sources arranged in series

changes.from: Use R = V/I.
changes.to: Recall and use the equation resistance = p.d. current R = V I

changes.from: Calculate combined resistance of resistors in series.
changes.to: Calculate the combined resistance of two or more resistors in series

changes.from: Draw circuit diagrams with cells, switches, resistors, heaters, lamps and motors.
changes.to: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams with cells, batteries, power supplies, switches, resistors (fixed and variable), heaters, thermistors (NTC only), light-dependent resistors (LDRs), lamps, motors, ammeters, voltmeters, coils, fuses, diodes and light-emitting diodes (LEDS)

changes.from: State common uses of electricity.
changes.to: State common uses of electricity, including heating, lighting, battery charging and powering motors and electronic systems

changes.from: Explain trip switches and fuses and choose ratings.
changes.to: Explain the use and operation of trip switches and fuses and choose appropriate fuse ratings and trip switch settings

changes.from: Define proton number and nucleon number and calculate neutrons.
changes.to: Define the terms (a) proton number/atomic number, Z (b) nucleon number/mass number, A and be able to calculate the number of neutrons in a nucleus

changes.from: Describe detecting alpha with cloud chamber or spark counter, and beta and gamma with a GM tube.
changes.to: Describe the detection of alpha particles (α-particles) using a cloud chamber or spark counter, and the detection of beta particles (β-particles) (β-particles will be taken to refer to β− ) and gamma radiation (γ-radiation) by using a Geiger-Müller (GM) tube and counter

unsureList.text: Describe the functions of these cell structures.
unsureList.best: Describe the functions of the above structures in animal and plant cells

unsureList.text: Explain that specialised cells have structures related to their function.
unsureList.best: Understand that cells can become specialised and that their structures are related to their specific functions, as illustrated by examples covered in the syllabus

unsureList.text: Explain diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient from random motion.
unsureList.best: Understand diffusion as the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration (i.e. down a concentration gradient), as a result of their random movement

unsureList.text: Describe a catalyst as a substance that speeds a reaction and is unchanged by it.
unsureList.best: Describe a catalyst as a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction

unsureList.text: Describe enzymes as protein biological catalysts that mostly act inside the cell that makes them.
unsureList.best: Describe enzymes as proteins that function as biological catalysts

unsureList.text: Investigate and explain how temperature and pH change enzyme activity, including denaturation and collisions.
unsureList.best: Investigate and explain the effects of changes of temperature and pH on enzyme activity in terms of kinetic energy, shape and fit, denaturation and the frequency of effective collisions

unsureList.text: State that chlorophyll in chloroplasts turns light energy into chemical energy.
unsureList.best: State that chlorophyll transfers light energy into chemical energy for the formation of glucose and other carbohydrates

unsureList.text: Outline use and storage of photosynthesis products: starch, cellulose, respiration, sucrose and other molecules.
unsureList.best: Outline the subsequent use and storage of the carbohydrates made in photosynthesis, limited to: (a) starch as an energy store (b) cellulose to build cell walls (c) glucose used in respiration to provide energy (d) sucrose for transport through the plant (e) glucose and mineral ions to synthesise other biological molecules e.g. proteins

unsureList.text: Identify the main regions of the digestive system.
unsureList.best: Identify the main regions of the digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum and ileum), pancreas, liver and large intestine (colon, rectum and anus)

unsureList.text: Explain why food must be digested before absorption.
unsureList.best: Explain why most foods must be digested before they can be absorbed

unsureList.text: Describe physical digestion and chemical digestion, and how physical digestion helps enzymes.

unsureList.best: Why choose this syllabus? Key benefits Cambridge O Level is typically for 14 to 16 year olds and is an internationally recognised qualification. It has been designed especially for an international market and is sensitive to the needs of different countries. Cambridge O Level is designed for learners whose first language may not be English, and this is acknowledged throughout the examination process. Our programmes balance a thorough knowledge and understanding of a subject and help to develop the skills learners need for their next steps in education or employment. Cambridge O Level English Language encourages learners to read a variety of texts and improve their use and style of language in a range of contexts. Learners develop the ability to understand and respond to what they read and to communicate effectively in writing. These skills equip them for progression to further study or employment. Our approach in Cambridge O Level English Language encourages learners to be: confident, exploring and evaluating ideas and arguments in a structured, critical and analytical way. They are able to communicate and defend views and opinions as well as respect those of others responsible, understanding how to use English language in different contexts and for different purposes to influence and affect the world around them reflective, critically reviewing their own work and identifying ways to improve. They develop successful learning strategies to consolidate their skills innovative, applying their knowledge and understanding to engage with a range of texts and styles of writing. They adapt their skills in order to respond to tasks in different contexts engaged, taking inspiration from, and being interested in, the variety of language around them. They read critically, learn from others and understand how their English Language learning fits within the wider context. School feedback: ‘Cambridge O Level has helped me develop thinking and analytical skills which will go a long way in helping me with advanced studies.’ Feedback from: Kamal Khan Virk, former student at Beaconhouse Garden Town Secondary School, Pakistan, who went on to study Actuarial Science at the London School of Economics Cambridge learner

unsureList.best: Assessment objectives The assessment objectives (AOs) are: AO1 Reading Candidates will be assessed on their ability to: R1 demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings R2 demonstrate understanding of implicit meanings and attitudes R3 analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text R4 demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers R5 select and use information for specific purposes. AO2 Writing Candidates will be assessed on their ability to: W1 articulate experience and express what is thought, felt and imagined W2 organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect W3 use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to context W4 use register appropriate to context W5 make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar. unsureList.best: Why choose this syllabus? Key benefits Cambridge O Level is typically for 14 to 16 year olds and is an internationally recognised qualification. It has been designed especially for an international market and is sensitive to the needs of different countries. Cambridge O Level is designed for learners whose first language may not be English, and this is acknowledged throughout the examination process. Our programmes promote a thorough knowledge and understanding of a subject and help to develop the skills learners need for their next steps in education or employment. Cambridge O Level Literature in English offers learners the opportunity to read, interpret, evaluate and respond to a range of literature in English. The range includes drama, prose and poetry from the works of Shakespeare to contemporary literature. This course enables learners to deepen their understanding and appreciation of the ways in which writers use English to express meaning and achieve effects. Cambridge O Level Literature in English will stimulate learners to read for pleasure and to explore wider and universal issues, promoting a better understanding of themselves and the world. unsureList.best: Why choose this syllabus? Key benefits Cambridge O Level is typically for 14 to 16 year olds and is an internationally recognised qualification. It has been designed especially for an international market and is sensitive to the needs of different countries. Cambridge O Level is designed for learners whose first language may not be English, and this is acknowledged throughout the examination process. Our programmes balance a thorough knowledge and understanding of a subject and help to develop the skills learners need for their next steps in education or employment. Cambridge O Level Global Perspectives gives learners the opportunity to think about significant global issues and to consider these from different perspectives. It develops a set of transferable skills in research, analysis, evaluation, communication, collaboration and reflection. It encourages learners to construct arguments, present views, work collaboratively, research, and reason and reflect on their place in a connected world. These transferable skills will support student learning across all of their studies. Our approach in Cambridge O Level Global Perspectives encourages learners to be: confident, making independent judgements and justifying opinions based on reasoning and evidence, allowing them to present ideas on and solutions to issues of global interest responsible, directing their own learning by exploring diverse and varied sources to present suggestions and courses of action to members of their local community reflective, developing an empathetic understanding by analysing why others have certain attitudes and take the positions they do, while understanding that there is a range of perspectives on any given issue, and so developing their own perspective innovative, using critical thinking to propose sustainable solutions to global issues at global, national and local levels engaged, collaborating, sharing new ideas and reaching mutual understanding of possible courses of action, allowing new ideas to be explored in unfamiliar contexts. School feedback: ‘Cambridge O Level has helped me develop thinking and analytical skills which will go a long way in helping me with advanced studies.’ Feedback from: Kamal Khan Virk, former student at Beaconhouse Garden Town Secondary School, Pakistan, who went on to study Actuarial Science at the London School of Economics Cambridge learner

changes.from: Solve quadratic equations and inequalities in one unknown by factorising, completing the square or the formula.
changes.to: solve quadratic equations, and quadratic inequalities, in one unknown By factorising, completing the square and using the formula.

changes.from: Solve by substitution a pair of simultaneous equations, one linear and one quadratic.
changes.to: solve by substitution a pair of simultaneous equations of which one is linear and one is quadratic e.g. x + y + 1 = 0 and x2 + y2 = 25, 2x + 3y = 7 and 3x2 = 4 + 4xy.

changes.from: Recognise and solve equations that are quadratic in some function of x.
changes.to: recognise and solve equations in x which are quadratic in some function of x. e.g. x4

changes.from: Understand function, domain, range, one-one function, inverse function and composition of functions.
changes.to: understand the terms function, domain, range, one-one function, inverse function and composition of functions Notes and examples

changes.from: Find the range of a simple function and the composition of two functions.
changes.to: identify the range of a given function in simple cases, and find the composition of two given functions e.g. range of: x x

changes.from: Understand and use transformations y = f(x) + a, f(x + a), af(x), f(ax) and simple combinations.
changes.to: understand and use the transformations of the graph of y = f(x) given by y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = af(x), y = f(ax) and simple combinations of these. Including use of the terms ‘translation’, ‘reflection’ and ‘stretch’ in describing transformations. Questions may involve algebraic or trigonometric functions, or other graphs with given features.

changes.from: Find the equation of a straight line from sufficient information.
changes.to: find the equation of a straight line given sufficient information Notes and examples e.g. given two points, or one point and the gradient.

changes.from: Use the forms y = mx + c, y - y1 = m(x - x1) and ax + by + c = 0, including distance, midpoint, parallel and perpendicular gradients.
changes.to: interpret and use any of the forms y = mx + c, y – y1 = m(x – x1 ), ax + by + c = 0 in solving problems Including calculations of distances, gradients, midpoints, points of intersection and use of the relationship between the gradients of parallel and perpendicular lines.

changes.from: Understand that (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 is a circle with centre (a, b) and radius r.
changes.to: understand that the equation (x – a)2 + (y – b)2 = r2 represents the circle with centre (a, b) and radius r Including use of the expanded form x2 + y2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0.

changes.from: Use exact trigonometric values for 30, 45 and 60 degrees and related angles.
changes.to: use the exact values of the sine, cosine and tangent of 30°, 45°, 60°, and related angles e.g., cos sin 150

changes.from: Use the notations sin^-1, cos^-1 and tan^-1 for principal values of inverse trigonometric functions.
changes.to: use the notations sin–1 x, cos­ –1 x, tan–1 x to denote the principal values of the inverse trigonometric relations No specialised knowledge of these functions is required, but understanding of them as examples of inverse functions is expected.

changes.from: Use the identities tan = sin/cos and sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.
changes.to: use the identities cos sin tan / i i i and sin cos 1 2 2 / i i + e.g. in proving identities, simplifying expressions and solving equations.

changes.from: Use the convergence condition and sum to infinity for a geometric progression.
changes.to: use the condition for the convergence of a geometric progression, and the formula for the sum to infinity of a convergent geometric progression.

changes.from: Apply differentiation to gradients, tangents, normals, increasing and decreasing functions and rates of change.
changes.to: apply differentiation to gradients, tangents and normals, increasing and decreasing functions and rates of change Including connected rates of change, e.g. given the rate of increase of the radius of a circle, find the rate of increase of the area for a specific value of one of the variables.

changes.from: Integrate (ax + b)^n for rational n except -1, with multiples, sums and differences.
changes.to: understand integration as the reverse process of differentiation, and integrate (ax + b)n (for any rational n except –1), together with constant multiples, sums and differences Notes and examples e.g. x x x 2 5 1 d 3 − +;^ h, x x

changes.from: Evaluate definite integrals, including simple improper integrals.
changes.to: evaluate definite integrals Including simple cases of ‘improper’ integrals, such as x x x x d and d

changes.from: Identify the forces acting in a situation, for example with a force diagram.
changes.to: identify the forces acting in a given situation Notes and examples e.g. by drawing a force diagram.

changes.from: Understand force as a vector and find and use components and resultants.
changes.to: understand the vector nature of force, and find and use components and resultants Calculations are always required, not approximate solutions by scale drawing.

changes.from: Understand a contact force as a normal component and a frictional component.
changes.to: understand that a contact force between two surfaces can be represented by two components, the normal component and the frictional component

changes.from: Use the smooth contact model and understand its limitations.
changes.to: use the model of a ‘smooth’ contact, and understand the limitations of this model

changes.from: Use differentiation and integration with respect to time for displacement, velocity and acceleration.
changes.to: use differentiation and integration with respect to time to solve simple problems concerning displacement, velocity and acceleration Calculus required is restricted to techniques from the content for Paper 1: Pure Mathematics 1.

changes.from: Use the relationship between mass and weight.
changes.to: use the relationship between mass and weight W = mg. In this component, questions are mainly numerical, and use of the approximate numerical value 10(ms–2 ) for g is expected.

changes.from: Understand work done and calculate it for a constant force with a displacement not parallel to the force.
changes.to: understand the concept of the work done by a force, and calculate the work done by a constant force when its point of application undergoes a displacement not necessarily parallel to the force Notes and examples cos W Fd i =; Use of the scalar product is not required.

changes.from: Understand gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy and use the formulae.
changes.to: understand the concepts of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, and use appropriate formulae

changes.from: Solve problems such as a car's instantaneous acceleration on a hill against resistance.
changes.to: solve problems involving, for example, the instantaneous acceleration of a car moving on a hill against a resistance.

changes.from: Draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams, box-and-whisker plots, histograms and cumulative frequency graphs.
changes.to: draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams, box-and-whisker plots, histograms and cumulative frequency graphs Including back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagrams.

changes.from: Use a cumulative frequency graph to estimate medians, quartiles, percentiles and proportions.
changes.to: use a cumulative frequency graph e.g. to estimate medians, quartiles, percentiles, the proportion of a distribution above (or below) a given value, or between two values.

changes.from: Understand and use measures of central tendency and variation, including standard deviation.
changes.to: understand and use different measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and variation (range, interquartile range, standard deviation) e.g. in comparing and contrasting sets of data.

changes.from: Understand permutation and combination and solve simple selection problems.
changes.to: understand the terms permutation and combination, and solve simple problems involving selections Notes and examples

changes.from: Use addition and multiplication of probabilities in simple cases.
changes.to: use addition and multiplication of probabilities, as appropriate, in simple cases Explicit use of the general formula A B A B A B P P P P, + − = + ^ ^ ^ ^ h h h h is not required.

changes.from: Understand exclusive and independent events, testing independence by comparing P(A and B) with P(A)P(B).
changes.to: understand the meaning of exclusive and independent events, including determination of whether events A and B are independent by comparing the values of A B P + ^ h and A B P P # ^ ^ h h

changes.from: Draw up a probability distribution table for a discrete random variable and calculate E(X) and Var(X).
changes.to: draw up a probability distribution table relating to a given situation involving a discrete random variable X, and calculate E(X) and Var(X) Notes and examples

changes.from: Use the expectation and variance formulae for the binomial distribution and the expectation for the geometric distribution.
changes.to: use formulae for the expectation and variance of the binomial distribution and for the expectation of the geometric distribution. Proofs of formulae are not required.

changes.from: Understand the normal distribution as a model for a continuous variable and use normal tables.
changes.to: understand the use of a normal distribution to model a continuous random variable, and use normal distribution tables Notes and examples Sketches of normal curves to illustrate distributions or probabilities may be required.

changes.from: Use the derivatives of e^x, ln x, sin x, cos x, tan x and tan^-1 x with multiples, sums, differences and composites.
changes.to: use the derivatives of ex, lnx, sinx, cosx, tanx, tan–1 x, together with constant multiples, sums, differences and composites Notes and examples Derivatives of sin–1 x and cos–1 x are not required.

changes.from: Use integration by parts when an integrand is a product.
changes.to: recognise when an integrand can usefully be regarded as a product, and use integration by parts e.g. integration of xsin2x, x2 e–x, lnx, x tan–1 x.

changes.from: Use a given substitution to simplify and evaluate definite or indefinite integrals.
changes.to: use a given substitution to simplify and evaluate either a definite or an indefinite integral. e.g. to integrate sin2 2xcosx using the substitution u = sinx.

changes.from: Calculate vector magnitudes and use unit, displacement and position vectors.
changes.to: calculate the magnitude of a vector, and use unit vectors, displacement vectors and position vectors In 2 or 3 dimensions.

changes.from: Interpret the solution of a differential equation in the modelled context.
changes.to: interpret the solution of a differential equation in the context of a problem being modelled by the equation. Where a differential equation is used to model a ‘real-life’ situation, no specialised knowledge of the context will be required.

changes.from: Represent complex numbers on an Argand diagram.
changes.to: represent complex numbers geometrically by means of an Argand diagram

changes.from: Find the two square roots of a complex number.
changes.to: find the two square roots of a complex number e.g. the square roots of 5 + 12i in exact Cartesian form. Full details of the working should be shown.

changes.from: Understand the geometrical effects of conjugating, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing complex numbers.
changes.to: understand in simple terms the geometrical effects of conjugating a complex number and of adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing two complex numbers

changes.from: Illustrate simple equations and inequalities with loci on an Argand diagram.
changes.to: illustrate simple equations and inequalities involving complex numbers by means of loci in an Argand diagram e.g. |z – a| < k, |z – a| = |z – b|, arg(z – a) = α.

changes.from: Understand how the Poisson distribution models random events, and use it as a model.
changes.to: understand the relevance of the Poisson distribution to the distribution of random events, and use the Poisson distribution as a model

changes.from: Use the normal distribution, with continuity correction, to approximate the Poisson where appropriate.
changes.to: use the normal distribution, with continuity correction, as an approximation to the Poisson distribution where appropriate. The condition that m is large should be known;

changes.from: Understand a continuous random variable and recall and use properties of a probability density function.
changes.to: understand the concept of a continuous random variable, and recall and use properties of a probability density function Notes and examples For density functions defined over a single interval only; the domain may be infinite, e.g. x

changes.from: Use a probability density function for probabilities, and to calculate mean and variance.
changes.to: use a probability density function to solve problems involving probabilities, and to calculate the mean and variance of a distribution. Including location of the median or other percentiles of a distribution by direct consideration of an area using the density function. Explicit knowledge of the cumulative distribution function is not included.

changes.from: Use the Central Limit Theorem where appropriate.
changes.to: use the Central Limit Theorem where appropriate Only an informal understanding of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is required; for large sample sizes, the distribution of a sample mean is approximately normal.

changes.from: Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance from raw or summarised data.
changes.to: calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance from a sample, using either raw or summarised data Only a simple understanding of the term ‘unbiased’ is required, e.g. that although individual estimates will vary the process gives an accurate result ‘on average’.

changes.from: Determine and interpret a confidence interval for a population mean with known variance or a large sample.
changes.to: determine and interpret a confidence interval for a population mean in cases where the population is normally distributed with known variance or where a large sample is used

changes.from: Carry out a hypothesis test for a population mean with known variance or a large sample.
changes.to: formulate hypotheses and carry out a hypothesis test concerning the population mean in cases where the population is normally distributed with known variance or where a large sample is used

changes.from: Calculate probabilities of Type I and Type II errors in specific normal, binomial or Poisson tests.
changes.to: calculate the probabilities of making Type I and Type II errors in specific situations involving tests based on a normal distribution or direct evaluation of binomial or Poisson probabilities.

unsureList.best: carry out the process of completing the square for a quadratic polynomial ax2 + bx + c and use a completed square form Notes and examples e.g. to locate the vertex of the graph of y = ax2 + bx + c or to sketch the graph

unsureList.text: Find the discriminant of a quadratic and use it to count real roots, including repeated roots.
unsureList.best: find the discriminant of a quadratic polynomial ax2 + bx + c and use the discriminant e.g. to determine the number of real roots of the equation ax2 + bx + c = 0. Knowledge of the term ‘repeated root’ is included.

unsureList.best: find all the solutions of simple trigonometrical equations lying in a specified interval (general forms of solution are not included). e.g. solve sin x x 3 2 1 0 for 1 1 − r r + =, sin cos 3 5 1 0 0 360 for 2 c c G G − − i i i =.

unsureList.text: Use the expansion of (a + b)^n for positive integer n, including nCr and factorial notation.
unsureList.best: use the expansion of (a + b)n, where n is a positive integer Notes and examples Including the notations n r f p and n! Knowledge of the greatest term and properties of the coefficients are not required.

unsureList.text: Use the nth term and sum formulae to solve problems on progressions.
unsureList.best: use the formulae for the nth term and for the sum of the first n terms to solve problems involving arithmetic or geometric progressions Including knowledge that numbers a, b, c are ‘in arithmetic progression’ if 2b = a + c (or equivalent) and are ‘in geometric progression’ if b2 = ac (or equivalent). Questions may involve more than one progression.

unsureList.text: Understand the gradient of a curve as a limit of chord gradients, and use the notations for first and second derivatives.
unsureList.best: for first and second derivatives Notes and examples Only an informal understanding of the idea of a limit is expected. e.g. includes consideration of the gradient of the chord joining the points with x coordinates 2 and (2 + h) on the curve y = x3. Formal use of the general method of differentiation from first principles is not required.

unsureList.text: Differentiate x^n for rational n, multiples, sums, differences and composites using the chain rule.
unsureList.best: use the derivative of xn (for any rational n), together with constant multiples, sums and differences of functions, and of composite functions using the chain rule e.g. find x y d d, given y x 2 5 3 = +.

unsureList.text: Locate stationary points, find their nature, and use them in sketching graphs.
unsureList.best: locate stationary points and determine their nature, and use information about stationary points in sketching graphs. Including use of the second derivative for identifying maxima and minima; alternatives may be used in questions where no method is specified. Knowledge of points of inflexion is not included.

unsureList.text: Understand modulus, sketch y = |ax + b| and use modulus relations to solve equations and inequalities.
unsureList.best: understand the meaning of |x|, sketch the graph of y = |ax + b| and use relations such as |a| = |b| ⇔ a2 = b2 and |x – a| < b ⇔ a – b < x < a + b when solving equations and inequalities Notes and examples Graphs of y = |f(x)| and y = f(|x|) for non-linear functions f are not included. e.g. |3x – 2| = |2x + 7|, 2x + 5 < |x + 1|

unsureList.text: Use the factor theorem and the remainder theorem.
unsureList.best: use the factor theorem and the remainder theorem. e.g. to find factors and remainders, solve polynomial equations or evaluate unknown coefficients. Including factors of the form (ax + b) in which the coefficient of x is not unity, and including calculation of remainders.

unsureList.text: Understand how logarithms relate to indices and use the laws of logarithms.
unsureList.best: understand the relationship between logarithms and indices, and use the laws of logarithms (excluding change of base) Notes and examples

unsureList.text: Understand the definition, properties and graphs of e^x and ln x as inverse functions.
unsureList.best: understand the definition and properties of ex and lnx, including their relationship as inverse functions and their graphs Including knowledge of the graph of y = ekx for both positive and negative values of k.

unsureList.text: Use logarithms to solve equations and inequalities where the unknown is in an index.
unsureList.best: use logarithms to solve equations and inequalities in which the unknown appears in indices e.g. 2 5 x

unsureList.text: Use logarithms to turn a relationship into linear form and find constants from gradient or intercept.
unsureList.best: use logarithms to transform a given relationship to linear form, and hence determine unknown constants by considering the gradient and/or intercept. e.g. y = kxn gives lny = lnk + nlnx which is linear in lnx and lny y = k(ax ) gives lny = lnk + x lna which is linear in x and lny.

unsureList.text: Understand sec, cosec and cot, and use properties and graphs of all six trigonometric functions for any angle.
unsureList.best: understand the relationship of the secant, cosecant and cotangent functions to cosine, sine and tangent, and use properties and graphs of all six trigonometric functions for angles of any magnitude Notes and examples

unsureList.text: Use trigonometric identities to simplify, evaluate exactly and solve equations, including compound angle, double angle and R sin(theta + alpha) forms.
unsureList.best: use algebraic methods to solve problems involving lines and circles Including use of elementary geometrical properties of circles, e.g. tangent perpendicular to radius, angle in a semicircle, symmetry. Implicit differentiation is not included.

unsureList.text: Use the derivatives of e^x, ln x, sin x, cos x and tan x with multiples, sums, differences and composites.
unsureList.best: use the derivatives of ex, lnx, sinx, cosx, tan x, together with constant multiples, sums, differences and composites Notes and examples

unsureList.text: Integrate e^(ax+b), 1/(ax+b), sin(ax+b), cos(ax+b) and sec^2(ax+b) by reversing differentiation.
unsureList.best: +, sin(ax + b), cos(ax + b) and sec2 (ax + b) Notes and examples Knowledge of the general method of integration by substitution is not required.

unsureList.text: Use trigonometric relationships, such as double-angle formulae, when integrating.
unsureList.best: use trigonometrical relationships in carrying out integration e.g. use of double-angle formulae to integrate sin2x or cos2 (2x).

unsureList.text: Understand and use the trapezium rule to estimate a definite integral, including whether it over- or under-estimates.
unsureList.best: understand and use the trapezium rule to estimate the value of a definite integral. Including use of sketch graphs in simple cases to determine whether the trapezium rule gives an over-estimate or an under-estimate.

unsureList.text: Locate a root approximately using graphs or a sign change.
unsureList.best: locate approximately a root of an equation, by means of graphical considerations and/or searching for a sign change Notes and examples e.g. finding a pair of consecutive integers between which a root lies.

unsureList.text: Use a given iterative formula x(n+1) = F(x(n)) to find a root to a given accuracy.
unsureList.best: understand how a given simple iterative formula of the form xn + 1 = F(xn) relates to the equation being solved, and use a given iteration, or an iteration based on a given rearrangement of an equation, to determine a root to a prescribed degree of accuracy. Knowledge of the condition for convergence is not included, but an understanding that an iteration may fail to converge is expected.

unsureList.text: Use equilibrium: the vector sum of forces, or components in any direction, is zero.
unsureList.best: use the principle that, when a particle is in equilibrium, the vector sum of the forces acting is zero, or equivalently, that the sum of the components in any direction is zero Solutions by resolving are usually expected, but equivalent methods (e.g. triangle of forces, Lami’s Theorem, where suitable) are also acceptable; these other methods are not required knowledge, and will not be referred to in questions.

unsureList.text: Understand limiting friction and limiting equilibrium, and use F = mu R or F <= mu R.
unsureList.best: understand the concepts of limiting friction and limiting equilibrium, recall the definition of coefficient of friction, and use the relationship F R n = or F R G n, as appropriate Terminology such as ‘about to slip’ may be used to mean ‘in limiting equilibrium’ in questions.

unsureList.text: Use Newton's third law.
unsureList.best: use Newton’s third law. e.g. the force exerted by a particle on the ground is equal and opposite to the force exerted by the ground on the particle.

unsureList.text: Understand distance and speed as scalars, and displacement, velocity and acceleration as vectors.
unsureList.best: understand the concepts of distance and speed as scalar quantities, and of displacement, velocity and acceleration as vector quantities Notes and examples Restricted to motion in one dimension only. The term ‘deceleration’ may sometimes be used in the context of decreasing speed.

unsureList.text: Sketch and interpret displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, including gradients and areas.
unsureList.best: sketch and interpret displacement–time graphs and velocity–time graphs, and in particular appreciate that

unsureList.text: Use constant acceleration formulae for straight-line motion.
unsureList.best: use appropriate formulae for motion with constant acceleration in a straight line. Questions may involve setting up more than one equation, using information about the motion of different particles.

unsureList.text: Use the definition of linear momentum and understand it is a vector.
unsureList.best: use the definition of linear momentum and show understanding of its vector nature Notes and examples For motion in one dimension only.

unsureList.text: Use conservation of linear momentum for direct impact of two bodies, including coalescence.

unsureList.best: Subject content This syllabus gives you the flexibility to design a course that will interest, challenge and engage your learners. Where appropriate you are responsible for selecting resources and examples to support your learners’ study. These should be appropriate for the learners’ age, cultural background and learning context as well as complying with your school policies and local legal requirements. AS content Computational thinking is developed using a structured approach that includes the use of programming and problem-solving skills to provide solutions to real life problems. It requires the manipulation and storage of different types of data and the communication of solutions over networks. Computational thinking is supported by developing an understanding of how computer architecture, hardware, systems software, security measures and communication systems, provide the infrastructure required in an efficient and ethical way. The syllabus supports opportunities for students to apply their skills in practical contexts that are required in the digital industry.

unsureList.best: Set poems and stories for examination in 2024 continued Poems and stories for examination in 2024 are listed below. William Blake: Selected Poems from Songs of Innocence and of Experience Paper 1, Section B Poetry Title: Introduction The Shepherd The Lamb The Little Black Boy The Chimney Sweeper The Little Boy Lost The Little Boy Found A Cradle Song The Divine Image Holy Thursday Spring Nurse’s Song A Dream On Anothers Sorrow Introduction Earth’s Answer Holy Thursday The Little Girl Lost The Little Girl Found The Chimney Sweeper Nurses Song The Fly The Angel The Tyger My Pretty Rose Tree The Little Vagabond London The Human Abstract A Poison Tree A Little Boy Lost The School Boy First line: Piping down the valleys wild How sweet is the Shepherds sweet lot, Little Lamb who made thee My mother bore me in the southern wild, When my mother died I was very young, Father, father, where are you going The little boy lost in the lonely fen, Sweet dreams form a shade, To Mercy Pity Peace and Love, Twas on a Holy Thursday their innocent faces clean Sound the Flute! When the voices of children are heard on the green Once a dream did weave a shade, Can I see anothers woe, Hear the voice of the Bard! Earth rais’d up her head, Is this a holy thing to see, In futurity All the night in woe A little black thing among the snow: When the voices of children, are heard on the green Little Fly I Dreamt a Dream! what can it mean? Tyger Tyger, burning bright, A flower was offerd to me; Dear Mother, dear Mother, the Church is cold. I wander thro’ each charter’d street, Pity would be no more, I was angry with my friend: Nought loves another as itself I love to rise in a summer morn,

unsureList.best: International recognition and acceptance Our expertise in curriculum, teaching and learning, and assessment is the basis for the recognition of our programmes and qualifications around the world. Every year thousands of students with Cambridge International AS & A Levels gain places at leading universities worldwide. A wide range of inspiring set texts have been carefully selected to offer a depth and breadth of literary study and to encourage lively and stimulating classroom discussion. At AS Level learners will study three set texts and prepare for one unseen text. At A Level they will study four further set texts. Throughout the AS and A Level course learners will be encouraged to practise their skills in close reading through the study of literary extracts and unseen texts; developing skills of analysis and interpretation of texts, alongside their expression of personal response to the texts studied. Learners will explore the conventions of genres of texts and the contexts in which works have been written, read and received. At A Level learners will further develop their subject knowledge through the evaluation of opinions and ideas, both their own and those of others. These are highly transferable skills and can help learners in other subject areas, as well as equipping them for higher education and/or employment. unsureList.best: Content overview Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English will provide learners with the opportunity to gain further knowledge and understanding of international poetry, prose and drama, with candidates studying all genres at both levels. A wide range of inspiring set texts have been carefully selected to offer a depth and breadth of literary study and to encourage lively and stimulating classroom discussion. At AS Level learners will study three set texts and prepare for one unseen text. At A Level they will study four further set texts. Throughout the AS and A Level course learners will be encouraged to practise their skills in close reading through the study of literary extracts and unseen texts; developing skills of analysis and interpretation of texts, alongside their expression of personal response to the texts studied. Learners will explore the conventions of genres of texts and the contexts in which works have been written, read and received. At A Level learners will further develop their subject knowledge through the evaluation of opinions and ideas, both their own and those of others. These are highly transferable skills and can help learners in other subject areas, as well as equipping them for higher education and/or employment. Support for Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English

unsureList.best: Subject content This syllabus gives you the flexibility to design a course that will interest, challenge and engage your learners. Where appropriate you are responsible for selecting texts, resources and examples to support your learners’ study. These should be appropriate for the learners’ age, cultural background and learning context as well as complying with your school policies and local legal requirements. At AS Level learners will study three set texts and prepare for one unseen text. At A Level they will study four further set texts. AS Level includes Paper 1 and Paper 2. A Level includes Paper 1, Paper 2, Paper 3 and Paper 4. Set texts for examination in 2024 The set texts listed below are for examination in 2024. Set texts regularly rotate on the syllabus and may change from one year of examination to the next. Before you begin teaching, check the set text list for the year in which your candidates will take their examinations. Here take my picture, though I bid farewell; Nature’s lay idiot, I taught thee to love, No spring, nor summer beauty hath such grace, Come, Madam, come, all rest my powers defy, As due by many titles I resign Oh my black soul! now thou art summoned This is my play’s last scene, here heavens appoint At the round earth’s imagined corners, blow If poisonous minerals, and if that tree, Death be not proud, though some have called thee Batter my heart, three-personed God; for, you Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt I scarce believe my love to be so pure Go, and catch a falling star, Sweetest love, I do not go, All kings, and all their favourites, When by thy scorn, O murderess, I am dead, Come live with me, and be my love, For God’s sake hold your tongue, and let me love, Dear love, for nothing less than thee Where, like a pillow on a bed, So, so, break off this last lamenting kiss, Mark but this flea, and mark in this, I wonder by my troth, what thou, and I When my grave is broke up again Busy old fool, unruly sun, I have done one braver thing Blasted with sighs, and surrounded with tears,

unsureList.best: Content overview Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English will provide learners with the opportunity to gain further knowledge and understanding of international poetry, prose and drama, with candidates studying all genres at both levels. A wide range of inspiring set texts have been carefully selected to offer a depth and breadth of literary study and to encourage lively and stimulating classroom discussion. At AS Level learners will study three set texts and prepare for one unseen text. At A Level they will study four further set texts. Throughout the AS and A Level course learners will be encouraged to practise their skills in close reading through the study of literary extracts and unseen texts; developing skills of analysis and interpretation of texts, alongside their expression of personal response to the texts studied. Learners will explore the conventions of genres of texts and the contexts in which works have been written, read and received. At A Level learners will further develop their subject knowledge through the evaluation of opinions and ideas, both their own and those of others. These are highly transferable skills and can help learners in other subject areas, as well as equipping them for higher education and/or employment. Support for Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English

unsureList.best: International recognition and acceptance Our expertise in curriculum, teaching and learning, and assessment is the basis for the recognition of our programmes and qualifications around the world. Every year thousands of students with Cambridge International AS & A Levels gain places at leading universities worldwide. Our programmes and qualifications are valued by top universities around the world including those in the UK, US (including Ivy League universities), Europe, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. UK NARIC, the national agency in the UK for the recognition and comparison of international qualifications and skills, has carried out an independent benchmarking study of Cambridge International AS & A Level and found it to be comparable to the standard of AS & A Level in the UK. This means students can be confident that their Cambridge International AS & A Level qualifications are accepted as equivalent, grade for grade, to UK AS & A Levels by leading universities worldwide. Cambridge International AS Level Literature in English makes up the first half of the Cambridge International A Level course in Literature in English and provides a foundation for the study of Literature in English at Cambridge International A Level. Depending on local university entrance requirements, students may be able to use it to progress directly to university courses in literature or some other subjects. It is also suitable as part of a course of general education. Cambridge International A Level Literature in English provides a foundation for the study of literature or related courses in higher education. Equally it is suitable as part of a course of general education. For more information about the relationship between the Cambridge International AS Level and Cambridge International A Level see the ‘Assessment overview’ section of the Syllabus overview. We recommend learners check the Cambridge recognition database and university websites to find the most up-to-date entry requirements for courses they wish to study.

unsureList.best: Content overview Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English will provide learners with the opportunity to gain further knowledge and understanding of international poetry, prose and drama, with candidates studying all genres at both levels. A wide range of inspiring set texts have been carefully selected to offer a depth and breadth of literary study and to encourage lively and stimulating classroom discussion. At AS Level learners will study three set texts and prepare for one unseen text. At A Level they will study four further set texts. Throughout the AS and A Level course learners will be encouraged to practise their skills in close reading through the study of literary extracts and unseen texts; developing skills of analysis and interpretation of texts, alongside their expression of personal response to the texts studied. Learners will explore the conventions of genres of texts and the contexts in which works have been written, read and received. At A Level learners will further develop their subject knowledge through the evaluation of opinions and ideas, both their own and those of others. These are highly transferable skills and can help learners in other subject areas, as well as equipping them for higher education and/or employment. Support for Cambridge International AS & A Level Literature in English
